World.title: Postcards from Mexico: On the Cabo San Lucas Marina
World.content:
CABO SAN LUCAS, Baja California Sur, Oct. 25 — It’s quiet and cool off the strip. The abarrotes are just opening, and there’s an old man in a vest up the block pushing a shopping cart full of empty beer cans. That might be mop-up duty from last night’s debauchery, or this morning’s. Stray dogs patrol the streets, trotting from one garbage pile to the next like derelict show ponies. In their glory days, they guarded the now-abandoned buildings that flank the street, too pure for this world with their barbed-wire crowns of thorns.

Baby birds are just waking up, warbling. They were promised a worm, like all early birds, but maybe they’ll settle for the gnats buzzing around my face, plentiful at these hours when it’s still not hot enough for the sun to burn them out of the air midflight.

It doesn’t take much to drown out the noise they make. Every half-minute, buses rattle up the sand-dusted Narciso Mendoza and down the Leona Vicario. As I turn onto Lázaro Cárdenas, I’m presented with a beautiful bouquet of belching tubas courtesy of the music blaring from the back of a black vocho. One doesn’t question who would blast banda music at this hour. “Reveille.” “La 4 x 4.” Same tiger, different stripes.

The soundtrack of the Cabo San Lucas Marina

The playlist in the Cabo San Lucas Marina is different. You might still hear some classics, depending on whose boat you walk by, but the shops and kiosks pander to a different demographic. I still haven’t quite figured out which. Daft Punk begets Murray Head, which begets Katy Perry. Speaking of which, Señor Frog’s is still thriving. Even at this hour, I spot a gringo retiree in board shorts and a tank top loitering in front, presumably curious about hours of operation. He’s in good company.

Along the esplanade, you hear far more English than Spanish. Much of that comes from merchants stumbling through back-of-the-napkin phrases they’ve committed to memory to entice newly arrived tourists to buy their wares. Though I also hear an old woman muttering something to her dog about one of the boats they pass by, so I guess even the dogs here are fluent.

‘A parking lot for yachts’

Along a wall, a line of men wearing Oakleys, long-sleeved shirts and visors sits idly, taking it easy before heading out on whatever excursions they’ll be leading. Nearby, a bored-looking clerk in a dockside store that looks like Cabo’s version of J. Peterman scrolls on his phone, unfazed about the urban sombrero sales quota he’ll need to meet by the end of the day. Even aboard the boats, on the eve of the world’s biggest marlin tournament, local fishermen prattle, hosing down decks and trying to be heard over the dull roar of idling boat engines.

This marina is like a Costco parking lot for yachts, though instead of an associate in a neon vest checking your ID, there’s a tall, wrought-iron gate with an entrance like a cage that only those with a key can get through. I pause to size it up, then look around to see who’s watching. “I could hop that,” I say to myself.

Ethan Jacobs is a freelance writer and writing coach based in Playa del Carmen. He has written extensively in narrative and short fiction formats, and his work has received recognition both domestically and internationally in microfiction, short fiction and narrative essay formats.

World.title: Is Chipotle in Mexico a good or bad idea? A ‘Confidently Wrong’ podcast
World.content:
Recently, and with much fanfare, Chipotle opened its first restaurant in Mexico. Perhaps not surprisingly, the opening spurred a polarizing debate and discussion about whether a U.S.-based Mexican restaurant chain would do well in the country. Years ago, Taco Bell entered the country and ultimately left in what was considered a disaster.

So what are the arguments for and against Chipotle coming to Mexico? Is it yet another unwanted assault of American culture on another country? Or is it a welcome sign of competition and choice for Mexicans?

Could it lead to lost business for local Mexican restaurants and reduced “authentic” Mexican food options? Or could it create a standard for the trifecta of affordability, service and quality that Chipotle is known for and oftentimes doesn’t exist in many restaurants today? Or perhaps it’s not that big of a deal, and people should move on?

And finally, what does the choice of a ritzy Monterrey suburb as the first restaurant location in the country tell us?

I will admit that while I have been a very frequent customer of Chipotle in the United States, I have actually eaten very few burritos here in Mexico. And the ones I have had have been very different.

In this week’s episode of Confidently Wrong, George and I talk through the arguments on each side of the debate and offer our own thoughts and opinions. Where do you stand on this issue? Check out the discussion here:

Confidently wrong about Chipotle: Episode 5 - Season 3

World.title: US sanctions more than 50 Jalisco cartel-linked individuals and businesses
World.content:
The U.S. Treasury on Thursday imposed sanctions on 39 Mexican individuals and 16 companies it alleges are linked to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), calling it “the largest action ever taken” against the notorious crime gang.

The measure targets the leadership of the cartel — designated by President Donald Trump as a foreign terrorist organization — and its illicit financing networks across Mexico.

The Treasury Department said in a statement that the goal of the sanctions is to limit the CJNG’s ability to traffic fentanyl and other drugs into the United States.

Shortly thereafter, Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF) reported it had identified “indicators related to possible operations with resources of illicit origin, including cash transactions, acquisition of high-end vehicles, jewelry and real estate,” as well as “international transfers, intensive use of credit and debit cards and transactions using virtual assets.”

As a result of this review, Mexico blocked the accounts of the same 55 individuals and companies sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department.

“The coordinated actions between Mexican and U.S. authorities strengthen mechanisms of international cooperation to prevent abuse of the financial system, combat money laundering and weaken the economic structures of organized crime,” the UIF said.

Among those sanctioned is Juan Carlos González, aka “El Pelón,” identified by U.S. authorities as the new leader of the CJNG following the February death of his stepfather, cartel founder, Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, who was killed in a federal operation.

The U.S. State Department has offered a reward of US $5 million for the capture of González, who holds both Mexican and U.S. citizenship.

Also sanctioned was the network of associates and subordinates linked to Audias Flores Silva, aka El Jardinero, who was arrested by Mexican authorities in April.

The UIF review found “inconsistencies” in tax records involving the accused, saying “they present characteristics of shell companies or with corporate structures of limited or no apparent economic activity.”

A complaint was filed with the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) and the 39 individuals — as well as eight others accused of being part of the same CJNG network — were added to the UIF’s Blocked Persons List (BPL).

The BPL is a public report identifying individuals and legal entities involved in money laundering or terrorist financing. All Mexican individuals and companies are required to immediately suspend any and all acts, operations or services with people or entities on the BPL.

With reports from EFE, Infobae, El Economista and La Jornada

World.title: Watching the 2026 World Cup Final in a Costa Rica Dive Bar
World.content:
Since moving to Costa Rica in 1990, I have not missed a World Cup final. I’ve watched them from a bar, from a friend’s house, and from the comfort of my own home. For 2026, I planned on something different. I took the trip over the mountain to San José, ready to attend the huge public party at La Sabana Park.

It seemed the perfect way to watch the match, surrounded by thousands of enthusiastic fans in an atmosphere of pure fiesta de fútbol. When I got to San José and informed my friend Roberto of my plans, he immediately set out to change my mind. The park would be packed with rowdy drunks and screaming kids, he said, and an older dude like myself would feel alone and out of place amid the throngs.

So I didn’t go to the big party. Instead, I joined my friend at one of his favorite San José dive bars. It was a casual, unpretentious, open-air place on a narrow street in a downtown barrio, with a 12-seat bar and several tables and chairs in an area next to the bar. The crowd was an assortment of older gringos and younger Ticos, with a couple of aging hookers completing the mix.

The bar had a representative liquor selection and Stella Artois beer in addition to the domestic brands. There were two TVs above the bar, but they were not in sync. One was a few seconds ahead of the other.

The largest-screen TV was in the separate part of the restaurant. This TV, which no one watched, was about 25 to 30 seconds ahead of the ones over the bar. I sat at the bar, turned at an angle to keep an eye on play. Any time there was an exciting run, I would look to the bar TV for a quick replay.

By the time Spain scored the winning goal, many of the clients had figured out that the TV with no sound was the one that was actually live. Spain completely dominated the game, and virtually everybody in the bar was happy with the result. In my small sampling, I was surprised by how few Ticos I spoke with were for Argentina.

Only two that I knew of supported them. One was a friend of mine who was actually born in Argentina, and the other was a huge fan of Lionel Messi. I thought more people would be rooting for the Argies, as they’re part of the Americas just like Costa Rica. Instead, I heard people complain of referee favoritism in their favor, calling them names like VARgentina and ArgenFIFA.

My younger daughter, who’s half Tica, half gringo and very proudly Latina, told me that people here are against Argentina because Argentinians reject being called Latinos. They consider themselves transplanted Euros and far superior to all the mestizos and mulattos to their north.

Another person told me that in 2014, the year of Costa Rica’s great run to the final eight, Diego Maradona appeared on ESPN before the Cup. When he looked at the group that Costa Rica was in, the so-called group of death that included three former world champions, Uruguay, England and Italy, he said Costa Rica should just take a gun, put it to their head and pull the trigger.

Alas, Maradona is dead, Messi is near retirement and Argentina has been dethroned as world champions. And until 2030, it’s Vive España!

Read more of Don Mateo’s writing from his newly published ebook.

World.title: Man detained after young woman’s frightening bathroom ordeal
World.content:
Man detained after young woman’s frightening bathroom ordeal

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A man is in police custody after a young woman reported a deeply disturbing incident at her Trial Farm home, alleging that her mother’s common-law husband tried to force his way into the bathing room while she bathed, then grabbed and pulled her as she tried to escape, leaving her with injuries certified as harm.

According to the Belize Police Department, the young woman, accompanied by her mother, visited the Trial Farm Police Station on Monday, July 20, 2026, to make the report.

She told police that on the morning of Sunday, July 19, she was at home alone with her mother’s common-law husband when she went to bathe at about 10:00 a.m. While in the bathing room, she saw a shadow approaching and looked out to see the man coming toward her. With no door to the room, she grabbed the side of the shower curtain to keep him out as he struggled against her to get in, telling her in Spanish to let him in to bathe with her.

She held the curtain firm. When the man moved to close a window she had opened, she seized the moment, dressed quickly, and ran for her mother’s room. He ran behind her, according to her report, forcing his way into the room before she could shut him out, then grabbed her left hand and pulled her toward him as she struggled to break free, gripping her so hard that her arm hurt.

She managed to pull loose and ran outside, where a neighbour who saw what was happening took her into her home. From there she called her mother, waited as told, and later noticed pain through her entire arm and scratches on her wrist where she had been held.

She made her formal report the following day, and a doctor certified her injuries as harm. She has requested court action.

Police recorded her statement, and the man was detained. As he has not been formally charged, his identity is being withheld, along with the identities of the complainant and her family.

World.title: One checkpoint stop, three traffic charges for Belmopan rider
World.content:
One checkpoint stop, three traffic charges for Belmopan rider

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A routine vehicular checkpoint in Belmopan turned up a motorcycle missing every piece of required paperwork, and its rider now faces three traffic charges and a date with the Magistrate Court.

According to the Department of Transport, on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at about 8:10 p.m., a traffic warden conducting a vehicular checkpoint on Cemetery Road in the Maya Mopan Area of Belmopan City observed a woman approaching on a black motorcycle and directed her to stop, which she did.

The warden introduced herself as a Department of Transport officer and explained that checks were being conducted to ensure vehicles on the public road carried proper documentation. Asked for her driver’s licence, the rider stated that she did not own one, and she was informed of the offence and cautioned.

The checks did not stop there. Further inspection of the motorcycle revealed that it carried no insurance and was not licensed, adding two more offences to the night’s tally. The rider was informed of all the offences, cautioned again, placed under arrest, and escorted to the Maya Mopan Precinct pending charges.

At the precinct, she was identified as 32-year-old Francine Vanessa Recinos, a self-employed resident of the Salvapan Area, Belmopan City. She was informed of her constitutional rights in custody.

That same date, she was formally arrested and charged with three traffic offences: driving a motor vehicle not covered by third-party risk insurance, driving an unlicensed motor vehicle, and driving a motor vehicle while not being the holder of a Belize driver’s licence. Cautioned once more, she chose to remain silent.

Bail was granted in the sum of $500, and she is to appear at the Belmopan Magistrate Court at 9:00 a.m. on Wednesday, July 29, 2026.

World.title: School bag search lands San Pedro man with cocaine charge
World.content:
School bag search lands San Pedro man with cocaine charge

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A San Pedro Town man is facing a drug charge after police say a late-night stop in the Boca del Rio Area turned up suspected cocaine in the front pocket of the school bag he was carrying.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at about 9:15 p.m., officers on mobile patrol near a grocery shop in the Boca del Rio Area observed a man walking on the street with a dark blue school bag on his back. Upon seeing the marked police mobile, police reported, the man hurriedly hid something behind his back.

Finding the movement suspicious, an officer exited the vehicle, identified himself, and informed the man that a search would be conducted for drugs and ammunition. A search of his person found nothing incriminating, but checks inside the school bag, with the aid of a flashlight, produced a small transparent ziplock bag containing a white powdery substance, suspected to be cocaine, in the bag’s front pocket.

The man was shown the find, informed of the offence, cautioned, arrested, and escorted to the San Pedro Police Station with the suspected drugs in his view at all times.

At the station, he was identified as 24-year-old Edi Anderi Aban, a labourer of the San Juan Area, San Pedro Town. The suspected cocaine was weighed in his presence on a scale shown to read zero beforehand, amounting to 0.5 grams, then sealed in a labelled envelope which he signed voluntarily. He was served his rights in custody and granted a telephone call.

On Friday, July 24, 2026, police formally arrested and charged Aban with possession of controlled drugs. Cautioned once more, he chose to remain silent.

World.title: SUV run off the road at Punta Gorda Junction, driver flees
World.content:
SUV run off the road at Punta Gorda Junction, driver flees

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A woman escaped injury after her SUV was sideswiped into a roadside drain near Punta Gorda Junction on Friday evening, and police are now searching for the driver of a black car who never stopped.

According to the Belize Police Department, officers responded to a report of a road traffic accident at Punta Gorda Junction at about 5:55 p.m. on Friday, July 24, 2026.

On arrival, police met a 46-year-old Orange Walk Town woman, who explained that she was driving her grey Nissan Murano SUV from Punta Gorda Junction toward Bella Vista Village. Upon reaching the area of the three speed bumps, she told police, she saw a black car ahead of her travelling in the same direction, put on her left indicator, and attempted to overtake.

As she did, according to her report, the black car swerved into her vehicle, striking it between the rear passenger door and the bumper. The impact caused her to lose control and run into the drain on the right-hand side of the road.

The driver of the black car, she told police, never stopped.

Fortunately, no one was injured in the collision. Police are actively investigating the matter, and the identity of the fleeing vehicle and its driver remains unknown.

Anyone who witnessed the collision near the speed bumps at Punta Gorda Junction on Friday evening, or who has information about a black car with fresh damage, is asked to contact the Independence police.

World.title: Woman bitten by dog, owner allegedly refused to help
World.content:
Woman bitten by dog, owner allegedly refused to help

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Cowpen Village woman is nursing a dog bite, and police are seeking the animal’s owner, after she reported that the dog ran from his yard, bit her on the leg, and that the owner refused to assist her when told.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 37-year-old domestic of the Stann Creek District village visited the Independence Police Station on Friday, July 24, 2026, to make the report.

She told police that on the night of Thursday, July 23, at about 8:30 p.m., she was walking along a street in the village when a black and brown dog ran toward her and bit her on the left leg. According to her report, the dog ran from a nearby yard, and when she informed the owner that his dog had bitten her and that she needed assistance, he refused.

Police recorded a statement from the woman and issued her medico-legal forms, which are yet to be retrieved. A man has been listed as wanted in connection with the matter, facing the potential charge of permitting an unmuzzled ferocious dog to be at large. As he has not been detained or charged, his identity is being withheld.

The matter remains under investigation.

World.title: Road safety must be more than just putting down concrete!
World.content:
Road safety must be more than just putting down concrete!

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Joe Awe: (Please note: I am no civil engineer. I am just a concerned citizen looking out for the better for the twin towns. I am not even interested in any mischief. I am willing to be corrected)

Let me start by saying something clearly: our children must be protected. Our pedestrians must be protected. And drivers must slow down.

There should be no argument about that.

But good road safety is not simply about installing a speed bump wherever there is a concern. Good road safety requires us to look at the entire road system: vehicles, pedestrians, intersections, emergency services and human behavior, and then make decisions based on proper traffic engineering.

That is why serious questions should be asked about the recently installed speed bump on Bullet Tree Road, reportedly about 300 yards from the four-way traffic lights at Joseph Andrews Drive.

This is a busy two-way roadway connected to a major signalized intersection. Vehicles turn from Joseph Andrews Drive onto Bullet Tree Road while other vehicles are approaching the intersection in the opposite direction. Any traffic-calming device placed along such a corridor should therefore be evaluated not only for the speed it reduces, but also for its effect on traffic flow, turning movements, sudden braking, vehicle queues and emergency access.

International traffic administration guidance itself treats speed humps as a traffic-engineering measure, not a one-size-fits-all solution. Their placement should consider the type of road, traffic volume, speed, intersection proximity and the role that road plays in the wider transportation network.

And there is another issue we cannot ignore: The San Ignacio Hospital is located down Bullet Tree Road. That changes the conversation.

Ambulances and other emergency vehicles may need to travel this corridor while transporting patients or responding to emergencies (and there are 5 speed bumps before the ambulance would get to this new one!). Research has documented that vertical traffic-calming devices can delay emergency vehicles, which is precisely why transportation guidance recommends special consideration for emergency routes and, where vertical traffic calming is necessary, alternatives such as speed cushions designed to allow larger emergency vehicles to pass with less disruption. – but there is no space for this engineering on this particular street.

So the question is not: “Do we care about children?” Of course we do. The real question is: Was this the safest solution available?

Because perhaps the bigger problem is standing only a few hundred yards away.

At the intersection of Joseph Andrews Drive and Bullet Tree Road, we already have a four-way traffic-light system and designated pedestrian-crossing infrastructure. That intersection should be one of the safest places for pedestrians, including schoolchildren, to cross.

But infrastructure alone does not educate people.

Do our children know exactly when to cross? Do pedestrians understand the pedestrian signals? Do motorists understand their responsibility when making left and right turns while pedestrians are crossing? Are the crossings clearly marked and visible? Is the timing adequate for children, older persons and slower pedestrians? Are we actively teaching people how to use that intersection safely? These questions matter.

International road safety guidance says pedestrian signals at signalized crossings are specifically intended to tell pedestrians when it is appropriate to cross, while proper signal timing must give people enough time to complete that crossing safely. Road-safety programs for children also combine engineering with education, supervision and other safety measures.

There is also a very real danger at intersections that we sometimes overlook: turning vehicles and pedestrians occupy the same space. Important pedestrian-safety materials specifically warn that drivers making left or right turns may fail to look for pedestrians. Modern signal strategies can even give pedestrians a head start before turning vehicles move, reducing conflicts between pedestrians and vehicles making left or right turns.

That is where our attention must also be focused.

A speed bump may slow a vehicle. Education changes behavior. A properly designed pedestrian system protects people at the precise location where they need to cross. Enforcement changes dangerous driving habits.

Good engineering anticipates what happens when an ambulance is rushing a patient to hospital, when two vehicles meet on a busy road, when a driver makes a right turn, and when a child steps into a crossing believing it is safe.

So perhaps it is time for the San Ignacio and Santa Elena Town Council to publicly explain the engineering reasoning behind this speed bump.

Was a traffic study conducted? Were ambulance and emergency-response movements considered? Was the hospital consulted? Were traffic volumes and vehicle queues studied? Were the turning movements from Joseph Andrews Drive assessed?

Were alternatives such as a raised pedestrian crossing, better markings, improved lighting or stronger enforcement considered?

And, critically, what sustained program is in place to teach our children and the wider public how to properly use the pedestrian crossing at the traffic lights?

These are not political questions. These are public-safety questions.

We should never have to choose between protecting a schoolchild and getting a patient to hospital quickly. A properly designed road-safety system should protect both.

Let us slow down where we need to slow down. Let us protect our children with everything we have. But let us also demand that every traffic-calming decision be based on sound engineering, public education, emergency access and the realities of how people actually use our roads.

Because sometimes the easiest thing to do is to build a speed bump. The harder, and more responsible thing is to build a complete culture of road safety.

And that is the conversation our Twin Towns need to have.

Touch lives. Change the world.

World.title: Shrimp production projected to rise to 3.3 million pounds, surpassing $20 million in value
World.content:
Shrimp production projected to rise to 3.3 million pounds, surpassing $20 million in value

By Hugh O’Brien: In 2020 shrimp production in Belize reached a low of just over one (1) million lbs after a rapid decline from 16 million lbs in 2014 due to the Early Mortality Syndrome (EMS) disease. However, thanks to the efforts of the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries and the Belize Agricultural Health Authority (BAHA), working closely with the Belize Shrimp Growers Association and the Belize Fisheries Department, the industry is on the rebound in line with Plan Belize 2.0. During this time of renewed growth BAHA is maintaining a strong surveillance programme to protect the industry from exotic diseases.

At the meeting, industry stakeholders reported that shrimp production in 2026 is projected to be 3.3 million lbs, valued at over $20 million for the first time since 2016. Production in 2025 was 2.3 million lbs valued at $16 million. More importantly the growth of the shrimp industry is geared more towards the larger and jumbo sized shrimp targeting the demand of the local tourism industry.

To support the industry’s regrowth, shrimp growers have procured faster growing and hardier genetics and more advanced technologies have been adopted. This has allowed the industry to better supply the growing local tourism market for larger and jumbo shrimps, and to be in a pivotal position to increase exports.

During the discussions, Minister Ferguson committed to continue supporting the growth of the shrimp industry, to work closely with the Fisheries Department to address contraband shrimp, to improve packaging and labeling requirements for shrimp destined for the retail market, and to bring the tourism industry and Cabinet fully on board with the recent growth and development of the local shrimp industry.

World.title: International News: Flávio Bolsonaro nominated to challenge Lula in Brazil’s 2026 Presidential Election
World.content:
International News: Flávio Bolsonaro nominated to challenge Lula in Brazil’s 2026 Presidential Election

By Zoila Palma: Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, has been formally nominated as the presidential candidate of his father’s Liberal Party, setting up a potential showdown with incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s October election.

Speaking at the party convention in São Paulo today, Flávio paid tribute to his father, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence over a plot to overturn his defeat in the 2022 election.

“Bolsonaro’s blood flows here,” he said, as he presented his candidacy and accused Lula and Brazil’s Supreme Court of targeting his family.

Flávio has received support from Argentine President Javier Milei and a message of backing from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while also seeking endorsements from allies of US President Donald Trump.

However, his campaign has faced early challenges, including criticism over an alleged request for financial support from a jailed banker to fund a film about his father and backlash over his efforts to seek US support after Washington imposed higher tariffs on Brazilian exports.

World.title: Woman among three fatally shot by police in Mandeville shootout
World.content:
MANCHESTER, Jamaica — Police have confirmed that a woman is among three people who were fatally shot during an alleged shootout on Caledonia Road in Mandeville Saturday afternoon.

Preliminary reports are that about 4:00 pm, police were alerted to a robbery spree and subsequently intercepted a getaway vehicle near Horseshoe Curve.

A highly placed police source said the occupants of the intercepted vehicle opened fire on the cops who then returned fire. A shootout ensued resulting in a prolonged standoff and running gun battle.

Police said a woman and two men were taken from the intercepted vehicle and taken to hospital where they were pronounced dead on arrival.

The incident happened in the vicinity of last Saturday’s double murder where nursing student Deenekia Pounall and Sadefa Henry were gunned down in a taxi by a gunman who posed as a passenger.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: MegaMart Catherine Hall property goes on sale for US$15 million
World.content:
The former MegaMart Catherine Hall location is on sale for US$15 million.

The property that once housed MegaMart’s Montego Bay operations has gone on sale for US$15.09 million, or $2.41 billion, nearly eight months following the impact of Hurricane Melissa on western Jamaica.

Cost Club Limited, trading as Megamart Wholesale Club, occupied the 89,674 square feet property since December 2007 when it first opened to customers in western Jamaica. However, the location was closed following the devastation caused by the Category 5 storm which flooded the location and left substantial damage.

The former Catherine Hall location is being offered on an ‘as-is’ basis, with realtor REMAX Elite Realty indicating that the property could be used for a range of commercial uses.

The property and building is being sold by Wilco Ltd which acquired the property in April 2015 for US$1.05 million ($119.63 million). The location was developed at a cost of US$20 million ($1.3 billion).

The MegaMart Catherine Hall and Portmore properties were sold to a group of pension funds in 2013 as part of a sale and leaseback transaction that was arranged by Scotia Investments Jamaica Limited (SIJL). That deal, which was reportedly valued at $2.3 billion, resulted in MegaMart maintaining operations at both locations and receiving cash from the transaction, but paying a monthly lease cost under a 15 year lease arrangement.

The Portmore location closed on June 30, 26 years after it opened in September 1999. The loss-making location was effectively subsidised by the operations of the Catherine Hall location. The closure of both locations resulted in the loss of more than 300 jobs as Cost Club undergoes a strategic consolidation for its remaining two locations.

The Portmore property was transferred in January 2013 for $1.05 billion. The owner is listed as Scotia Investments Jamaica on the property title, but transfer documents lists the National Insurance Fund (NIF), SIJL NCB Insurance Company Limited, Montego Bay I.T. Centre Limited, Grace, Kennedy & Co. Limited Pension Scheme, Jamaica Money Market Brokers Limited (JMMB) and Appliance Traders Group Pension Scheme as paying a transfer tax. The future of this property is unknown at this time.

Scojampen Limited, The Bank of Nova Scotia Pension Fund, owns the MegaMart Mandeville location while Lord Nelson Investment Limited owns the Waterloo Road location in St Andrew.

World.title: Cape Verde star goalkeeper Vozinha heads to Chile
World.content:
Cape Verde’s goalkeeper Vozinha celebrates with his national flag after their 1-1 draw with Spain during the FIFA World Cup. (Photo: AFP)

SANTIAGO, Chile (AFP) — Vozinha, the 40-year-old goalkeeper who was one of the heroes of Cape Verde’s fairytale run at the World Cup, is signing for Colo Colo, the Chilean club announced.

“Vozinha is set to become a Colo Colo player; he will arrive in Chile in the coming days, undergo the necessary medical tests and will then be presented here at the Monumental Stadium,” club president Anibal Mosa told reporters ahead of a league match on Friday evening.

Vozinha starred at the World Cup with heroic displays in a 0-0 group-stage draw against eventual champions Spain and in a 3-2 extra-time loss to finalists Argentina in the knock-out rounds.

The goalie, whose full name is Josimar Jose Evora Dias, will move to Chile from Chaves of the Portuguese second division. Although he did not sign his first professional contract until he was 26, he has also played in Cyprus, Slovakia, Moldova and Angola.

“He’s in very good form; that’s why we’re signing him,” said Mosa.

Vozinha has also become a social media star, with help from Brazilian influencer Casimiro. The goalkeeper’s Instagram following has soared from 50,000 to nearly 30 million.

Colo Colo, 34-time Chilean champions, hold a comfortable lead in the table midway through the current season.

World.title: Hitman’s appeal denied
World.content:
Simone Campbell-Collymore, whose confessed killer Wade Blackwood had his appeal rejected on Friday.

THE Court of Appeal on Friday upheld the sentence and conviction of killer Wade Blackwood, who in 2021 was sentenced to life in prison after confessing to being the trigger man in the 2018 murder of 32-year-old businesswoman Simone Campbell-Collymore.

The then 24-year-old, in a confession, detailed how he had been subcontracted to kill Campbell-Collymore in a $2-million murder-for-hire plot hatched by her then husband Omar “Best” Collymore.

Thirty-six-year-old taxi driver Winston Walters was also killed during the incident which took place outside Campbell-Collymore’s Forest Ridge apartment in Red Hills, St Andrew, on January 2, 2018.

The two men involved in the shooting that day were identified by the police, from closed-circuit television footage in the vicinity, as Blackwood and a now-deceased Corporate Area don who went by the name Jim.

Blackwood, who had been held by cops in April 2018, had pleaded guilty in January 2021 to two counts of murder and one count of illegal possession of firearm before the Home Circuit Court in downtown Kingston.

He was sentenced to life imprisonment for his role in the murders, ahead of the other individuals involved in the plot, with 35 years on each count of murder before eligibility for parole, and eight years and six months for illegal possession of firearm. Those sentences, however, were to run concurrently, making it so that he would serve 35 years before applying for parole.

Friday, the Appeal Court, which heard the matter over two days, in handing down its decision ruled that based on the fact that Blackwood was resentenced on February 9, 2024, after a plea agreement was reached, the basis of his appeal was obsolete.

Blackwood, through his attorney Shenieka Sparks, in supplemental grounds of appeal filed this year, had contended that a discount for his guilty plea was “unreasoned and inadequate”.

He further argued that the sentencing judge had erred in setting 30 years as a starting point to arrive at his ultimate sentence. According to Blackwood, compared to other similar cases, the discount was “out of parity”.

The Jamaica Observer was told that when Blackwood was advised of the decision of the Appeal Court he accepted that he would not continue challenging his sentence and a notice of abandonment was filed on his behalf.

As such, Blackwood will serve 20 years before he is eligible for parole, as was the sentence imposed on following his plea deal.

In February 2024, Blackwood — who testified against his co-accused following a deal with prosecutors — claimed he was pressured into committing the act by Jim, who was supposedly the leader of a gang his brother had been involved with.

Blackwood claimed that Jim, in levelling death threats at him and his family, told him that he had to carry out the killing to repay his brother’s debt for a firearm that had been seized by the police.

Blackwood, in negotiating with the prosecution, had 15 years shaved off his sentence, which now makes him eligible for parole after 20 years.

At the end of the substantive trial, Collymore, who was slapped with two life sentences, was also sentenced to one year and six months for conspiracy and ordered to serve 46 years and six months before becoming eligible for parole. His co-conspirators Dwayne Pink, Michael Adams, and Shaquille Edwards were also handed life sentences.

In the highly publicised incident, Campbell-Collymore and Walters were ambushed and shot dead outside the apartment complex where she lived with her then husband and children.

The Crown, at the close of its case, established that Collymore ordered the hit to claim his wife’s multimillion-dollar life insurance policies from which their two children were entitled to 15 per cent each while Collymore was entitled to 70 per cent of the benefits.

He was also listed as trustee for the children and their portion. Those policies were taken out by the couple three months before the murders.

Collymore was collared by cops at Norman Manley International Airport while attempting to flee the island a day before his wife’s funeral.

Earlier this month, Collymore, alongside his co-accused Pink, Adams, and Edwards, appeared before the Home Circuit Court again where they are all facing charges of illegal possession of firearm, shooting with intent, and conspiracy to murder with respect to an unnamed woman the businessman was in a relationship with at the time he orchestrated his wife’s death.

A new conspirator, Carey Jonas, is also named on the indictment with respect to the new matter.

On Thursday, Edwards, who had entered into plea negotiations with the prosecution and pleaded guilty to the new charges, was sentenced to six years and nine months for his part in that crime.

Edwards, however, has already spent more than seven years in custody and is set to be released.

World.title: No ease in honey shortage
World.content:
President of the St James Bee Farmers Association Dennis McKay with two bottles of honey, on Tuesday.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — The nation could be facing a severe honey shortage by the end of the year as the long-term effects of last October’s Hurricane Melissa continue to cripple the beekeeping industry, according to president of the St James Bee Farmers’ Association Dennis McKay.

He said even the intense heat now being felt across the country pales in comparison to the lingering effects of the Category 5 storm.

“It’s not so much the heat that is the crisis for the bees. Probably the major problem at this time is the impact of the hurricane and the trees that are missing. The storm turned down all the trees that provide the nectar and the pollen that support the bees. They are unable to get the nectar, so they cannot get enough nectar to store that we can get honey,” McKay told the Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

He explained that this period would ordinarily be the height of the honey-producing season, when beekeepers harvest their largest volumes. However, with many nectar-producing trees destroyed and only now beginning to recover, bees are gathering just enough food to sustain their colonies rather than building honey reserves.

“As the bees get the little nectar, it is only enough to feed them, not enough to store. So that is the major crisis as it relates to where the beekeeping and the honey business is going to go,” he said.

The dramatic decline in production has left many farmers with only a fraction of their usual harvest.

“A man used to get maybe 100 bottles from an apiary, [now] he only gets four bottles,” McKay said, adding that even large commercial operators who previously sold honey by the drum are now only able to provide a few bottles.

“He’s not getting enough that he can be selling by the drum, like before,” he added.

McKay also noted that many beekeepers suffered another devastating blow when they lost entire colonies during the hurricane.

“We are heading into a honey crisis,” he warned.

According to McKay, the dwindling supply has already sent up retail prices.

“Right now, honey used to be selling for $3,000 a bottle. I went into a supermarket and see it for $4,800, before tax added. This is the middle of the honey season; this is a time when everybody get honey,” he said.

McKay predicted that prices could climb even higher by Christmas.

“Going down to December, you might be paying $7,000 per bottle,” he cautioned.

While some damaged trees are beginning to regenerate, McKay said recovery is likely to be gradual and warned that another major weather event could worsen the situation.

“The existing trees now that are coming up, they may blossom next year, or we might have to start talking about importation of honey,” he said.

However, he expressed concern about relying on imported supplies, arguing that consumers cannot always be certain of their authenticity.

“I am seeing online where honey is made without bees. It’s only when you buy your local honey [that] you can have certain confidence that at least it come from bees,” McKay said.

Following the hurricane, the Government distributed sugar to beekeepers to help sustain weakened colonies. McKay said the assistance was useful when nectar was scarce.

“Bees don’t make honey with sugar. They use the sugar syrup to feed their young. As soon as trees start to blossom they don’t want that sugar water anymore,” he underscored.

He also suggested that support programmes should have included replacing lost colonies, noting that while some districts still have flowering trees, many of the bees needed to pollinate them and produce honey were wiped out during the hurricane.

“We have to be concerned because some people depend on that for a living,” McKay said.

World.title: Job scam victims repaid in court but case not closed
World.content:
MONTEGO BAY, St James — Decarlos Christie, who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud, has repaid a total of $200,000 to two women who fell prey to a job scam.

With the payment, part of his case has been resolved but he has been remanded as he still owes one of the women $57,000. There is also a third alleged victim.

Decarlos, who is jointly charged with his brother Bryan Christie, appeared before Judge Kaysha Grant-Pryce in the St James Parish Court on Wednesday. Two of three complainants attended the hearing. One was repaid the full $52,000 she had paid while another received $148,000 of the $205,000 of which she was allegedly defrauded. Judge Grant-Pryce has directed that efforts be made to contact the third complainant

Following Wednesday’s guilty plea Decarlos was admonished and discharged in relation to the matter involving the complainant who received full restitution. He is expected to pay the outstanding balance owed to the second complainant by July 29, when the matter will next be before the court. While he was remanded in custody, his brother’s bail was extended.

During the hearing Decarlos maintained that his brother, Bryan, used his personal information without his knowledge or consent to carry out the transactions while he was in custody in St Ann on unrelated matters. Decarlos insisted that he had no involvement in the alleged scheme.

According to the allegations, in January the first complainant was introduced by telephone to a man identifying himself only as “Mr Campbell”, who claimed to be offering overseas job placement opportunities. She was allegedly instructed to deposit $52,000 into a bank account registered to Decarlos Christie.

Police say a second complainant later deposited $205,000 into the same account for the same purpose, while a third complainant transferred $10,000. Investigators allege the complainants were subsequently assured they would travel to Kingston as part of the overseas employment programme. However, the promised arrangements did not materialise, prompting reports to the police.

During the investigation, police reportedly found that Decarlos’s bank card and account information were in Bryan’s possession, leading to the former being charged. Police further allege that Bryan was the individual who communicated with the complainants while posing as “Mr Campbell” and offering the overseas job opportunities.

World.title: Rvssian continues to rise on Billboard Latin charts
World.content:
From left: Rauw Alejandro, Wizkid and Rvssian.

Jamaican producer Tarik “Rvssian” Johnston continues to make moves on the Billboard Latin charts with his latest entry PONGO, which features Rauw Alejandro and Wizkid.

On Hot Latin Rhythm Songs, PONGO bolts from #22 to #14 in its 9th week. This is Rvssian’s first entry on this particular Billboard chart.

However, on Latin Airplay, the song which peaked at #41 in May, steps up a notch from #47 to #46. This is his fifth entry on Latin Airplay, with Nostalgico being his highest peak at #9 in 2021.

PONGO re-enters Hot Latin Songs at #38 and becomes the eighth entry on the chart for the Head Concussion Records/Rich Immigrants boss. His highest peak on this chart came in 2017 with Kippy Kush, featuring Farruko, Nicki Minaj, Bad Bunny, and 21 Savage stalling at #5.

The song becomes Rvssian’s sixth entry on Latin Rhythm Airplay, cruising from #13 to #11 in its 16th week. Both Santa and Nostalgico are his biggest hits on this chart, with each peaking at #6.

Echo (FIFA World Cup 2026) by Daddy Yankee and Shenseea, which rose to #1 three weeks ago on Latin Airplay, tumbles from #6 to #28.

Spin by American R&B singer Kevin Ross, which was produced by Jamaican producer Kheilstone, remains at #5 on Billboard’s Hot Adult R&B Airplay, while staying firm at #22 on Billboard’s R&B/Hip Hop Airplay chart.

Jamaican (Bam Bam), a reconstructed house/Afrobeats/dance version of Sister Nancy’s 1982 hit Bam Bam (credited to producers HUGEL and SOLTO) backtracks from #14 to #15 on Billboard’s Warm Global Dance Radio chart (it peaked at #4), while on Hot Dance/Electronic Songs chart it rises from #19 to #17 in its 24th week.

The song dances from #31 to #28 in its 17th week on Billboard’s Global Excluding US chart, and bullets from #63 to #53 on Billboard’s Global 200.

Still on Global 200, (When You Gonna) Give it Up to Me by Sean Paul and Keyshia Cole moves from #117 to #110. Sean Paul’s other entry, Cheap Thrills, with Sia, inches up from #139 to #138.

Sean Paul continues the double on Global Excluding US, with Cheap Thrills firm at #90 and (When You Gonna) Give it Up to Me inching up from #71 to #68.

Over on the Billboard Reggae Albums chart, Legend by Bob Marley and the Wailers remains at #1 for 340 non-consecutive weeks, while Best of Shaggy: The Boombastic Collection by Shaggy and Sean Paul’s The Trinity at #2 and #3 respectively.

World.title: Hill wary of call for ganja amnesty
World.content:
HILL...I have to remind you all that ganja is a Schedule 1 drug. It’s the same thing as fentanyl, the same thing as cocaine

SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — While a key stakeholder in the cannabis industry continues to call for an amnesty to regularise farmers operating outside the regulated sector, Minister of Industry, Investment and Commerce Senator Aubyn Hill has sounded a cautionary note. He pointed to the complex international legal landscape in explaining his stance on the matter.

“I have to remind you all that ganja is a Schedule 1 drug. It’s the same thing as fentanyl, the same thing as cocaine. It’s in the same category as heroin. It is seen as a bad drug,” the minister stressed.

He was addressing a Westmoreland Chamber of Commerce and Industry meeting at the Hotel Commingle in Savanna-la-Mar on Wednesday. He gave a breakdown on the implications for international trade and travel.

“Even today, because it’s a Schedule 1 drug, if you fly in the airspace of the United States, you are illegal. You can be taken out. You see what happened to those guys out there in the sea? That can happen to a ganja plane flying in the airspace of the United States, legally,” warned the minister.

He further emphasised that strict compliance with international drug laws is essential to maintaining Jamaica’s standing in global trade.

Hill was responding to questions posed by Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) board member Verald Vassell, better known as Ras Iyah V. The Westmoreland ganja advocate — who served on the CLA board from 2016 to 2021 and returned in 2024 — has consistently pointed to the need for an amnesty to transition illicit farmers into the legal medical cannabis industry.

During Wednesday night’s meeting Ras Iyah V highlighted what he said was continued harassment farmers face at the hands of the police.

“As the minister in charge of the CLA, what are the plans? Because I know the regulation has been amended recently. But what are the plans, the road map, and if you can explain how this is going to work? Because, as for me, I see a certain approach that creates a glut in the market, and then there is no market… Can you explain what is the road map going forward to bring our ganja farmers from being considered illegal into the legal industry? Because most of these farmers have been out-financed,” stated Ras Iyah V.

Acknowledging the concerns raised by the advocate, Hill outlined recent legislative changes aimed at easing operational restrictions for small-scale cultivators.

“Under my leadership with the permanent secretary and the people in the ministry, we changed the law. Because the very small farmer was constantly complaining of being put upon, [saying] they can’t get their things done. And we said, ‘Alright, you must have a fence of… five feet,” relayed Hill.

The minister pointed out that these regulatory adjustments provide greater flexibility for traditional farmers and workers trying to satisfy compliance requirements.

Addressing the issue of a market glut, Hill attributed the surplus to the initial surge of interest following the decriminalisation of cannabis.

“Understand that the glut that is developing is because when ganja was decriminalised, the euphoria that came around it encouraged people to go into it. Everybody was in it. There was one firm in Canada that seemed to have made a lot of money and then the thing collapsed. But that euphoria took a lot of people in,” the minister said.

Under the Dangerous Drugs Act, which came into effect on April 15, 2015, provisions were implemented for the possession and smoking of ganja; the use of ganja by those of the Rastafarian faith; and the use of ganja for medical, therapeutic, and scientific purposes.

“Our law allows people who use ganja for their religious practices to be exempt. But they have to go through a process,” explained Hill.

Regarding ongoing police enforcement, he noted that while adults are permitted to possess up to two ounces of ganja without criminal charges, the police must act whenever boundaries are breached.

World.title: Romanian airspace violated twice in 2 days
World.content:
Romanian Air Force F-16 fighter jets waiting for an aerial refueling, while they participate in an exercice. | Clement Mahoudeau/AFP via Getty Images

Romanian fighter jets shot down drones in separate incidents on Friday and Saturday.

Romanian fighter jets on Friday and Saturday morning shot down two drones that were violating the country's airspace.

On Saturday morning, Romanian radar "detected another unauthorized penetration of the national airspace by a drone operating in the vicinity of the Ukrainian border" and two Romanian F-16 jets shot it down in an unpopulated area close to the border, the Romanian defense ministry said in a statement. Romania already shot down another drone on Friday.

Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said that the drone shot down on Friday "was a Shahed-type drone, the same kind Russia launches, night after night, against Ukraine."

"Two incursions in 48 hours are not an accident, they are a pattern, and our answer to that pattern is consistency: detection, interception, protection of our citizens, full transparency with our allies," Toiu said.

In a social media post, European Council President António Costa "commend[ed] the Romanian authorities for their swift and effective response."

World.title: Record-breaking wildfires burned nearly 100,000 hectares in France, interior minister says
World.content:
Nearly 200,000 people have been evacuated because of the fires in southwestern France out of which more than 167,000 are in Gironde, the department of Bordeaux, and around 30,000 in the nearby Landes department.

French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday announced that he requested the activation of an EU emergency mechanism, which has prompted other EU countries including Portugal, Croatia, Slovakia and Sweden to send airplanes and helicopters to help France.

"Europe stands with France and Spain against the devastating wildfires that are hitting them," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote in a social media post on Saturday, stressing that France is already benefitting from five planes and two helicopters provided by other EU countries while four planes will arrive in Spain on Saturday.

France's Nuñez confirmed that Saturday afternoon an Airbus A400 military plane will start throwing a fire retardant product at the wildfires. That is on the top of Canadair and other French and European aircraft.

The wildfires have been the subject of political controversy in France in recent days, with both the hard-left France Unbowed and the far-right National Rally accusing Macron of underinvesting.

Spain has declared the state of emergency in the Madrid and Ávila regions.

"Our priority is to save lives, protect communities, and fight the fires," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Saturday. Around 80,000 people have been evacuated or are confined because of the wildfires, Spanish media report.

World.title: Italy’s defense minister offered adviser job to ousted Ukrainian defense chief
World.content:
The Italian minister said Fedorov was "moved" by the proposal and saw it as "a mark of respect and friendship," but he didn't elaborate on whether Fedorov accepted or not.

Crosetto strongly praised Fedorov, who has been credited with bringing a technology overhaul to Ukraine's military but also clashed with top generals.

“Fedorov embodies innovation; he is one of those who has completely changed the rules of the game on the battlefield, enabling Ukraine first to hold its ground and then to take the initiative,” Crosetto said, adding that Fedorov was faced with "a resistance to change" that is also a problem in Italy, France and Germany.

Fedorov hasn't responded publicly to Crosetto's offer.

Crosetto, who is a top figure in Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's Brothers of Italy party, also made clear that he is in favor of continuing to borrow via EU loans from the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) scheme rather than financing defense spending through national public debt. But he made clear that it was up for the Treasury to make that decision.

Crosetto's comments come as the Italian government is mulling applying for only €5 billion to €7 billion under the SAFE scheme, instead of €15 billion, as initially planned.

World.title: NATO intern arrested over espionage suspicions
World.content:
The Canadian national of Chinese origin is suspected of spying for a third country and being part of a criminal organization.

Belgian police on Friday arrested an intern at NATO's strategic headquarters of the Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE,) suspecting her of "spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization," the Belgian Federal Prosecutor Office wrote in a statement on Saturday.

The intern, a Canadian national of Chinese origins, "had come to the attention" of the security services of SHAPE, NATO’s strategic command for operations in Mons, Belgium.

Belgian authorities searched her home and office on Thursday.

Belgian prosecutors gave no further details on what the woman is suspected of.

Camille Gijs contributed to this report.

World.title: ICC member states remove chief prosecutor over sexual misconduct claims
World.content:
“I have no other way to describe it but an escalation of attempts,” she said in the interview, adding that she feared for her job and hence was afraid to say “no” to Khan’s advances.

Khan has denied any wrongdoing and, according to Reuters, called the Friday vote “unlawful, procedurally unfair and unsupported by evidence.”

The vote to fire Khan comes a week after the U.S. administration announced a campaign to dismantle what it called a “threat posed by the ICC to U.S. sovereignty.” Washington argues that the court should not have the authority to investigate and prosecute U.S. citizens.

Last year, the U.S. sanctioned Khan and other ICC employees after they issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes in Gaza.

World.title: We’ve fallen in love with drones, but they’re not the sole answer
World.content:
They are not. But nor are they mere bit players.

The enthusiasm for drones is understandable. According to the Kyiv Post, on July 9 alone “Ukraine said it struck 14 Russian vessels overnight in the Sea of Azov, including 12 tankers allegedly belonging to Moscow’s sanctioned ‘shadow fleet.’ Ukraine’s drone commander said a total of 35 ships had been hit over the previous 96 hours, while Ukrainian forces also targeted 45 military sites in occupied Crimea and southern Ukraine.”

It’s as if Ukrainian drones are everywhere. And not only is Ukraine using them to hit Russian targets without causing devastating losses to human life the way, say, missiles would; it’s also able to do so at enormous distances.

Drones hit Russian shadow vessels in the Black Sea. They hit Russian shadow vessels in the Mediterranean. They hit Russia’s oil refineries. They hit Russia’s Baltic Sea oil terminals. They’re causing constant problems for the Russian military, and have hit Russia itself. Earlier this month they even struck an oil refinery in Siberia.

In fact, Ukraine’s drones have become such a success that they’re triggering increasingly loud demands for NATO’s European members to shift their focus to these mostly small and cheap weapons. Look at how drones have helped Ukraine shift the course of the war! Look at how much you can achieve at relatively small expense! Drones are the future! Our governments are behind the curve! That’s how the argument goes.

But while drones are indisputably part of the future of warfare, they’re also still experimental and lack clear rules of engagement.

World.title: Hungary opens fairy tale themed 4.5-hectare corn maze for visitors to explore
World.content:
Children wander through a maize field, in Hungary, near the Romanian border, yet their parents remain calm. These adventurous youngsters aren’t lost – they’re exploring Central Europe’s largest maize maze.

 

This year, organisers have carved storybook characters, a castle and a unicorn shape into the 4.5-hectare maize field at Kiszombor.

The design was created by Dávid Nagy on his computer in a spreadsheet, and the maize plants were cut back while they only reached knee height. That made it easier to see the whole layout, and drones helped with the final tweaks.

Children get a map to help them find their way, but it’s still no easy task. The 2.5-kilometre-long maze is full of dead ends, and it’s easy to get lost.

The maze was first created 18 years ago in nearby Kukutyin by volunteers from the Kiss Mária Hortensia Local History Circle, in a bid to lure visitors back to the depopulating area. Since then, two to three thousand people a year have been coming here to try traditional skill games and lose themselves in the maize field.

According to the head of the local history circle and of the project, Erzsébet Endrész, the main aim throughout has been to put Kiszombor on the map for Hungarians and other Europeans who enjoy puzzles. After all, it’s essentially a giant escape room.

The maize maze is open to visitors until 22 August.

World.title: India's 'Cockroach' movement ends protests after education minister resigns
World.content:
India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan announced his resignation on Saturday after weeks of mass youth-led protests over alleged exam paper leaks and irregularities in the education system.

 

"I am pained to see the events of the past 10 days. This is not a matter of personal prestige for me," Pradhan said in a statement posted on social media platform X.

"I have sent my resignation letter to the prime minister," Pradhan said in his letter in Hindi.

The social media-driven Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leading the protests said after Pradhan's resignation that all their demands had been met in another round of talks and that they were calling off the protests that were centred on the Jantar Mantar demonstration site in central New Delhi.

A protester holds a placard after India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned following nationwide protests in Mumbai, India, Saturday, July 25, 2026. AP Photo/Rafiq Maqbool

“We urge everyone to peacefully withdraw from protest sites,” Ashutosh Ranka, spokesperson of the CJP, which launched the protest movement, said at a news briefing in New Delhi.

The "Cockroach'" movement began more than a month ago after allegations of leaks in some of India’s biggest entrance exams. It started as a call for education reforms but grew into a broader protest over unemployment, government accountability and economic opportunities. Students, professionals, families and activists joined rallies in New Delhi and other cities across India.

Pradhan's resignation marks the first significant concession by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government to one of the most visible waves of public dissent it has faced in recent years.

Protesters react after India's education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned following nationwide "Cockroach" demonstrations in New Delhi, India, Saturday, July 25, 2026. AP Photo/Prabhat Mehrotra

The government has rarely yielded to sustained public pressure during Modi's more than 12 years in office. The most notable exception came in 2021, when it was forced to withdraw controversial farm laws after a yearlong farmers’ protest.

News of Pradhan’s resignation sparked celebrations among the thousands of protesters who have camped at New Delhi’s protest site for more than a month. Many embraced each other and waved the Indian flag.

Tensions escalated on Monday when police moved to disperse thousands of protesters marching toward Parliament. Several students were injured in the crackdown, intensifying anger among demonstrators.

Protesters participate in a demonstration demanding educational reforms as part of the Cockroach Janta Party's ongoing protest movement in New Delhi, India, July 25, 2026. AP Photo/Vipin

Modi’s government had earlier sought to ease tensions by announcing fast-track courts for cases involving exam paper leaks and saying it would introduce legislation to strengthen measures against cheating and corruption in the examination system.

The measures failed to satisfy protesters, who said they did not address government accountability. Opposition parties, which rallied behind the protests, said Pradhan’s resignation showed the government had bowed to sustained public pressure.

World.title: Russian central bank cuts GDP growth forecast to zero, expects faster inflation
World.content:
The Central Bank of Russia expects inflation at 6–7% in 2026 "due to the significant increase in fuel prices that has already occurred".

 

Previously, the regulator had expected it to slow to 4.5–5.5%.

Inflation expectations among households, businesses and financial market participants have risen. Their persistence at elevated levels may impede a sustained slowdown in inflation, the Bank of Russia said in a press release.

"The fuel situation falls into what is known as supply shocks," admitted Elvira Nabiullina, the head of the Bank of Russia, at a press conference on the same day.

Since mid-May, fuel price growth has accelerated, and in June several Russian regions faced shortages after Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries in Russia in response to the war launched by the Kremlin.

At the same time, some analysts forecast that by the end of the year inflation in Russia could turn out even higher, including as a result of strikes by the Ukrainian Armed Forces on Russian logistics centres.

The forecast for Russian GDP growth in 2026 has been cut from 0.5–1.5% to 0.0–1.0%, including the projection for the fourth quarter (from 1.0–2.0% to 0.0–1.5% year-on-year).

"Companies expect demand to slow, as follows from the real-time data. Taking into account the temporary reduction in capacity in the economy, we have lowered our GDP growth forecast," the head of the Bank of Russia commented.

The Central Bank expects that "fuel production capacity will gradually be restored by the end of the year", but Ukraine continues to use its "long-range sanctions" in response to Russian attacks.

On Saturday, Ukrainian drones struck an oil refinery in Tyumen, a logistics facility in Yekaterinburg and a fuel and lubricants depot in Rostov-on-Don.

World.title: Goes berry picking, finds traces of mysterious Allied plane wreck in Poland
World.content:
It was meant to be a simple walk in the forest to pick berries. Instead of woodland fruit, a resident of Świnoujście found something that could help solve one of the mysteries of the war.

 

In woodland not far from facilities belonging to the Museum of Coastal Defence - Fort Gerhard, the man came across an unusual depression in the ground. Around it lay numerous fragments of a metal structure. They did not look like random scrap. Among the scattered pieces you could see sections of aluminium sheets, parts of a structure and the remains of burnt ammunition.

One of the fragments was handed over to museum staff. That was the beginning of a story that may have started more than eighty years ago, during the Second World War.

"Even a first look showed that this was not random scrap metal. The nature of the sheet metal, the way it was riveted, traces of aircraft structures and burnt ammunition all suggested we might be dealing with the remains of an aircraft," explained Wiktor Czeszewski from the Museum of Coastal Defence in Świnoujście.

The first lead pointed to the British air force

One of the most important finds turned out to be the ammunition remains. Initial identification showed it was calibre .303 British - a round used, among other things, in British Browning aircraft machine guns.

This was the first strong indication that the recovered parts might have come from a machine belonging to Allied air forces.

The real breakthrough came once the recovered pieces had been cleaned more thoroughly. On one of the small fragments - a copper tube - an alphanumeric marking was found.

The symbol T7 turned out to be the key to further research. According to British RAF technical documentation, it denoted a type of seamless copper tubing used in oil, fuel and gas systems and other on-board installations.

Even more intriguing was the end fitting of the pipe. Everything indicates that it was an Avimo-type component, a high-pressure coupling used in British aircraft, including in systems connected to the legendary Rolls-Royce Merlin engines.

These power units were installed in many of the RAF's best-known aircraft, including Lancaster bombers.

A Lancaster near Świnoujście? History may be coming full circle

For now, the museum team is being cautious about identifying the exact type of aircraft. There is still no absolute certainty as to whether the wreck that has been found is a Lancaster, a Mosquito or another aircraft using similar technical solutions.

Yet an extremely interesting lead has emerged.

The Museum of Coastal Defence already holds a large, roughly five-metre-long section of a Lancaster bomber wing. It was hauled out of the Baltic in 2009 by fishermen.

What is particularly intriguing is that the site of the current discovery lies only about a kilometre in a straight line from where the wing was found.

"It could be the same aircraft," said Piotr Piwowarczyk, director of the Museum of Coastal Defence - Fort Gerhard.

The wing section recovered years ago was thoroughly examined. Thanks to the analysis, researchers were able to establish the names of three crew members. They were airmen who, in the final phase of the war, flew over the Szczecin and Police area, home to key German industrial plants and port infrastructure.

Do the remains found in the forest belong to that same aircraft? The answer will take time.

The forest still guards its secret

The discovery site has been secured. The Voivodeship Monument Conservator, the Międzyzdroje Forest District and institutions responsible for war graves have been notified.

The area has not been specially marked so as not to attract passers-by, souvenir hunters or collectors.

The crash site itself is striking. The ground is clearly shaped in an unnatural way, and a larger piece of embedded structure can be seen in the soil.

"We expect that the main part of the aircraft came down there," said Piotr Piwowarczyk.

That means further parts of the aircraft may lie several metres below the surface. The hardest scenario cannot be ruled out either: that the remains of crew members may still be in the ground.

"The site has to be examined professionally. We cannot rule out that crew remains are buried underground," museum representatives stress.

An inconspicuous tube may open up a big story

Sometimes major discoveries begin with small objects. In this case it was a small copper tube which, once cleaned, revealed a marking pointing to British aviation technology.

Does the forest near Świnoujście conceal the wreck of an Allied Lancaster? Will it be possible to identify the names of its crew? Will the fragments found on land be linked to the wing raised years ago from the sea?

Only further archaeological work and expert assessments will answer these questions.

One thing, however, is certain: the history of this place has just begun to reveal another secret. And it all started with a man who went into the forest to pick berries and found traces of an aircraft from the time of the greatest conflict in human history.

World.title: German teacher ill for 17 years fights in court for full salary
World.content:
For years, the case of a teacher from North Rhine-Westphalia has been making headlines across Germany. The 62-year-old has been on long-term sick leavesince 2009, but throughout this period she has continued to receive her full salary as a civil servant teacher. She is now taking legal action against being forced into retirement – because that would mean she would only receive her pension in the future.

 

Most recently, the teacher worked at a vocational college in Wesel. According to WDR and Spiegel, she submitted medical certificates over many years citing a psychological condition. An official medical assessment was not initially ordered. It was only this year that a public health officer concluded that a return to teaching within the next six months could not be expected.

The Düsseldorf district government then ordered at the end of May that the civil servant be placed into retirement. The 62-year-old has since filed a lawsuit against this decision with the Düsseldorf Administrative Court, the court has confirmed.

Until a ruling is made on the lawsuit, she will receive payments equivalent to her pension. According to the district government, any amount exceeding her pension entitlement are currently being withheld. If the teacher succeeds with her claim, these payments would have to be paid out retrospectively.

Suspected fraud and disciplinary proceedings

At the same time, the case is also occupying the law enforcement authorities. The Duisburg public prosecutor's office is investigating on suspicion of commercial fraud. There is suspicion that the teacher at least temporarilyfalsely claimed to be unfit for dutyand worked as an alternative health practitioner while on sick leave.

Back in March, investigators searched her home and seized documents and digital storage devices. According to Spiegel, potentially relevant evidence was found, which is currently being analysed. The investigations cover a period of four years, as any older alleged offences may now be time-barred.

Disciplinary proceedings are also under way against the teacher and against an employee of the Düsseldorf district government. He is accused of having failed for years to initiate a proper review of the alleged permanent incapacity for service.

The case has sparked a nationwide debate on checks on civil servants who are on long-term sick leave. North Rhine-Westphalia's education minister Dorothee Feller (CDU) described the events as "inexcusable" and "incomprehensible in its scale" as long ago as last year.

World.title: Greek Patriot battery intercepts Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Tensions in the Middle East are on the rise again, as Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen launched attacks against Saudi Arabia.

 

According to Greek military sources, one of the attacks targeted a major refinery installation in the Yanbu area. The Greek Patriot missile battery deployed there as part of the Hellenic Force in Saudi Arabia intercepted the attack, which was launched from Yemeni territory.

The Greek battery later also shot down a drone approaching from Yemen.

The battery is part of the “Integrated Air Missile Defense Concept” initiative, aimed at supporting Saudi Arabia's air defences.

Houthi retaliation

Earlier, Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan.

Riyadh did not immediately comment on reports shared by Houthi-affiliated media channels on Telegram on Saturday claiming that a “missile attack from Yemen” had caused fires in Jizan.

However, Riyadh's civil protection agency issued brief warnings on Saturday to residents of the city, as well as those in Yanbu.

The warnings came after strikes by the Saudi-led coalition on Houthi military installations in Yemen.

The operation was carried out in retaliation to Houthi attacks on commercial vessels in the area, coalition spokesperson Air Vice-Marshal Turki al-Maliki said.

The coalition responded "decisively and forcefully" by hitting Houthi military sites after "their terrorist forces targeted commercial ships in the Red Sea", Turki al-Maliki said in a statement on X, adding that the military operation had now been completed.

The Houthis had accused Riyadh of "dangerous escalation".

A Yemeni security source told AFP that a naval base in the port of Hodeidah and a military camp on the island of Kamaran were among the Saudi targets.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for attacks on two Saudi vessels earlier this week, with Saudi Arabia confirming one of the attacks in the Red Sea.

The latest escalation in the Middle East opens a new front in the war that began after US-Israeli strikes on Tehran in February.
