World.title: Another activist in Georgia convicted over insulting Facebook post: doctor Giorgi Akhobadze
World.content:
Georgia: activist Giorgi Akhobadze sentenced over FB post

On July 24, another person in Georgia was sentenced to administrative detention over a Facebook post containing profanity. Giorgi Akhobadze, a doctor and active participant in the country’s pro-European protests, was sentenced to 25 days in detention.

Giorgi Akhobadze

The ruling was issued by Tbilisi City Court. Giorgi Akhobadze did not attend the hearing.

He was represented by his lawyer, Mikheil Zakareishvili.

A few hours after the ruling, Akhobadze was arrested during a special police operation at his home.

Administrative proceedings against Giorgi Akhobadze were initiated following a complaint by the Interior Ministry’s recently established Department for Monitoring Hate Speech.

Akhobadze was sentenced over a Facebook post in which he used profanity to insult police officers who had testified against him in an earlier criminal case.

In December 2024, Akhobadze was returning home from a pro-European protest (which has continued in Georgia for nearly two years) when he was detained by police. He was searched and charged with purchasing and possessing drugs.

Akhobadze and his lawyers maintained that the drugs had been planted on him during the arrest. After an eight-month trial, he was acquitted and released from the courtroom in August 2025.

The Facebook post that led to his current administrative sentence referred specifically to the police officers whom Akhobadze accuses of planting the drugs.

“I stand by every word of that post,” Akhobadze told TV Pirveli after learning of the court’s decision, repeating the profane insult directed at the police officers.

“I’ll spend 25 days in a cell, get some rest, and if they think I’ll come out thinking differently, they’re very much mistaken,” Akhobadze said before his arrest.

On fines and detention for offensive social media posts

Giorgi Akhobadze is the second person to receive a jail sentence over comments posted on social media.

A few days earlier, on July 22, Tbilisi City Court sentenced well-known journalist and Formula TV host Vakho Sanaia to 14 days of administrative detention.

Sanaia had published a Facebook post containing profane and insulting language directed at senior officials of the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Administrative cases over opinions expressed in public are being initiated on the basis of reports filed by the Interior Ministry’s new Department for Monitoring Hate Speech, which began operating on June 1.

The department’s mandate is to monitor and proactively identify statements that violate human dignity, are insulting, or incite hatred, where they may constitute an administrative offence.

According to the Georgian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, between June 1 and July 2 the department identified 170 alleged administrative offences and referred 150 cases to court.

Courts have already ruled on 33 of those cases: 31 people were fined and two received verbal warnings. Most of those fined are activists taking part in the mass protests demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenian police see rise in domestic violence reports: Data and analysis
World.content:
Domestic violence reports in Armenia

In the first half of 2026, Armenia‘s police received 1,375 reports of domestic and family violence. That is 78 more cases than during the same period last year.

Police say that for many years incidents of domestic violence went unreported because families kept them hidden. Now, however, many victims are choosing to contact the police. Law enforcement officials attribute this to people’s growing confidence that “their voices will be heard and their safety and rights will be protected.”

Representatives of civil society have also noticed a change in people’s behaviour. Nare Hayrapetyan, head of the Kotayk regional NGO Women’s Empowerment Resource Centre, describes it as a “victory” that even people who previously categorically rejected the idea are now turning to law enforcement for help.

“Trust in both the state and the institutions responsible for providing protection has increased,” she says.

Police register 1,155 perpetrators

In the first six months of 2026, Armenian police registered 1,155 people who committed violence against family members, up from 1,011 during the same period last year.

In response to the identified cases of domestic violence, police took the following measures:

325 perpetrators received an official warning (compared with 304 last year);

961 emergency intervention orders were issued (up from 833 last year).

Civil society’s role in preventing domestic violence

The Interior Ministry says cooperation between civil society organisations and the police is key to preventing domestic violence. To strengthen that cooperation, regular meetings are held in Yerevan and the regions to assess the effectiveness of joint efforts and identify existing challenges.

“Our cooperation with the police is at a very high level,” says Anahit Abgaryan, head of the NGO Talin-Huys.

According to her, many more people are now turning to the police, which she also sees as a result of growing trust in the system.

“In the past, we encouraged victims to go to the police. We explained that we could not guarantee their safety in the same way the police could. But they refused,” Abgaryan says.

Protecting victims is the priority

According to Georgy Khachatryan, head of the Police Department for Professional Methodological Support, police respond promptly to every report of domestic violence.

“For a police officer working in the community, protecting victims of violence is the priority,” he says.

He outlined the police’s main responsibilities:

identifying and preventing all forms of violence;

protecting every person subjected to violence;

taking the necessary measures to reduce the risk of repeat violence.

Khachatryan argues that the increase in domestic violence reports should not be viewed as a negative indicator.

“Domestic violence is, in fact, a hidden crime. Therefore, the increase in detected cases does not necessarily mean there are more incidents of violence. Rather, these crimes are now coming to the attention of law enforcement authorities,” he says.

To improve the speed of emergency responses, the SAFE YOU app has been operating since 2025 as part of a partnership between the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) and the Armenian police.

“When an alert is triggered, it ensures the simultaneous involvement of all relevant state agencies. This is crucial both for a rapid response and for organising protection measures,” Khachatryan said.

World.title: Landslide hits village in Georgia, leaving two families worst affected
World.content:
Major landslide hits Georgian village

A landslide struck the mountainous village of Gomaro in Georgia’s Adigeni municipality. Rocks and debris swept down the mountainside, damaging residents’ homes and cars. No injuries were reported.

The incident occurred late on 23 July. The first photos and videos from the scene were published by local outlet TOK TV.

Footage from the scene shows that the debris that crashed into one of the houses piled up to nearly half the height of the building.

A pickup truck parked beside the house was completely buried under rocks and mud.

The homeowner told TOK TV that the debris reached the level of the windows. A surge of water smashed a window and flooded the rooms.

“A torrent suddenly came rushing through and swept everything away. The whole house is flooded. The fridge, the gas supply—everything has been damaged,” the young man said.

The Siradze family’s home was among the hardest hit. Its owners told the reporter that the house had also been damaged by a landslide in the same area last year.

Local residents say last year’s landslide was less severe. This time, a much larger torrent of water and rocks came crashing down from the forest, damaging more homes than in the previous landslide.

Another local outlet, Samkhretis Karibche, reported that the family was not at home when the landslide struck.

“My father is ill, and we had gone to Batumi to visit him. Our neighbours called and told me to come back. When I arrived, I saw they were using pumps to drain water from the houses and had torn down walls… I have nothing left. The fridge, the gas supply, all the household appliances—everything that could be plugged into the electricity… The beds and the floor have been ripped out. Nothing is left.”

According to a local resident, officials at the mayor’s office said it would take time to resolve the problems in Gomaro. Geologists from Tbilisi first need to assess the situation. After that, “it will take millions to build bridges and retaining walls.”

“If we try to repair the bridges and retaining walls ourselves, we’ll be the ones held responsible. We’ve already been waiting for a year,” the young woman said.

Heavy machinery was brought into Gomaro on Thursday evening, and part of the affected area has already been cleared. Cleanup operations are set to continue the following day.

Flooded home in the village of Gomaro. Photo: Sknews

Flooded home in the village of Gomaro. Photo: Sknews

The village of Gomaro on the second day after the landslide. Photo: Sknews

The village of Gomaro on the second day after the landslide. Photo: Sknews

Statement from the authorities

The Adigeni Municipality administration released an official statement on the second day after the disaster.

According to the statement, heavy rainfall across the region caused damage in three villages: Gomaro, Kvemo Enteli and Shoka.

The administration said the landslide in Gomaro damaged two residential homes, while a car was buried under debris. In Kvemo Enteli, agricultural land was damaged, while in Shoka both road infrastructure and farmland were affected.

“As a result of the emergency response, the riverbed in the village of Gomaro has been restored to its original course, while road clearance operations are continuing in the village of Shoka. At the same time, a special commission established by the municipal administration continues to assess the extent of the damage,” the administration said in its statement.

Major landslide hits Georgian village

World.title: Georgian Foreign Ministry expresses ‘regret’ over EU sanctions on Kulevi plant
World.content:
Georgia on EU’s 21st sanctions package

In an official statement, Georgia‘s Foreign Ministry expressed regret over the inclusion of the Kulevi oil terminal in the EU’s 21st sanctions package. The ministry said that “there are neither factual nor legal grounds for placing the Kulevi oil terminal on the sanctions list.”

On 23 July, the European Union’s 21st sanctions package against Russia was announced. It includes the Kulevi oil terminal in Georgia and several cryptocurrency platforms.

The ban on transactions with the Kulevi oil terminal will take effect in six months unless the facility changes its operating practices.

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry said the country fully takes into account the EU sanctions regime, “the context of that regime”, and is taking all necessary measures to ensure that Georgian territory is not used to circumvent sanctions.

The statement also stresses that cooperation with the EU in this area is based on transparency and openness. Georgian authorities, it says, consistently provide EU institutions with all necessary information and clarifications in a timely manner.

The ministry also said that, to date, authorities have not recorded any cases of EU sanctions being circumvented through Georgian territory.

“During preparations for the EU’s 21st sanctions package, the Georgian side provided the European Commission with comprehensive information and supporting documentation clearly demonstrating that there are neither factual nor legal grounds for placing the Kulevi oil terminal on the sanctions list,” the statement says.

The Foreign Ministry also expressed hope that the relevant departments of the European Commission and EU member states “will be guided by the principle of fairness and review the decision” within the next six months.

A brief overview of the new sanctions package

The EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia, which is due to take effect shortly, received final approval from the permanent representatives of the EU member states on 23 July 2026.

The sanctions are expected to enter into force on 23 July following approval by EU leaders and their official publication.

The measures target sectors of the Russian economy that provide the greatest financial support for the war in Ukraine, including energy, financial services and the cryptocurrency sector.

The package also imposes sanctions on more than 50 companies and organisations that supply military equipment and weapons to Russia.

It also includes the largest set of individual sanctions to date, targeting a total of 218 entities: 48 individuals and 170 legal entities.

It marks one of the largest expansions of EU sanctions over the past four years.

Georgia on EU’s 21st sanctions package

World.title: Armenia’s labour market trends: Social media replaces employment agencies as jobs and wages grow
World.content:
Analysis of labour market trends in Armenia

Armenia‘s unemployment rate fell only slightly in 2025, declining to 11.8% from 13.3% in 2024. At the same time, according to the country’s Statistical Committee, wages continued to rise, with the average monthly salary increasing by 5.6% over the same period to 303,140 drams ($828).

Compared with 2021, the average nominal monthly salary has increased by 48.6%, the number of employees has grown by 22.4%, and the unemployment rate has fallen by 2.7 percentage points.

Employment remains highest in the wholesale and retail trade sectors, as well as in education and manufacturing. By contrast, employment is lower in the arts and culture, scientific research, and real estate sectors.

An analysis of online job platforms shows that employers are currently seeking couriers, waiters, accountants, assistants, sales and marketing specialists, and fundraising professionals.

At the same time, job seekers are increasingly drawn to international, foreign, and joint ventures, attracted by both higher salaries and better working environments.

“The labour market has become more coordinated”

Until 2016, Naira Piloyan ran an employment agency that helped many people find jobs and earned a reputation as a reliable partner for local organisations. Over the past decade, however, she says the labour market has changed. Employers now search for candidates through online platforms, using their own social media pages and job websites. As a result, she had to close her agency. She now works as a human resources specialist at a pharmaceutical company.

She says every medium-sized and large company in Armenia now employs HR specialists. They use online platforms and professional networks to find qualified candidates.

“I closely follow developments in the labour market. From my own experience, I can say that local professionals have become much better at presenting themselves during the hiring process. Employers have also become more selective when recruiting staff. The whole process is now far more streamlined and coordinated,” she says.

At the same time, she notes that personal connections and recommendations from friends or acquaintances still influence hiring decisions.

However, serious companies have realised that hiring unqualified staff creates a “time bomb” for their future development.

Instead, they rely on candidates’ experience, references from previous employers and personal interviews.

“Over the past few years, salaries at our company have increased by around 30% on average. Higher levels of professionalism among staff have largely driven that increase. Every employee takes professional development courses or retrains in a new field. As people gain knowledge and experience, they expect higher pay. If they don’t receive the salary they believe they deserve, they start looking for another job. That staff turnover has become a major challenge for large companies,” the HR specialist explains.

She says employers have also started investing more in their employees’ skills. Many companies now pay for foreign language courses, mainly English, as well as training abroad in manufacturing, technology and other fields.

She believes this growing coordination has improved the quality of Armenia’s labour market. When someone from another company applies for a job with her employer, she can now openly discuss the candidate’s abilities and professional qualities with HR managers at their previous workplace.

“In the past, asking someone for an opinion about a job applicant felt awkward. Now I simply send an email and receive a reply within a few days. The only real difficulty today is finding highly specialised professionals and technical staff. Problems usually arise when we urgently need to hire someone like a driver, security guard or cleaner. Candidates for these jobs tend to be very conservative. For example, if they need to stay just 10 minutes beyond the end of their shift, they often show little flexibility. Some may even leave work during the day without informing anyone.”

According to her, wages for these positions have risen by a larger percentage than salaries for many higher-skilled professions, including finance specialists and translators.

Working conditions are more attractive at foreign companies

Ilona Khachatryan is a logistics specialist. She now works for an American company and earns four times more than she did two years ago in the same role at a local firm. But salary is only part of the reason she left. She says unhealthy relations with management at her former company also played a major role. More broadly, she is critical of hiring practices and personnel management at many local organisations.

“At the company where I worked, it was extremely difficult to receive the bonuses that management itself had promised. To avoid paying them, they would even falsify hourly timesheets.

I applied for jobs at other local companies as well. I attended interviews and then waited for months without hearing back. Even if they decide not to hire you, shouldn’t they at least tell you? After all, you invest your time and effort preparing for those interviews. Foreign companies treat candidates much more fairly. They make transparent hiring decisions. If they decide not to hire someone, they explain in detail why they cannot move forward with the candidate.”

Ilona says her current employer hired her after the first interview. The company immediately explained the salary, holiday entitlement, employment rights and job responsibilities.

“Hearing the words ‘thank you for your work’ genuinely motivates me. It gives me energy and makes me work with greater enthusiasm and commitment. And when your employer also recognises your achievements, you realise just how undervalued professionals are in the local labour market.”

Analysis of labour market trends in Armenia

World.title: Azerbaijan changes status of internally displaced people: What do new rules provide?
World.content:
The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

On 23 July, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed into law amendments to the Law on the Status of Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons and the Law on the Social Protection of Internally Displaced Persons and Persons Equated with Them.

The amendments to the Housing Code provide for the creation of a Permanent Resettlement Fund in the territories liberated from occupation. Housing from the fund will be used to resettle internally displaced persons (IDPs) to the reclaimed territories and will later be transferred to them as private property.

The legislation also clarifies the grounds on which a person may lose IDP status. This applies to those who refuse housing offered by the state, as well as to those who are provided with alternative housing that meets the officially established housing standard for the relevant region instead of accommodation in their previous place of residence. At the same time, social protection measures will remain in place for three years after a person loses or voluntarily relinquishes their IDP status.

The changes are intended to strengthen the legal framework for the Great Return programme. In practice, however, they could significantly affect the lives of hundreds of thousands of people who have spent decades building their lives in Baku and other parts of Azerbaijan.

The purpose of the law and the benefits linked to IDP status

Under the previous legislation, internally displaced person (IDP) status entitled holders to a range of social benefits, including a monthly allowance of 60 manats (about $35) for each family member, state-funded tuition at fee-paying departments of public universities, and exemptions from certain government fees and utility payments.

For people forced to flee their homes in the early 1990s and who had spent decades living in dormitories, temporary housing units or other makeshift accommodation, these benefits represented a basic form of social support. The status also carried legal significance, as it formally recognised that they had been displaced against their will.

Under the new rules, the state is deemed to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers an internally displaced person permanent housing. If the person accepts the apartment, ownership is transferred to them, but they simultaneously lose their IDP status. Those who refuse the offer also lose their status and may forfeit the temporary accommodation provided to them in Baku or another city.

During a three-year transition period, only social support measures, including financial assistance and education benefits, will remain in place. The legal status itself, along with the other rights and guarantees associated with it, will cease to apply.

Freedom of choice and the problem of “any available housing”

The law refers to “alternative housing that complies with the standards established for the region of residence”. In practice, this means that internally displaced people are not necessarily offered housing in their native village or on their ancestral land.

For example, a person who owned several hectares of farmland before being displaced may now be offered a house in a newly built settlement with a plot of only 100–200 square metres. Ownership of their original land is not restored, as the state provides housing only. As a result, the concept of “returning home” is significantly narrowed.

According to dozens of families whose accounts have been shared on social media and in public appeals, many of the homes offered to them suffer from poor construction. They report leaking roofs during rainfall, flooded yards, and repeated disruptions to gas, water and electricity supplies. In some cases, applicants say they have been told verbally: “You’ve been given a house — be grateful, or you’ll lose that too.”

Similar complaints have also been submitted through official grievance mechanisms, although the issue has yet to generate wider public debate.

Life in Baku after three decades of integration

A large proportion of Azerbaijan’s internally displaced people have spent more than 30 years living in Baku and other major economic centres. Over that time, they have found employment, received an education, gained access to healthcare and established stable social networks. After losing their homes in the early 1990s, they were provided with temporary accommodation by the state, including places in dormitories, unfinished buildings and container settlements, as well as apartments in purpose-built residential complexes.

Under the new rules, however, this housing may be reclaimed once a person loses IDP status. As a result, many people face a difficult choice: accept an apartment in Karabakh and leave behind the life they have built in Baku, or lose both their IDP status and the accommodation provided to them by the state.

International human rights standards, including the UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement, require that return be voluntary, safe and carried out in dignity. These principles are based on freedom of choice, the provision of adequate housing and, wherever possible, the restoration of rights to former property. Under Azerbaijan’s new legislation, however, the state is considered to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers housing, while refusing that offer results in the loss of IDP status. This weakens the principle that return should be voluntary.

Official position and expert assessments

Pro-government media outlets, including Milli.az, Report.az and APA, have presented the amendments in a positive light, using phrases such as “restoring property rights”, “sustainable social support” and “providing a legal framework for the Great Return programme”.

MP Vugar Bayramov has also argued that the three-year transition period demonstrates the state’s continued commitment to social support. Official statements emphasise that the new housing is transferred into private ownership rather than provided on a rental basis, which the authorities say will encourage people to settle permanently in the region.

At the same time, independent observers and some human rights advocates argue that the changes restrict freedom of choice, fail to fully restore land rights and raise other concerns. They also point to the contrast between the urban lifestyles that many IDPs have built over the past three decades and the newly established rural settlements, as well as the risks of unemployment and inadequate infrastructure.

The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

World.title: EU’s 21st sanctions package targets Kulevi oil terminal and cryptocurrency platforms in Georgia
World.content:
Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

The European Union’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia includes an oil refinery in the Georgian town of Kulevi and several cryptocurrency platforms.

The sanctions against the Kulevi refinery, which processes and sells Russian oil, include a six-month grace period. The ban on transactions will take effect after six months unless the refinery changes its business practices.

The Kulevi refinery had previously been considered for inclusion in the EU’s 20th package of sanctions against Russia, but was ultimately removed from the sanctions list.

At the time, the EU said that “the Georgian authorities and the port operator had made positive commitments.” This was stated in a letter from the EU’s Special Envoy, David O’Sullivan, to Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili.

What does the new sanctions package include?

The EU’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia, which is expected to take effect shortly, was formally approved by the permanent representatives of the EU member states on 23 July 2026.

The sanctions are expected to enter into force on 23 July following approval by EU leaders and their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

The measures target sectors of the Russian economy that generate significant revenue for Moscow’s war in Ukraine, including energy, financial services and the cryptocurrency sector.

The package also imposes sanctions on more than 50 companies and organisations involved in supplying military goods and weapons to Russia.

It includes the EU’s largest-ever round of individual sanctions, targeting a total of 218 entities — 48 individuals and 170 legal entities.

It is one of the most significant expansions of the EU’s sanctions regime in the past four years.

Sanctions against the Kulevi refinery

“The package introduces the possibility of banning transactions with oil refineries listed in Russia and third countries that process Russian crude oil and petroleum products. Under these measures, the EU is imposing a ban on transactions with the Georgian oil refinery in Kulevi, which processes and trades Russian oil. The ban will take effect in six months,” the EU said in a statement.

According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, citing a source familiar with the matter, the introduction of a six-month deadline is unprecedented in EU sanctions policy.

The same source said the decision reflected Tbilisi’s willingness to meet the EU’s requirements, which became apparent during discussions over sanctions related to the port.

This means that if the Kulevi refinery continues processing Russian oil over the next six months, it will become subject to EU sanctions. The refinery’s owner, Black Sea Petroleum, announced on 1 July 2026 that it would begin full-scale processing of non-Russian crude from August or September.

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, domestic exports rose sharply in January 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, driven largely by exports of petroleum products.

Petroleum and petroleum products ranked as Georgia’s second-largest export category in January 2026, with exports worth $58.7 million, accounting for 12.2% of the country’s total exports.

Cryptocurrency platforms added to the sanctions list

The EU has imposed transaction bans on 14 cryptocurrency platforms based in Georgia, Panama, the United Arab Emirates, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus and the Marshall Islands.

For the first time, the EU has introduced a mechanism allowing it to impose a complete ban on transactions between EU companies and cryptocurrency platforms that help Russia circumvent sanctions.

The measure also applies to crypto service providers operating in third countries if they facilitate activities that serve Russian interests.

What does the inclusion of Georgian companies in the sanctions package mean for Georgia?

The inclusion of the Kulevi refinery in the EU’s 21st sanctions package has already sparked debate in Georgia.

“The EU’s 21st sanctions package is a national disgrace: Georgian assets are being used as cannon fodder for Russia’s war machine. By allowing the Kremlin to circumvent sanctions, those in power are betraying our sovereignty. Georgia’s place is in Europe — we will never become a loophole for Russian aggression,” Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zourabichvili, wrote on X.

Analyst Lela Djedjelava said sanctions against such an important economic asset would have an impact on the Georgian economy.

“The consequences will become increasingly visible over time. The reality is that the Kulevi refinery is probably not the only facility that could be exposed for cooperating with Russia. If other businesses in Georgia are also hit by sanctions, it will naturally have a very negative impact on the country.”

Gedevan Popkhadze, one of the leaders of the opposition Coalition for Change, said the EU sanctions against the Kulevi refinery were the result of the Georgian government’s inaction.

“If you are not helping Ukraine, why are you helping Russia? If you do not want war, why are you acting in favour of one of the parties to the conflict? We must clearly understand that these sanctions are not a message to the Kulevi refinery itself — they are a message to Georgia’s de facto government. It should realise that claiming to be neutral is hypocrisy.”

Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

World.title: Opinion: ‘There is no longer peace in Georgia’
World.content:
Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

Professor at Ilia State University and literary critic Zaal Andronikashvili comments on the events that unfolded in Georgia on 22 July 2026, including the arrest of a journalist, a shooting in central Tbilisi, and an attack on an opposition stand-up comedian.

He writes that there is no longer peace in Georgia and blames Bidzina Ivanishvili and his Georgian Dream party.

Journalist Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 14 days of administrative detention over satirical social media posts about members of the Georgian Dream party. A shooting took place in central Tbilisi on 22 July, leaving four people injured, including two minors. One of the minors later died in hospital. Comedian Onise Okriashvili, a critic of the government, was brutally beaten at his home. Before the attack, he had been the target of a disinformation campaign on pro-government television channels.

Zaal Andronikashvili: “It is important to find the right name for what is happening in Georgia. The situation is new, and historical parallels apply only in part.

Since at least 2019, during the ‘Gavrilov Night’ protests, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have done everything possible to prevent a peaceful transfer of power. Some scholars describe this as a ‘coup from above’.”

This “coup from above” is not peaceful.

Anyone who believes that Georgia is at peace today is deeply mistaken. Beyond dragging Georgia into a geopolitical confrontation on Russia’s side — at an enormous cost to the country — Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are waging an asymmetric, hybrid civil war against the overwhelming majority of the Georgian population.

Part of this hybrid civil war consists of unlawful restrictive legislation enforced only against certain groups of citizens and against civil society as a whole.

There is also financial repression aimed at depriving opponents of the regime of their livelihoods, as well as the deliberate destruction of education and culture. Alongside this come aggression, hopelessness, and an absence of love and empathy elevated to the level of state policy.

There is micro-level violence — encouraging crime and fostering a culture of impunity that ultimately erodes trust in the law, the justice system, and the very idea of justice. There is macro-level violence carried out by the police and special forces, along with many other elements.

“I repeat: this is not peace.

It is a hybrid civil war waged by a regime that controls the police, the legislature and the country’s financial resources against the majority of Georgia’s population, especially its most active citizens. Its goal is to suppress, subjugate and ultimately enslave them.

The other side has nothing but the truth and peaceful resistance. But the truth is a powerful, almost invincible weapon — and it can never truly be defeated.

Despite this asymmetric civil war, whose domestic objective is to cement the regime permanently in power and make the current government irreplaceable, while its foreign policy goal is to sever Georgia once and for all from the European values-based community and turn it into a banana republic under a quasi-colonial regime, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have failed to win this unequal conflict.

Peaceful resistance is alive. The people have not been broken. They have not been intimidated.

Those who support the regime today, or choose silent complicity, should look at Russia.

People there also believed that if they kept quiet and buried their heads in a bowl of caviar, none of it would affect them. Other people’s children would die, someone else would go to prison, someone else’s life would be ruined. Perhaps someone would stop greeting them, but they could live with that.

In reality, supporting injustice always comes at a price. Injustice and lawlessness may begin by targeting only selected groups, but they very quickly spread to everyone.

By supporting injustice, you create an environment in which that injustice will inevitably reach you in one form or another.

But people are willing to ignore it until it affects them personally. There is a powerful metaphor in the Gospel of Matthew (26:52): ‘All who draw the sword will die by the sword.’ This is not really about the sword itself, but more broadly about the laws of social reality and their universal nature.

There is no peace in Georgia. Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are responsible for that.”

Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

World.title: How young fan's 'celebrity crush' on YouTube sensation ended in rape trial
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains details some readers may find distressing, including allegations of sexual assault.

He was a YouTube sensation with millions of followers on social media, a UK celebrity and sometime BBC presenter who had branched out into a successful music career.

She was a starstruck young woman who thought her wildest dreams had come true when her idol not only came to her small city on the other side of the world for a gig, but also singled her out in the crowd for special attention.

"My future husband!" she shrieks excitedly in a video recorded by her best friend in the toilets of the venue, just before the concert begins shortly before midnight on September 27, 2024.

But there was to be no fairytale ending.

UK rapper Yung Filly has been accused of raping and assaulting one of his young fans. (Facebook: Yung Filly)

Instead, the alleged events of that fateful night have been replayed in sordid detail in Perth's District Court this week, where Yung Filly, whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, is on trial on charges of rape and assault against that devoted 20-year-old fan.

Growing celebrity

When Mr Barrientos came to Perth in September 2024, he was at the height of his fame.

Born in Colombia in 1995 but raised in the UK, he'd begun his career as a comedy sketch artist whose YouTube videos had first begun attracting serious attention in 2013.

In 2017, he released his first single, and more would follow in subsequent years, notching two UK Top 40 hits.

He continued making YouTube videos, not only on his own channel but also in collaboration with other popular content creators such as Beta Squad, amassing millions of views.

Yung Filly came to Perth for a gig in September 2024. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

He hosted and appeared in a slew of prime-time TV shows in the UK, including Race Across the UK, the Great British Bake Off and Hot Property.

And with growing stardom came luxury cars, holidays and jewellery, if his social media accounts were anything to go by.

An age-old story

But in the judicial surroundings of Court 3.1 of the District Court, the glamour and the glitz and the trappings of fame fell away, leaving Mr Barrientos sitting alone in the dock, just like any of the other accused offenders that pass through the same court.

Yung Filly pictured at the Perth Magistrates Court. (ABC News: Phoebe Pin)

And ultimately, the story told by the prosecution is the same one juries in this court have heard countless times before: the story of a young woman allegedly raped by an older, more powerful man.

Her word versus his.

The 'lucky' white top

Her version of events laid out before the court this week was a harrowing one.

Court hears Yung Filly choked, sexually assaulted young fan A Perth court hears disturbing details of the YouTube personality's alleged sexual assault of a young woman who had a "celebrity crush" on him.

A long-time fan of Yung Filly, she had been thrilled when she heard he was coming to Perth to perform at Bar One, a nightclub in Perth's northern suburbs overlooking Hillarys marina, along a pristine stretch of white sandy beaches popular with the UK expatriate community.

She had carefully selected her "lucky" white top to wear for the occasion, the court heard, teamed with a pair of light-coloured denim jeans.

That innocuous sleeveless top would turn out to be anything but lucky for her, as the state prosecutor would later tell the jury.

'I'm gonna marry him'

Never meet your idols, they say.

But it's doubtful that even Gustave Flaubert, who first coined the phrase in Madame Bovary back in the 19th century to warn of the essential fallibility of humans, even very famous ones, could have conceived of a celebrity encounter characterised by this level of alleged depravity.

It didn't start out that way.

Yung Filly has also hosted and appeared in a slew of prime-time TV shows in the UK. (Instagram: yungfilly)

In videos shown to the court and recorded on the phone of her best friend at the gig, the bright-eyed young women are animatedly discussing the rapper and the night ahead.

Brimming with excitement, the short videos record the 20-year-old telling of her "celebrity crush" on Mr Barrientos, whom she thought of as her "future husband".

"I'm gonna marry him!" she yells as the music thumps behind her in the crowded nightclub.

Later she will tell a court she had envisaged a "David Beckham and Victoria Beckham future" for herself and the rapper.

Dream begins to unravel

The women eventually manage to get access to the VIP area of the club, where they enjoy free drinks and are ultimately able to mingle with Mr Barrientos himself once he comes offstage.

She will later tell the court she noticed his "vampire-like teeth".

The 20-year-old met with Yung Filly at the VIP area of the club once he came offstage. (Facebook: Yung Filly)

It's at this point that her dream appears to begin to brush up against a harsher reality, according to what she told the court.

Chatting with Mr Barrientos, the starstruck 20-year-old testified that he put his hands down the back of her pants and told her, "you're coming home with me tonight".

She pushed his hands away, only to have him grab one of her breasts, according to her testimony.

"I'm not like that," are the words she recalls telling him.

" You can't do that. "

"It really shows your age," is what she remembers him saying.

No afterparty

By 3:30am, Mr Barrientos and his entourage are leaving the club, and so is the still eager 20-year-old fan.

CCTV footage played to the court shows her climbing into a Kia Carnival with Mr Barrientos and five other men in his entourage.

Yung Filly pictured at the Perth Magistrates Court. (ABC News: Phoebe Pin)

She thought she was going to an afterparty, she would later tell the court, but instead, they drove straight to his hotel, the InterContinental in Hay Street, in the heart of the city's CBD.

Some 22 months later, she would be testifying against him in a courtroom less than a kilometre away on the same street, about exactly what happened that evening.

Evening takes dark turn

Once in his room, the pair had consensual sex, the court heard, before things allegedly took a much darker turn.

"It was then that the accused started to become more aggressive and forceful," state prosecutor Danielle Clarke told the court.

Graphic injury photos shown at Yung Filly rape trial A doctor testifies at a sexual assault trial about the injuries allegedly inflicted by an internationally renowned YouTube star on an infatuated fan in his Perth hotel room after a concert.

He began to bite her, hard, on the neck and cheek, Ms Clarke said, and when the young woman objected, he bit her harder and told her to stop talking.

It would get even worse from there, according to the prosecution's case.

The young fan was subsequently slapped repeatedly across the face without warning as she tried to put her hand up to protect herself, while Mr Barrientos ordered her to say, "I'm Filly's dirty whore and fat pig," Ms Clarke said.

Mr Barrientos, she said, put his hand around the 20-year-old's throat, choking her for several seconds, spat in her mouth and proceeded to rape her multiple times, "despite her explicitly saying 'no'".

"The accused then called room service and ordered himself a burger," she said.

'Pack of lies'

Mr Barrientos denies all 10 charges against him.

While we don't know exactly what his version of events is, since his barrister David Edwardson KC declined to give an opening address to the jury, it's clear he vehemently disputes the alleged victim's account.

"A pack of lies" is the way Mr Edwardson described key parts of the 20-year-old's testimony about what happened in the hotel room.

Mr Edwardson has alluded that the 20-year-old was lying in her testimony about what happened in the hotel room. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Cross-examining witnesses, he has focused on the events in the aftermath of the alleged rape, including later that same day, when she and her best friend attended a music festival.

"You were having a wonderful time, weren't you?" he asked the friend, showing the court videos taken from her phone of the two women dancing and drinking in the mosh pit.

YouTube rapper accused of rape allowed to fly home on bail British YouTube content creator Yung Filly, who's facing trial in Perth on sex assault charges, is granted permission to travel home.

While not denying there had been moments of levity, the friend said it had "felt really heavy, like there was an elephant in the room with us," and that the happier moments had been undercut by her friend's distress, including spending long periods of time in the toilets crying.

He got Detective Constable Luke Schatke to admit the importance of "anything you can capture which shows how she presents after the alleged incident" and whether "she displays distress or not distress".

Mr Edwardson has also sought to question the adequacy of the police investigation, showing the court videos captured of the alleged victim leaving Mr Barrientos's hotel about 5am on September 28 and receiving a phone call, then getting into an Uber.

While Detective Constable Schatke said it "can be" critical for police to interview the people the alleged victim spoke to immediately after leaving Mr Barrientos's hotel room, he also admitted he did not know if police had spoken to either the person the 20-year-old took a phone call from, or her Uber driver.

Yung Filly has denied all 10 charges against him. (ABC News: Phoebe Pin)

Investigating officer Sergeant Melissa James later confirmed the Uber driver had not been interviewed because he did not return police phone calls and messages, and neither had Mr Barrientos's bodyguard Mohammed Ali, who confiscated the alleged victim's phone on the night.

Mr Ali had been rude and uncooperative, she said, although she agreed with Mr Edwardson that he could potentially have been a "highly relevant" witness.

"Were you genuinely interested in being impartial?" Mr Edwardson asked.

"In chasing down all the relevant pieces of information that might be important for a jury?"

"Yes," she replied.

Yung Filly to testify

The prosecution's case finished on Friday, with the defence set to call witnesses from Monday — including Mr Barrientos himself, Mr Edwardson confirmed late on Friday.

Yung Filly will be called as one of the defence's witnesses next week. (ABC News: David Weber)

The courtroom has been close to capacity most days, with family and associates of Mr Barrientos present throughout, along with a smattering of young fans, mostly men in their teens or early 20s and some in school uniform.

Friends and family of the complainant have also been closely following from the gallery.

The trial, before Judge Linda Black, will resume on Monday and is scheduled to wrap up by the end of next week.

World.title: Idle, aging oil platform raises alarm for Dongara's fishers
World.content:
An abandoned oil drilling rig off the coast of Western Australia's Midwest is at the centre of a storm about who pays the clean-up bill after the company that owned it went into administration.

Local fishermen and conservation groups are demanding the federal government take action over the Cliff Head oil platform before crayfishing grounds are put at risk.

Pilot Energy was working with Triangle Energy to repurpose the rig, which sits 11 kilometres off the coast of Dongara, about 350 kilometres north of Perth.

But in July both companies, which had a combined value of about $9 million, went bust, leaving a decommissioning bill of $200 million.

Cray fisher Mike Butcher worries what will now happen to the unused Cliff Head platform sitting idly at sea. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Platform 'mothballed'

Dongara cray fisherman Michael Butcher said connection to the coast was one of the most sacred things to residents.

"I'd say fishing is pretty much the most important thing in Dongara, or just the ocean in general," he said.

"It's the main industry in town. [The ocean] is definitely part of our culture."

Mr Butcher, who fishes near the rig regularly, said he had not noticed anyone maintaining the platform recently.

According to local fishers, the aging, ocean-worn Cliff Head platform is falling into neglect. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"There's no-one coming out here on a daily basis checking on it [the platform]," he said.

"You can see for yourself, it's not been very loved or well maintained.

"It's just been mothballed."

Lobster fisher Jonathon Buist, or "Moggy" as he's locally called. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Fellow cray fisherman Jonathon "Moggy" Buist said the area around the platform was home to an "abundance" of marine life and it was important to local businesses that the rig was not left to degrade in the ocean.

"There's an abundance of fish life and caves that rock lobsters live in [near the platform] so it's a really important part of our fishery," Mr Buist said.

" The actual rig doesn't bother me too much because it's a bit of a navigation aid for us, but it's the pipework underneath we'd like to [keep] tidy. "

Crayfish or western rock lobsters can be found in caves near the Cliff Head oil platform. (ABC News: Chris Lewis)

'Canary in the coalmine'

In a written statement, federal Resources Minister Madeline King said taxpayers were not expected to foot the decommissioning bill and if needed it would extend an emergency sector-wide levy.

"Titleholders are obligated by Australian law to pay all costs associated with decommissioning," she said.

"In the event of companies being unable to pay I will have no hesitation in extending the Northern Endeavor levy or taking other measures to cover all costs of decommissioning.

" Under no circumstances will taxpayers be left on the hook. "

The Cliff Head platform sits abandoned following the voluntary administration of operators Triangle Energy and Pilot Energy. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Ms King also said the safety regulator would ensure protections were in place for the marine environment.

"The offshore safety regulator has taken a number of steps to ensure the Cliff Head facility does not pose an immediate threat to the marine environment," she said.

But Conservation Council of WA executive director Matt Roberts said the uncertainty exposed vulnerabilities in the decommissioning system.

"We have $60 billion worth of infrastructure off the coast of WA and this is that canary in the coal mine moment that indicates what else is at risk out there," he said.

"They've [the federal government] talked about having a financial assurances regime. When is that going to be passed and enforced?"

CCWA's Matt Roberts says better systems need to be in place for decommissioning infrastructure at sea. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Concern for other projects

Decommissioning the Cliff Head oil platform was not the only question front of mind for fishers.

Before the company fell into voluntary administration, protests began to stop Pilot Energy testing the surrounding sea bed, home to valuable rock lobster, for oil and gas reserves.

"I'm part of the Dongara against seismic blasting group and that involves a range of people … that are worried about the local environment," Mr Butcher said.

Dongara community members are opposing seismic testing and potential damage to the valuable rock lobster fishery. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

The lobby group started in 2025 after Pilot Energy was approved to begin its Eureka 3D Marine Seismic Survey.

Seismic blasting involves releasing a bubble of compressed air that produces low-frequency noise, penetrating rock layers below the surface.

The project, which was set to begin in February this year, was delayed for 12 months after Pilot failed to secure a suitable survey vessel.

With Pilot Energy entering administration, Dongara residents are hoping plans for offshore seismic testing will be abandoned. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Mr Butcher said fishers had been left in the lurch wondering if a project of similar calibre could return.

"We haven't had any consultation from government, [the] National Offshore Petroleum Safety and Enviromental Management Authority, nothing really regarding where we're going in the future," he said.

" But we've got to catch fish so we go to work. "

Pilot Energy administrators Cor Cordis said in a written statement they had begun assessing the rig's future.

"We recognise the strategic importance of the Cliff Head project and will work constructively with all stakeholders … as we assess all the available pathways," they said.

World.title: Albanese personally opposed to Labor push on voluntary assisted dying
World.content:
A Labor push to allow Australians to access voluntary assisted dying through telehealth does not have the personal support of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who fears it would undermine the system.

Mr Albanese is in favour of voluntary euthanasia but said he was "yet to be convinced" allowing people to consult with doctors via phone or video about the process was the right move.

"I think it is important that people have the right to die … with dignity," he said.

"But it's also important that protections be placed around it."

The policy platform adopted at Labor's 50th national conference included a commitment to expand voluntary assisted dying (VAD) access to telehealth, while a pledge to always allow a conscience vote on the issue was enshrined in the party's constitution.

Mr Albanese told ABC's Insiders on Sunday his personal concern with the proposal was the potential for "misuse" or that it would "undermine the system in itself".

"That's my position," he said. "I respect the fact that there are different views on this."

VAD telehealth endorsed at ALP conference A Labor push to lift the ban on accessing voluntary assisted dying through telehealth has triggered a warning about unintended consequences for vulnerable Australians.

Australia currently bans people from using telehealth for voluntary assisted dying (VAD) consultations, with doctors facing fines of up to $300,000 for contravening the law.

Advocates have argued the restriction unfairly impacts Australians in remote and regional areas and welcomed the amendment to Labor's platform pledging to remove "barriers" to accessing end-of-life care.

But Mr Albanese said it would be up to his cabinet, in consultation with the caucus, as to whether the matter was put before the parliament for a vote.

"Governments determine what governments do … what the conference does has put general direction of what they want, and it's clear that is a matter of conscience," the prime minister said.

Albanese defends orderly Labor conference

Reflecting on Labor's conference, which wrapped up in Adelaide on Saturday, Mr Albanese rejected criticism that internal deals had ensured all disagreements were handled behind closed doors.

He said the support for the party's platform showed there was "broad consensus" among Labor members about "the direction in which we're taking the government".

"We know who we are and what we stand for, and the direction in which we want to take the country," he said.

Husic lashes Labor culture A push to recognise claims of genocide in Gaza failed to gain enough support for a debate on the floor of Labor's national conference.

Asked about a failed push led by outspoken backbench MP Ed Husic to debate a resolution more critical of the Israeli government, Mr Albanese said he believed the party's platform "got the balance right".

"I support the right of Israel to exist within secure borders," he said.

"I also support the legitimate aspirations of Palestinians for their own state, and to live in peace and security with prosperity."

Mr Albanese said Mr Husic had a "right to come along and pursue whatever they say is or see is their objective".

"That's fine by me," the prime minister said.

"I have no problem with any delegate to the conference, having their say and making their contribution."

Labor's 50th conference has raised questions about whether debate now occurs behind closed doors, which Mr Albanese denied. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

But he rejected criticism of the party's efforts to avoid debate at the conference, arguing the motions that reached the floor had already gone through a lengthy internal process.

"The party has changed, and one of the things that's happened in the party is we are more cohesive, more united than we've ever been before," he said.

"And I think that's a good thing."

Albanese vows to challenge Trump on tariffs

On the 12.5 per cent export tariffs placed on Australia by the US, Mr Albanese said he would "absolutely" be raising his concerns with President Donald Trump.

"Those are unjustified," he said.

"We'll raise it at every level of the Australia-US relationship."

Mr Albanese acknowledged the impact of the ongoing US war with Iran and closure of the Strait of Hormuz on oil prices but did not indicate the cut to the fuel excise would be extended beyond July.

"That's not in our planning at this point in time," he said.

Anthony Albanese says he will "absolutely raise" the 12.5 per cent export tariffs placed on Australia with US President Donald Trump. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

Mr Albanese also revealed it was his hope the federal government would produce an exposure draft of legislation outlining standards for data centres built in Australia by the end of the year.

The prime minister is due to discuss the issue with premiers at a meeting of national cabinet next month and is aiming to have the final legislation introduced to parliament in early 2027.

Mr Albanese was pressed on reports in the Nine papers about his attendance at a dinner in Sydney last week hosted by Felix Lee, whose billionaire father Phillip Dong Fang Lee is accused by the Australian Tax Office of funnelling money from China into Australian bank accounts.

The prime minister said he attended "lots of functions".

"I attend lots of dinners in lots of places, and I don't talk about private dinners," he said.

Labor conference concludes with agreement on local councils

On the final day of the Labor conference, delegates endorsed changes to the platform committing Labor to a federation compact between local governments and the Commonwealth to increase federal funding.

Councils had been pushing for an effective doubling of untied funding that would cost the federal government about $3.5 billion a year.

Unions and local governments had been threatening to pursue the issue on the floor of the conference, but last-minute negotiations secured a deal and avoided debate.

United Services Union secretary Graeme Kelly said the commitment would give councils the certainty to "plan, to keep skilled people in secure local jobs and to deliver the services people across the state rely on".

Australian Services Union national secretary Emeline Gaske said it was an acknowledgment of the critical community services provided by librarians, parks, sanitation and other council workers.

Labor cuts deal on AI for workers Labor will respond to growing anxiety about the rise of artificial intelligence with a new taskforce to give Australian workers a greater say in how the technology shapes the nation.

Sydney's Inner West Mayor Darcy Byrne welcomed the commitment to restore adequate funding to councils across Australia.

"The crisis in local government funding is real and this new national agreement is exactly what's needed to secure basic, local services in municipalities across the country," he said.

"Australians rely on councils every day to deliver the grassroots services and infrastructure that keep local communities running."

Across the conference delegates backed changes to Labor's platform covering artificial intelligence, workers' rights, tougher gambling reforms, decarbonisation disincentives, the expansion of dental coverage in Medicare and a range of other issues.

Debates about a tax on gas exports or Labor's stance on the AUKUS defence pact did not eventuate.

World.title: 'Gonna bury him in his van': Ice Cream King marks 40 years
World.content:
Alex Deak would rather not think about how many times he's heard the distinctive 16th-century melody that blasts out of his ice cream van.

For 40 years Greensleeves has alerted those hankering for a cold treat to the arrival of "the Ice Cream King".

"If I would listen to it all the time, I reckon I would be mental by now," the 86-year-old says, adding he's learnt to tune it out.

Alex Deak struggles to find parts for his 53-year-old van. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

Since 1986 Mr Deak and his pink and white van have reigned in Mount Gambier.

Despite the 1972-model Bedford CF van being emblazoned with "Ice Cream King", Mr Deak insists he's "not king".

"I'm not blue blood at all," he says.

The Hungarian migrant is also known to locals as "Mr Whippy".

Among them is customer Trevor Smith, who recalls having "the one with flake in it" growing up Mount Gambier in the 1980s.

"You're talking three, four generations of kids and adults," he says.

"He's well-known … and a bit of character".

The journey to the throne

Mr Deak was born during World War II in Csongrád, southern Hungary.

He recalls almost getting "wiped out" by aerial fighters as a four-year-old and his first encounter with an ice cream man.

Alex Deak intends to keep running the van until he's 90. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

"'Ding-a-ling-a-ling' … everybody came out from the side street … we just loved the guy," he says.

" I just went and became an ice cream man. "

After fleeing to Austria as a teenager, he studied business in Germany before heading to Australia in the 1960s and working as a pine faller in Mount Gambier.

Into a different world

Byron Deak said his father always worked hard, be it in farming, forestry or factory jobs, but he didn't expect the midlife career change.

Alex bought the ice cream business in his mid-40s, which Byron's mates found amusing.

"There's a lot of jokes … it's like, 'Oh, your dad's Mr Whippy,'" Byron says.

Byron Deak was surprised by his father's career shift. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

"[Locals have] always got a story about chasing him … I've talked to people and they said that they've chased him up numerous hills for kilometres and he hadn't noticed them.

"But he didn't run them over, which is good."

Byron says he once expected to be asked to take over the ice cream van but he's no longer bracing for the tap on the shoulder.

"My mother wanted him to retire a few years ago and he just wouldn't. It's kind of part of him now," he says.

"I think we're gonna have to bury him in it."

Giving him life

Alex Deak says he enjoys being an ice cream man "immensely" and is keen to start his 40th season when the weather warms up.

"[Running the business] keeps me alive … because I'm mentally and physically active," he says.

Inside the van, he demonstrates how the suspension of the 53-year-old vehicle gives his back some rare respite.

"Because I haven't got a disc there, bone on bone, it is like an angel's wings," he says, springing his knees up and down with a smile.

Byron Deak's mates had a chuckle when his dad bought the van. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

Byron says his dad has always been someone who is happy in his own company, rather than being "a pub man".

"He sits here and plays his chess computer and whatnot, and he loves his grandchildren," he says.

"But his community is the people from that ice cream van."

A record innings?

According to Guiness World Records, the longest career of an ice cream distributer (male) is 67 years.

But Byron notes the record-holder was operating his vehicle for 37 years, while his dad has been selling ice cream out of his van for 40 years, which could be a record in itself.

"Forty years is a pretty good trot … if it's an Australian record, it'd be really nice," Byron says.

Guiness World Records did not respond to a request for comment, but Alex Deak says he's "privileged" to have spent four decades as Mr Whippy and is not concerned about breaking records.

"I do it till I'm 90," he says.

"And then I retire."

World.title: 'Bottomless pit of styles' on display at Gold Coast tattoo exhibition
World.content:
Benji Tobin's career as a tattoo artist began in 1993 with a bottle of liquid courage and a few scribbles on a mate's leg.

"We made a tattoo machine out of an electric shaver [but] my lines were way off and I said, 'Mate, this isn't going to turn out the way we thought,'" he said.

"Unfortunately, all my mates I grew up with have got the worst tattoos I've ever done."

Now Tobin has co-curated an art exhibition called Made to Suit, which reflects how much the art form has transformed since tattoos became mainstream.

"It was the bikies, the crims, the naughty boys," he said.

" Now you can go and get a coffee and the barista has a face tattoo. "

Benji Tobin says there is a huge diversity of styles in the tattooing world. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

'I have to nail this'

Tobin started Made to Suit five years ago as a way to bring the "cliquey" tattoo community together and highlight the vast diversity of styles.

"What I tattoo isn't what I get — what I like and what I get are two different things," he said.

"I'm covered in black and grey but I tattoo in colour."

Dan Johnston with his piece for the Made to Suit exhibition. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

The exhibition recreates more than 30 full-body tattoos on canvas.

Co-curator Dan Johnston submitted his own canvas this year, which demonstrates of how tattoos reflect the artists who draw them.

"After the last Made to Suit, my wife found out she has brain cancer," he said.

(ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Johnston's piece shows 13 samurai-inspired crabs climbing up a body, united in the fight against a symbol of cancer.

"I tried to make it a little bit about a journey that's happening in my life," he said.

"It was personal and I thought, 'I have to nail this and get it out.'"

'A bottomless pit of styles'

Stephanie King says she has seen trends come and go since she started tattooing 14 years ago.

"There's trends at the moment, like the fine lines, sticker ones — I feel like that's boomed," she said.

Stephanie King says the tattoo business is very different to what it once was. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

King has built a reputation for creating hyper-realistic black and white tattoos but has changed up her style for Made to Suit.

"You used to walk into a shop and you picked a design off the wall. The people doing the tattoos were probably pretty scary and fitted into a stereotype," she said.

"It's changed quite a bit, there's a lot more women in the industry now."

Tony Nguyen says he feels relaxed when he is under the needle. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

King's work in last year's exhibition was found online by New York lawyer Tony Nguyen, who wanted to get a full bodysuit for his first tattoo.

"I was really picky about who my artist was going to be," he said.

"When I first dipped my toe into it, it was a bottomless pit of styles, regions and histories — I got lost in it."

Mr Nguyen said King's art spoke to him so much that he travelled all the way to her Gold Coast studio.

"It was very fluid, there was something not strict, or an airy feel about it," he said.

'A way to tell a story'

It has taken King 12 days to tattoo Mr Nguyen's torso and she has his arms and legs still to go.

But he has no thoughts of turning back.

"It makes me feel at ease. It makes me feel the way I feel inside but it's on my skin and I can see it," Mr Nguyen said.

Stephanie King has been tattooing Tony Nguyen in her Gold Coast studio. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Tobin says people get tattoos for different reasons, but more customers are choosing artists for their distinctive style and giving greater thought to how one tattoo complements the next.

"They don't just go, 'Give me this, give me that' and [I] think, 'Shit, what am I going to do with all this?'" he said.

"They'll come in and go, 'Hey, I like your work, I want to get a sleeve', and that will extend into something bigger."

Lost Woods Tattoo by James Wood is on display at 2026 Made to Suit exhibition. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

King said there was more freedom than ever for tattoo artists to be creative and evolve.

"You go for a walk and you see things in nature that inspire you … I love going to galleries and museums," she said.

"People see it as art. It's a way to tell a story."

World.title: No more tears left to cry as Godwin goes from hell to the mountaintop
World.content:
Four years ago, Georgia Godwin was at the peak of her powers as she led Australia to silver in the women's team final at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games.

She performed all four of the apparatus and had the highest score in three of them.

This time around, her first two rotations were just OK, aided by brilliant performances by Kate McDonald, whose 14.200 was the best uneven bars score of the day; and Breanna Scott on beam.

They backed it up on the floor, with first Scott, then McDonald posting the day's second-best scores on the apparatus.

Godwin was a picture of composure. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Then Godwin reminded the world of her class with a stunning routine that earned her a 13.350 and left Australia in top spot with only the vault to come.

"There was a lot going through my head before that floor routine and the girls before me absolutely nailed their floors. I just really wanted to help the team and with all of that head noise and all of that pressure I just started feeling a bit overwhelmed," she said.

"So before I started floor, I went to my plans and grounded myself and I was so happy for that to be my first floor routine back at a big international event."

The moment her music faded out, the emotions came rushing into Godwin and out onto her face.

Georgia Godwin burst into tears immediately after her floor routine. (Getty Images: Owen Humphreys/PA Images)

Some mixture of pride and relief. Then the tears as she embraced every member of the team who had helped her get back.

The Achilles she tore two and a half years ago hadn't just held up, it had propelled her and her team towards almost certain gold in Glasgow.

Athletes often talk of resilience gained and lessons learned through adversity, but sometimes it just sucks to be unceremoniously kicked off the mountaintop, have your livelihood threatened and independence taken away.

"I'm gonna be completely honest, it's been a horrible, horrible road back," she said.

"My support team has been absolutely amazing, but the mental challenges I've had to go through have been the hardest I've been through in my life.

"But I want to finish this sport on my own terms and I wanted to do one more big event with these amazing girls.

The village got Georgia Godwin through hell. (Getty Images: Matthias Hangst)

"I've said it before and I'll say it over and over again, but it takes a village and I'm so lucky to have my special village."

That village includes her parents, who were in the stands to watch, her teammates, her coaches, physio, trainers, and of course puppy Remy.

Unsurprisingly, there were times when she thought she wouldn't be able to get back.

Too old, too sore, too hard. Just all too much.

It was too much again on Saturday night at the Glasgow International Arena.

The energy was high from the Australians throughout the final. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Asked about her mindset as she stepped onto the floor, the emotions came for her again.

"I'm gonna have no tears left by the end of this," she laughed.

A solid 20 seconds of overwhelm later, she said she wasn't performing for herself but those dozens, hundreds of people who have helped her get back on the mat, the bars, the vault and the floor.

Five seconds later she was laughing about becoming Australia's most decorated female gymnast, and joking at the expense of Allana Slater.

It was another reminder of her ability to compartmentalise, albeit slightly less impressive than when she managed to compose herself after the ultimate release of sticking that floor routine to pull off a similarly superb 13.550 vault.

In a competition where they won gold by 1.1 point, a half misstep or misalignment could have seen the ultimate goal slip through her fingers again.

Georgia Godwin has returned to the top of the world. (Gety Images: Naomi Baker)

"My emotions don't come up very often but when they do I'm very good at suppressing them if I've got a job to do," she said.

"I think it's so important to feel your emotions but there's also a time and place, so I took the moment, got myself into a quiet corner and just laid down and tried to calm myself back down and did the job."

Job done, but not really.

Still ahead of her in Glasgow are gold medal defences in the all-around and vault finals, and a floor final.

But today isn't about any of that.

Today is about reminding her who she is, what she can do, and why she does it.

"I think everything is all good," she said.

"We can move on and I've really taken a step today."
