World.title: 17yo killed in alleged DV murder remembered as 'sweet' girl finishing school
World.content:
Galiwin'ku residents say a teenage girl who was killed in an alleged domestic violence murder in the remote Northern Territory community earlier this month was a "sweet", "gentle" person who was "more than a statistic".

The 17-year-old girl, who cannot be named for cultural reasons, was found dead in a home on Elcho Island, 500 kilometres east of Darwin, on July 6, from what police allege were blunt force injuries.

Jordan Garrawurra, 34, has since been charged with her murder, with police alleging they were in a "domestic relationship" at the time of her death.

The East Arnhem Regional Council has since united local authority members across the region to urge family and community members to call out domestic violence.

'Sweet' girl remembered

Ganygulpa Dhurrkay, a family member of the girl who died, says her loss has left her devastated. (Supplied: East Arnhem Regional Council)

East Arnhem Regional Council member Ganygulpa Dhurrkay said the girl was "more than a statistic, more than a number", she was a family member.

"I though these were just things that happen in movies but it's not," she said.

"She was only a girl and that hurts so much.

"When I was shown a photo of her, I remembered her, I know her.

"She was beautiful, her smile; when I saw the photo that was shown to me, I just couldn't hold back, I screamed 'no, not her'.

"I used to visit her grandmother's bigger sister, we are cousins, [and] she used to be hanging around that place — I was so devastated.

"She was sweet, gentle."

The community of Galiwin'ku is in mourning for the girl. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Council Deputy President Stephen Dhamarrandji has been in Galiwin’ku since the girl’s death and said the community, especially the school, had been in mourning.

"The school [had] the smoking ceremony because this was her last year to finish year 12," he said.

"The family at the moment are having the silent grieving, but they are showing the love that overflows from their heart."

'No more, not on my watch'

Council President Lapulung Dhamarrandji is one of three councillors who are urging local authority members from across the region to help stamp out domestic violence in the wake of the tragedy.

"We need to bring that awareness that it will never happen again in the lives of our own people," he said.

"We need to preserve our young people, our next generation, heart to heart, soul to soul, by taking care and respecting each other."

At the recent meetings with local authorities, the councillors called on residents to speak up against domestic violence when they saw it.

Lapulung Dhamarrandji says communities in the region need to take care of their young people. (Supplied: East Arnhem Regional Council)

Ms Dhurrkay said locals could no longer afford to keep waiting for someone else to solve the problem.

"I was so hurt and angry, but also feeling this is no time to just be sad and cry and say that nothing would happen, no,” she said.

"To say no more, not on my watch.

"We can rise up to this giant.

"It's time to do action, it's time to say no more will I put it under the carpet."

Mr Dhamarrandji said the East Arnhem community, as well as the wider Australian community, needed to promote respect.

"We, as the members of the community, the family, we have to stand up and find the solution, find the best [way] we can make a pathway,” he said.

"We all have a role to play."

World.title: Quick hits: Photographer watches partner win gold, tiny nation makes history
World.content:
The partner of an Australian gold medallist nervously watches his final while working on the pool deck, while a swimmer loses her cap in the middle of a race.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Picture perfect moment

Sam Williamson (right) celebrates with his partner Linnea Lindberg after winning gold. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Spare a thought for Sam Williamson's partner Linnea Lindberg.

As Williamson powered to an emotional victory in the men's 100m breaststroke final, Lindberg was forced to nervously watch on in her professional capacity.

You see, Lindberg is working at the Comm Games as an accredited photographer.

Williamson joked after his final he was not sure about the quality of any snaps she took during his race.

"I can't imagine they'll be good," Williamson joked to the Seven Network.

"I reckon she's got more tears in her eyes than I do at the moment … if we get one good photo from tonight, it's all worth it."

Sam Williamson (left) and Linnea Lindberg caught the eye of poolside photographers. (Reuters: Andrew Couldridge)

Williamson and Lindberg were able to catch up and celebrate on the pool deck, much to the delight of the other photographers working at the swimming.

2. Aussie loses swimming cap

Sienna Toohey lost one of her swimming caps during her 100m breaststroke heat. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

No doubt Sienna Toohey thought she was ready for any challenge thrown at her at the Commonwealth Games.

That was until one of her swimming caps fell off mid-race during the heats of the women's 100m breaststroke.

"I got to the end [of my heat] and they [officials] were like, 'Has anyone lost a cap?', and I was like, 'Yeah, that's me,'" Toohey said.

She said officials told her she could dive back in the pool and retrieve the cap, but there was only one problem.

"I couldn't find it anywhere in the pool," Toohey said.

"I was thinking: 'I've got to get this cap back, I need it for tonight.'"

Toohey eventually found the cap, with the Tollcross International Swimming Centre crowd giving her a warm round of applause.

The "wardrobe malfunction" did delay the heats program, although no-one seemed bothered.

For the record, Toohey won her heat in a time of 1:07.30.

3. Diamonds put out call to Outlander star

Scottish actor Sam Heughan is in demand. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

The Australian netball team has laid down a challenge to Scottish actor Sam Heughan.

The Diamonds want to meet up with Heughan, who plays Jamie Fraser in the Outlander series, after he was spotted at a Scottish team training session.

Kiera Austin and Courtney Bruce are among the Diamonds players who have taken to Instagram asking Heughan — who featured in the opening ceremony — to come and watch the netball competition.

It seems their wishes may well be granted.

Loading Instagram content

We'll keep you posted on whether a meeting eventuates.

4. McCanns watch son compete

Kate and Gerry McCann watch their son Sean McCann compete in the swimming heats on day two. (Getty Images/SNS Group: Ross MacDonald)

From all reports, Kate and Gerry McCann avoided being accosted when they watched their son, Sean, compete in the men's 400m freestyle at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre.

The McCanns were the centre of a media frenzy when their three-year-old daughter Madeline went missing during a family holiday in Portugal in 2007.

It remains one of the most high-profile international missing-persons cases and is still under investigation.

The parents and Sean's twin sister, Amelie, sat in the stands for both the heats and final.

Sean McCann, who was two when Madeleine disappeared, finished fourth in his heat but snuck into the final, where he placed eighth.

5. Jersey breaks medal drought

Swimmer Filip Nowacki broke through for Jersey with his silver medal. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

The nation of Jersey has reason to celebrate after claiming its first Commonwealth Games medal in 36 years.

Filip Nowacki won silver behind Williamson in the men's 100m breaststroke final, beating world record holder Adam Ramsay-Peaty into third place.

"I'm really happy with that swim," the 18-year-old told BBC Jersey.

"It was just a touch outside my personal best, but it's a true privilege racing Adam, the Aussies and the very best in the world in a senior environment."

Nowacki's medal was only the fifth Jersey has won in Commonwealth Games history.

The last medal came at the 1990 Games in Auckland, when Colin Mallett topped the podium in the full-bore rifle.

World.title: Woman caught in crossfire as police shoot armed man during stand-off
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCrime Woman caught in crossfire as police shoot armed man during stand-off Catherine Strohfeldt July 26, 2026 — 10:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A bystander to a tense police stand-off has been shot after officers discharged multiple rounds at a 28-year-old man carrying knives. Both a 50-year-old woman and the armed man suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries following the incident in the Cairns suburb of Mount Sheridan. Both remained in hospital on Sunday. Assistant Commissioner Graeme Paine said the “very dynamic” situation had escalated quickly. Loading About 5pm on Saturday, multiple residents near Benjamina Street called Triple Zero to report a man in the street armed with knives.



Paine said the 28-year-old had broken into two residences. “The man was confronted by occupants during those break-ins, and it’s alleged that he has stolen two large knives before moving out onto the street,” Paine said. The assistant commissioner said the man was reported to have had blood on him. Polair, the dog squad, and general and tactical officers were sent to the scene. Officers found the man armed with knives about 5.30pm at a nearby roundabout connecting Hardy Road, Foster Road and Lizard Street.



Paine said the roundabout was a “busy residential and traffic area”, and officers first yelled out to the man to drop the weapons, before trying to use their vehicles to block his exits. Far Northern Region Assistant Commissioner Graeme Paine. Queensland Police “The male person was still mobile and still in possession of the knives,” Paine said. Three officers fired at the man, he said. A 50-year-old woman standing by the front door of her nearby property was struck by a stray bullet in the lower leg.



Paine said the 28-year-old man was shot in the elbow and upper leg, suffering “serious but non-life-threatening injuries”. No police officers were injured during the incident. The assistant commissioner would not be drawn on whether the 28-year-old had been moving towards the three officers when they opened fire, but he said he was satisfied they had responded appropriately. “The officers were confronted with a very challenging situation – a dynamic situation with a significant threat level,” Paine said. He said the incident would be “holistically” investigated by the Ethical Standards Command.



“There will be significant investigative strategies implemented, and that will incorporate everything from the versions of the officers, witness statements [and] CCTV.” The Queensland Police Union issued a statement on Saturday night confirming it was providing on-the-ground support for the three officers. Investigations into the alleged break-ins on Benjamina Street were also continuing on Sunday. Police declared crime scenes at the two homes on Saturday, with forensic specialists examining the properties on Sunday morning. Paine said he could not detail anything else that might have been taken from the homes, and urged anyone who had dashcam or CCTV footage, or who might have heard anything, to come forward. World.title: Battered, bruised, then banned from seeing her kids. How did Virginia Giuffre get here?
World.content:
Every day, inside the Perth Magistrates Court, judges make decisions that have life-changing consequences. For Virginia Giuffre, one made without her knowledge on January 14, 2025, was especially devastating. On January 9, the prominent Jeffrey Epstein accuser was allegedly assaulted by her husband, Robbie Giuffre, during a family holiday in coastal town Dunsborough, in Western Australia. Bruised and battered, Virginia later went to the local hospital, alleging he cracked her sternum. When Robbie walked out of the court five days later, it was with a family violence restraining order. But it wasn’t against him. Instead, Virginia had been banned from seeing their children for six months. How?



That question is what Good Weekend senior writer and Walkley Award-winner Melissa Fyfe, and WAtoday journalist Carla Hildebrandt, examine in episode three of The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald’s investigative podcast, Virginia. Robbie had not been charged with assault by police following the events of January 9, but they did serve him with a 72-hour restraining order.



That expired just hours before Robbie went inside the court on January 14, but that information wasn’t disclosed to the magistrate – nor was an incident in Colorado in 2015, when Robbie was charged with assault, jailed and temporarily banned from seeing Virginia by local law enforcement. Related Article Visual story

Domestic violence ‘Mommy pls call’: The secret ‘scrapbook’ of Virginia Giuffre Like many services in Western Australia, the Perth Magistrates Court is under strain from the sheer scale of domestic violence. WA Police attend about 80,000 family and domestic violence related call-outs each year, or one every six minutes. In 2024, the Australian Bureau of Statistics found the state had Australia’s worst rate of family and domestic assaults. In the 20-minute ex parte hearing – done in the absence of alleged abusers in the interest of keeping victims safe – Robbie told the magistrate that he feared Virginia and that his children were at risk.



The magistrate heard Robbie’s case and granted him the order, which meant Virginia couldn’t return home or contact her two youngest children, who were aged 15 and 17, for six months. Virginia and Robbie Giuffre in Europe in October 2023, 18 months before her death. Instagram Virginia sent messages about her marriage to family and friends after the January 2025 incident. Instagram “[The six-month family violence restraining order] was the worst thing that could have happened to her,” says Amanda Roberts, who is married to Virginia’s brother Sky Roberts. “Her children were her life … That was the biggest damage that was done.”



Immediately once she found out, Virginia objected to the order. But because of delays, Virginia’s court hearing was set for six months later, on July 11, 2025. The same length as the order itself. Virginia died before that hearing could take place. New episodes of Virginia are released every Saturday across The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age, WAToday, or wherever you get your podcasts. Listen to the third episode – where hosts Fyfe and Hildebrandt reveal how Virginia and Robbie’s family life in Perth ended in such a bitter place, the contents of Robbie’s seven-page affidavit that made the family violence order possible, and how the Australian legal system is failing domestic violence victims – in the player above, or click here.



A statement released to us by Robbie’s lawyer says: “Due to Virginia’s behaviour in January 2025, it was necessary for the courts to impose protective measures to safeguard Robert and the children from harm.” Robbie’s lawyer also said in a statement that Virginia suffered “significant mental health issues and overreliance on prescription medication” due to the pressure of being in the public eye, and that “this may have led to Virginia’s change of perspective.” Robbie was limited in responding to “various unfounded allegations,” for legal reasons, the statement says, but he and the children just want to “remember Virginia as a loving wife and mother.” If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: Chickens, Chairman Mao and spiced tea with the neighbours: Welcome to ‘the real China’
World.content:
WorldAsiaChina relations Chickens, Chairman Mao and spiced tea with the neighbours: Welcome to ‘the real China’ Lisa Visentin July 26, 2026 — 9:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What in the World, a free weekly newsletter from our foreign correspondents, is sent every Thursday. Below is an excerpt. Sign up to get the whole newsletter delivered to your inbox. Xingming village, China: Perched atop a hill in a small village in central China, Li Zhiying’s family guesthouse has a spectacular view. Just beyond the front door is a vista of a pristine reservoir, ringed by pine forests and framed by mountain ranges flossed with low-hanging clouds. Li Zhiying grew up in poverty in Hunan province in central China and later returned to his hometown to open a guesthouse. Lisa Visentin Along the cul-de-sac that winds past his house, Li’s neighbours tend crops of beans, chillies, pumpkin and corn in small plots near their homes.



Village dogs bark and scrap in the street and chickens roam freely. By the roadside, an elderly man is picking the Sichuan peppercorns that will spice the tea and tingle the tongues of neighbours who will pop by in the evening for a daily ritual of gossip and card-playing. I’ve come to Li’s hometown of Xingming in China’s central Hunan province to spend three days exploring a different side of the modern China story that frequently makes headlines. The ordinariness of rural life. Xingming village, in Hunan Province, central China. Lisa Visentin A snapshot of the so-called “real China” that’s more representative of everyday life for millions of Chinese people than dancing robots, drone light shows and the breakneck speed of AI development that is reshaping tech hubs in Beijing, Shenzhen and Hangzhou. The evening I arrive, we wander down the street to the home of the retired village party secretary, a local Communist Party official, whose wife is serving slices of watermelon and tea in plastic cups to any neighbour who stops for a chat.



“Hello Australia, welcome, please enjoy our village,” one elder tells me, using a translation app. Neighbours pop by in the evening for a daily ritual of gossip and card-playing. Lisa Visentin This is Chairman Mao country, where portraits of China’s former supreme leader hang in the homes of older villagers, his reputation unspoiled by history’s verdict – in the West at least – of the calamity caused by the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution. “Mao is like a god to us,” a local party cadre from the neighbouring province tells me over lunch at the guesthouse. “He understood the ordinary people.” The nearest market is 5 kilometres away in a small, unremarkable township, where everyone is curious about the visiting foreigner (me). There’s plenty of pointing and waving and lots of smiles.



“Never!” an old villager running a pork stall responds when I ask how often foreigners come to the market. Nearby, a man is loading hunks of fresh meat into the boot of his car lined with just a piece of cardboard. Another vendor is selling a freshly slaughtered whole dog, its fur shaved off but skin intact. It’s a confronting sight for the uninitiated, though Li tells me he has never seen dog meat for sale here before. By his own admission, Li forewarns would-be guests that his home is located in a remote rural village that most Chinese people have never heard of. There’s no tourist infrastructure, and quotidian village life is slow-paced and perhaps even boring.



“If you are looking for a comfortable, easy introduction to China, this may not be the place,” he says on the guesthouse website. But he believes visitors will be charmed by the warmth and authenticity of the locals, and the unrefined beauty of the Chinese countryside. Li Zhiying and his friend, Li Mi, paddling on the reservoir that sustains the local village. Lisa Visentin For the most part, this is not the side of China that has bedazzled the wave of influencers who have arrived under the government’s soft-power masterstroke of visa-free travel, which has now been extended to more than 70 countries, Australia included. They have flooded Instagram and TikTok with effusive videos about China’s smartphone-powered megacities, with a cashless economy, gleaming skyscrapers, robots that deliver food to the hotel door, and futuristic electric vehicles that cruise silently around clean streets.



The comparison is stark. There’s little tangible wealth in villages such as Xingming, but community bonds are strong. People eat what they grow, or fish from the reservoir, and share what they have with their neighbours. Some of the older generation speak patchy Mandarin, preferring their local dialect. This has tethered them to their home province and added to the language barriers with outsiders who arrive, as I have, reliant on AI tools to navigate them. ChatGPT, though an impressive translator, struggles with dialects. Villagers fish from the reservoir. Lisa Visentin Younger people, meanwhile, have decamped for the cities looking for work, often leaving behind their children to be raised by their grandparents. “My children have gone to work in the 3D printing industry,” one woman says, as she picks beans from her garden while her granddaughter plays nearby.



But the crushing poverty that once afflicted Xingming, and mired families such as Li’s in destitution, has largely been eliminated. To get to Xingming from Beijing, it’s a five-hour journey on high-speed rail to the nearest station in Yueyang – a small, lower-tier city by Chinese standards with only 5 million people (about the size of Sydney). Then it’s an hour-long drive through the countryside. I’ve come specifically to meet Li, a softly spoken 36-year-old architect turned aspiring AI developer, whose life has skirted the same grooves as China’s own recent trajectory in many ways. Portraits of Mao Zedong are a common sight in the homes of older residents in parts of rural China. Lisa Visentin He rose out of poverty off the back of China’s economic juggernaut, which from the 1990s onwards lifted hundreds of millions of people like him with it. Li then crested the wave of the country’s property boom before crashing with its collapse, shuttering his own construction company within six months of opening it in 2022.



Since then, he’s looked for ways to reinvent himself, firstly in e-commerce, joining a friend’s large online company selling adult products to consumers all over the world on platforms like Amazon and Taobao – a lucrative pivot that was especially profitable in the US market until US President Donald Trump’s tariff war upended global supply chains. Now he’s dabbling in the emerging tech economy, splitting his time between Xingming and Shenzhen – the gravitational epicentre of China’s entrepreneurial classes – where he is teaching himself AI and building a small online game. At the same time, he has been running the guesthouse. The 14-bedroom homestay is a relatively new addition to Xingming, one he designed himself, overseeing its construction in 2016 during the runaway years of China’s real estate bubble. To build it, he scrimped, saved and borrowed money from friends in a bid to deliver on his parents’ dream for their son to return home and share his success with the family. Its minimalist open-plan aesthetic – with sharp lines, exposed brick, timber panelling and floor-to-ceiling glass windows – is a strikingly incongruous landmark in the small village.



It’s also an unrecognisable improvement on the basic brick flat that once stood in the same spot and where his mother cooked over an open wood stove that doubled as heating. As a child, his family was too poor to afford a bicycle, so he and his brother walked two hours through the mountains to attend school, a journey they made twice a week, sleeping at the school quarters in between. “We could only afford to eat meat a handful of times a year. As for clothes, we often wore the same clothes for five or six years, unless we literally outgrew them,” he tells me. “I think everyone in China has felt the economic growth, and people in rural areas have felt it very noticeably too. North Asia correspondent Lisa Visentin has lunch with Li Zhiying’s family and neighbours at the guesthouse in Xingming village. “If you had visited rural China 30 years ago, there was basically not a single paved or asphalt road in most rural areas. All the toilets in the countryside were simple pit latrines. Our waste was used to fertilise the vegetables.”



These days the roads are sealed, and the village has reliable power and sewerage systems. Many of his neighbours have rebuilt bigger, multi-storey houses in recent years, and many families have at least one car. Li’s ticket out was that he was academically gifted, won a scholarship to study architectural design at university and was supported by government policies that helped low-income families. He graduated into a rapacious property market, at one point securing a well-paid job with Country Garden, China’s biggest real estate developer. Related Article China relations Not a solo performance, but a symphony: What China’s leader thinks about AI Laden with billions of dollars of debt, Country Garden has been teetering on the brink of collapse since 2023. Its crisis, along with the implosion of other major developers, has hollowed out China’s middle-class wealth and left an economic wound so deep that even the nation’s breakout AI industries haven’t come close to healing it. When Li’s guesthouse first opened before COVID-19 hit, it was fully booked on weekends, but since then, the slow post-pandemic recovery and lagging domestic economy have seen bookings dwindle as Chinese consumers sit on their savings.



During my stay last weekend, I was the only guest, although more travellers arrived the day I checked out. As China opens up to foreign tourists, Li hopes more will find their way to villages such as Xingming. “If you travel China, 70 to 80 per cent of the places are like this. It is also very beautiful here. Although the big cities are also a real part of China, this is what China truly is.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: This revolutionary rule change would kick-start global domination for NRL
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion This revolutionary rule change would kick-start global domination for NRL Roy Masters Sports Columnist July 26, 2026 — 9:30am

July 26, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NRL boss Peter V’landys thinks big. So, here is a radical, revolutionary suggestion for him to capitalise on his $5.3 billion broadcasting rights war chest and achieve his dream of “global domination” for the code: Allow one attacking kick, or a forward pass, to an offside receiver per set of six tackles. NRL halfbacks are so accurate at finding wingers, often on the run, with pinpoint kicks. They can execute with the boot what an NFL quarterback can with a pass to a deep, wide receiver. Allowing one kick per set to an attacking player in an offside position would make the game more attractive to overseas markets. Getty Images Consider the scenario of, say, tackle three in an NRL game with one offside kick/pass per set. A pair of outside backs rush downfield, quickly followed by defenders. Instead of kicking the ball, the half decides to pass it laterally against a depleted defensive line. The ball is then carried deep into opposition territory. The attack still has the one kick to an offside player to use. If the ball is caught and grounded in goal by a teammate who was onside at tackle three, it’s a try. V’landys has nominated Europe, dominated by soccer, and the USA where NFL wide receivers score most touchdowns, as homes of NRL franchises in the year 2050.



Ask soccer supporters their problem with rugby league and they’ll say “passing backwards”. Ask NFL fans what they admire about rugby league and they’ll say, “playing without helmets and pads.” Allow one kick to a deep offside player per set of six, and the 13 aside game would appeal to Europeans and Americans. Most of the football codes (soccer/American football/Gaelic football) allow forward passes. Peter V’landys is a big thinker and has never been scared to make big calls in the game’s best interests. Dominic Lorrimer However, if V’landys wants to accelerate global domination, he has to apply my suggested rule change to his international franchises. Pay TV partner DAZN, the global streaming company which broadcasts rugby league via Foxtel, has 100 million subscribers. Nearly 30 years from today, it could broadcast the game’s best showing off their skills in New York, London or Miami.



However, back in Australia in the mid-2020s, let’s play with the rules and focus more on the Barassi Line than flirting with the advantage line. The line, named after former Australian Rules VFL champion Ron Barassi, refers to the territory divide between rugby union and league within the states otherwise dominated by Aussie Rules. An accurate NRL kicker could take on an NFL quarterback-style role. AP The line has moved well north of the Murray River since Melbourne academic Ian Turner coined the term in a lecture in 1978. The AFL has teams in NSW (Swans and GWS) and Queensland (Lions and Suns). However, unlike the NRL, which grants the same amount of money to all its 17 clubs, the AFL heavily subsides the Giants and Suns. Furthermore, the AFL pledged to spend 10 per cent of all football revenue on the grassroots game, and is targeting Queensland.



NSW Riverina towns such as Temora, which produced league stars like Liam Martin, Trent Barrett, Zac Lomax and Ryan Hinchcliffe, now have an even split between rugby league and AFL. Yet when their fathers played, the 13-a-side code was dominant. There is some irony in V’landys boasting the NRL’s TV deal has bested the AFL’s contract and then investing in overseas expansion, while the AFL raids the game at home. Zac Lomax would be a beneficiary of my suggested rule change. Getty Images The AFL is on the back foot with the women’s game. Chair Craig Drummond was shocked on the morning of May 15 when he learned that the TV ratings for the second women’s State of Origin match eclipsed the AFL’s top game (Lions vs Geelong) played the same Thursday, 1,009,000 to 663,000. And NRLW will continue to eclipse the TV ratings of AFLW, especially when it moves to two full rounds and is potentially screened midweek. However, the major reason the NRL must invest its TV windfall result in development is to deepen the player talent pool.



NRL players are great athletes but many lack football IQ. Some games produce more tries bombed than scored. Ask any former players the following question: is the top 36 at your club as good as it was 10 years ago? I have posed it many times recently, and the replies were mainly in the negative. Those who prevaricated conceded defence as a skill, as in both tackling and positional play, has declined. Injuries have exposed a weakness in depth at most clubs. The NRL will expand to 18 teams next year with the inclusion of Perth; 19 the following year with the addition of PNG, and is anticipated to move to 20 soon after. We need an extra 108 players to field these three clubs at a time the talent pathways are not producing players as skilful as a decade ago. The choice of Christchurch as the 20th team would certainly help because it would harvest rugby union players. Another source for the NRL is Victoria, where the game broke through the Barassi Line in 1998 and established the Melbourne Storm. The club has been one of the benchmarks in the competition for generating commercial revenues, but has consistently lobbied the NRL for increased investment in participation and pathways to grow the game in Victoria.



Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Benji Marshall has total control at the Tigers. The club thinks that needs to change Danny Weidler Sport columnist Perhaps that’s why the Storm are considering partnering with private equity to raise funds. Cynics would suggest private equity is traditionally interested in profit and the money would be better coming from V’landys’ war chest. Recently departed NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo was always confident he would land a big TV deal. “I knew that our growth strategy would work and that the fundamental valuation would be strong,” he said. “So being able to get the timing right, having implemented the strategy first, was an advantage to us.” The AFL will also go to the broadcasting market with an expansionist strategy in approximately three years, just as V’landys secured his $5.3b during the AFL’s current deal (2025-31).



After all, the most important TV deal is always, as Abdo suggests, the next one. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Iran war spreads to Red Sea and Caspian, Gulf quiet as US forgoes strikes
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Iran war spreads to Red Sea and Caspian, Gulf quiet as US forgoes strikes Raphael Satter and Lefteris Papadimas July 26, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Signs of the Iran war’s spread emerged this weekend despite a pause in US strikes, as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Saudi oil installations along the Red Sea coast and Iran accused Ukraine of targeting an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea. The US military said on Saturday (Washington time) that its naval blockade against Iran “remains in full effect” but did not explain why it halted a streak of 13 nights of escalating strikes. Asked about the pause, a senior official in Donald Trump’s administration said the US president “has always been clear that his preference is diplomacy, but he has shown Iran what will happen if they fail to come to the table in a serious way”. There were also no reports of attacks from Iran on neighbouring countries, like those that have been taking place daily in response to the US attacks. Houthi supporters hold a rally in Sanaa, Yemen, this month against the Saudi-led coalition. The banner in Arabic reads, “All Saudi oil facilities are targets to our missiles and drones”. AP Photo/Osamah Abdulrahman On Friday, Trump told US news site Axios he was considering a “massive attack” on Iran to force it to negotiate a peace deal. But The New York Times reported on Saturday (New York time) that the president had set aside those plans, at least for now, amid concern that ramping up the war could dangerously drain the Pentagon’s shrinking inventory of Patriot interceptors and other air defences.



Despite the lull in the Gulf, fighting between Iran’s Houthi allies and Saudi Arabia on Saturday indicated the war, which has already disrupted energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz,

could affect a second major shipping route and reignite Yemen’s civil war. Related Article Updated

Middle East at war Trump warns of ‘massive attack’ on Iran, Australians urged to rethink travel plans Separately, Iran’s Foreign Ministry accused Ukraine of attacking an Iranian commercial vessel in the ​Caspian Sea, saying it resulted in an explosion that killed ‌a sailor and injured another. Earlier on Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky used a social media post to praise the results of “long-range strikes” in the Caspian Sea, alluding to vessels shipping military cargo, but did not identify the nationality of the targets. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group struck sites belonging to Saudi state oil company Aramco in Jizan and Yanbu. Video shared on social media showed a large column of smoke rising from the direction of the Aramco refinery in Jizan.



Two Asia-based trading sources said they had been informed of potential damage to fuel and oil storage sites at Jizan. Aramco did not respond to requests for comment. In Yanbu, two ballistic missiles aimed at oil installations were intercepted by a US-made Patriot battery operated in Saudi Arabia by the Greek military under an agreement with Riyadh, Greek security sources said. Loading Yanbu, Saudi Arabia’s main Red Sea oil port, has become a key route for Saudi oil skirting the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has blockaded. Up to 400,000 barrels can be processed daily at the oil refinery in Jizan, a city on the Red Sea close to the Yemeni border. In Yemen, the air force of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, which has opposed the Houthis for more than a decade, struck Houthi launch sites and arms depots in the

Marib and al-Jawf provinces, Yemeni officials said.



Earlier, the Saudi-led military alliance said it bombed Houthi military positions on Friday in the Red Sea port of Hodeidah. The Yemeni officials said both sides in Yemen’s civil war were mobilising forces along the front. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea is another crucial global shipping passage. Graphic: Nathan Perri Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling the Houthis for more than a decade since the Iran-aligned fighters captured Yemen’s capital, Sanaa. The Yemeni civil war, during which hundreds of thousands of people died from fighting and famine, has been paused under a ceasefire since 2022. But that truce broke down this month, with the Houthis effectively joining the wider war their Iranian allies have waged since being attacked by the US and Israel.



The Houthis have declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia over the past week, and Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi said all Saudi oil facilities could be targets. On Thursday, the Houthis struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea. American forces recently resumed their own blockade on Iranian ports. US Central Command, whose coverage area includes the Middle East, said it disabled a ship whose crew attempted to run the blockade despite “repeated warnings” on Friday in the Gulf of Oman. An interim truce effectively collapsed two weeks ago, with US forces striking targets in southern Iran in response to Iranian disruption of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. On Friday, Trump said the ‌US and Iran were in talks to ​negotiate an end ​to their conflict, but ⁠repeated that Tehran ​was not yet ready ​for a deal. World.title: Tim Tszyu almost quit boxing. Now he has the chance to cement his legacy
World.content:
SportBoxingWorld Boxing Tim Tszyu almost quit boxing. Now he has the chance to cement his legacy Adrian Proszenko July 26, 2026 — 9:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There was once a time, when his record was unblemished, that boxer Tim Tszyu spoke about retiring his opponents. And yet, it wasn’t so long ago that Tszyu himself almost quit. Worn down by boxing politics, family fractures and a series of beat-downs – including the loss of his world title belt – the Sydney-based pugilist lost the love of a sport that has been his life. Loading “It wasn’t from my losses,” Tszyu explained. “To a certain extent it was the politics of sport, I was thinking, ‘This is not worth it.’ “I joined the sport for the love of it, the thrill of it, the challenge of it. There are a lot of obstacles at certain times trying to stop me from doing that.



“That’s a time when I was thinking of retirement and giving it up … I won’t go into detail, it was just life.” There were several low points. His first loss, at short notice, to Sebastian Fundora, in which a horrific head cut cost him a chance of retaining the WBO super-welterweight world title he had wanted so much. His devastating knockout defeat to Russian Bakhram Murtazaliev, followed by a subsequent KO loss in his rematch with Fundora. Tim Tszyu shadow boxes ahead of his fight against Errol Spence Jnr. Sam Mooy “There were a lot of people in the change room after victory in the Tony Harrison fight, a lot of people for that,” Tszyu recalled, referring to his defeat of the American in 2023 to claim the interim WBO super welterweight belt. “But after what I went through in the Bakhram fight, there weren’t many people in the hospital, let’s just say that. You learn who is there and who is not. You learn about the ugly truth about the sport.”



But Tszyu’s decision to endure has been rewarded. After overhauling his mindset and team – legendary boxer-turned-trainer Jeff Fenech is in his corner – Tszyu will on Sunday step into the ring for the biggest fight of his career. The 31-year-old will take on Errol “The Truth” Spence Jnr in a blockbuster middleweight bout at Sydney’s Afterpay Arena. Spence is a future hall-of-famer, whose only loss was against Terence “Bud” Crawford, who became the first undisputed welterweight champion of the four-belt era. Tim Tszyu is ready for business. Sam Mooy While a world title isn’t at stake, it is a chance for Tszyu to take on the opponent who has been at the top of his hit list. “This is way bigger than a world title,” Tszyu said. “This is hall-of-fame status, we’re talking about one of the fighters of our generation. I get to take him on and cement myself. It’s a blessing.”



When he first rose to prominence, Tszyu was dubbed “The Soul Taker”. But after a wretched run that included three loses in four fights, he has been rebranded as “The Phoenix”. “All these nicknames – I’m Tim Tszyu,” he said. “The Phoenix was like a new chapter in my life to burn from the ashes from what happened and go onto the new. That’s what it is, this new phase of my life.” Tim Tszyu poses for a photograph at the Overseas Passenger Terminal ahead of the fight against Errol “The Truth” Spence Jr. on Sunday. Sam Mooy After a series of team changes, in a bid to start “controlling the narrative more” in his career, Tszyu has settled on Fenech as his mentor. “There’s not many people you can ask for advice who have been there and done that,” Tszyu said. “I’ve never been in a team where someone has felt exactly what I felt.”



It appears a peculiar comment given his father is hall-of-famer Kostya Tszyu, while his brother Nikita is an undefeated fighter closing in on his own world title shot. However, except for grandfather Boris – “he’s stayed with me through thick and thin” – Tszyu has a complex relationship with his family. Kostya has for a long time lived in Russia, there has been a falling out with Nikita and there has been tension with others who were close to him. Errol Spence Jnr has arrived in Sydney in supreme shape. Sam Mooy “Everyone goes through different issues in their families,” Tszyu said. “We are going to get through this fight and then we need to sit down and hug it out.” Fenech, a hall-of-famer who won four world titles in four weight divisions, has noticed a change in Tszyu since becoming his trainer.



“The person I saw in Tim prior to this is someone who had 110 things in his head, said some stupid things about opponents,” Fenech said. “I told him the only thing that will sell fights is not publicity, it’s not shit talk. Your fists will sell fights. “I’m not trying to change Tim. I’m just trying to make him a better Tim. The one thing I have changed is I have a happy guy.” Errol “The Truth” Spence Jr. shadow boxes at the Overseas Passenger Terminal. Sam Mooy Given Spence’s long lay-off – he hasn’t fought for three years – and Tszyu’s poor record in big fights, the loser could be forced into premature retirement. Having previously contemplated walking away from the sport, the Australian believes he is about to leave his mark on it. “I still believed in myself, I still got through it,” Tszyu said. “And here we are, on the verge of doing something special.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Sydney teens are looking back to the ’90s to ‘live in the moment’
World.content:
Olive Berlach, 15, in her bedroom filled with DIY items and mixed media.

Despite their digital childhoods – or perhaps because of it – many young people are increasingly rejecting technology and embracing analog culture.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In 15-year-old Olive Berlach’s Central Coast bedroom, knick-knacks from a distant era live strewn across every surface and wall. A Dirty Dancing vinyl, stacks of CDs, a Vogue magazine collection, jars of sea glass and shells, a Luke’s Diner coaster from Gilmore Girls, a lamp with coloured scarves sewn into it and posters of teen heartthrobs (young Johnny Depp and Australian singer Ruel). Olive wants to live like she’s “in the ’90s”. The front cover of her first self-published magazine, Olive, says it’s “for teens who want to live offline”. Inside, there’s a kaleidoscope of ideas and topics. There’s a pancake recipe you can cook at “your bestie’s house”, a profile on Allana Ferguson (Olive’s favourite rugby player), as well as Su-Elise Nash from 2000s girl band Mis-Teeq, ’90s fashion tips, a guide to a perfect screen-free day (and how to “put it down. Seriously”), a skincare edit and an interview with her mum, Emily. Olive reading her magazine, Olive. Audrey Richardson Olive is wearing an outfit inspired by a ’90s Katie Holmes, featured on the magazine page about ’90s street style. It’s pinned on her bedroom wall. Audrey Richardson With a dream to one day work at Vogue, Olive has spent two months putting together her first issue, which retails for $20 and costs roughly $8 to print. Olive sold out of her first run of 100 issues after one week – and is halfway through the second, called The Cosy Issue. “I am doing a photoshoot with my friends this weekend for the cover of the next issue. I interviewed Eleanor Pendleton. I’m doing a showcase with Luke Shadbolt’s photos. He was like an early noughties bodyboard photographer,” she says.



Olive, who doesn’t have a smartphone but uses a computer to create her magazine, says a lot of her peers are “really addicted to their phones”. “They’ll be like texting their boyfriends, scrolling TikTok while we’re hanging out, and I just don’t think that’s very fun, and I think there was a lot more freedom in the ’90s with not having the opinions of so many other people just pinging at you while you’re with your friends. “I just thought I would try to bring back living in the moment.” Teens like Olive have never known a world without social networks like Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and the phones that house them. They are, by all accounts, true digital natives – even as the Australian government has moved to change this through its world-first social media ban (the UK looks set to follow suit). In the six months since Australia’s social media ban came into effect, about 70 per cent of children retained their social media accounts – mostly because platforms hadn’t asked them to verify their age.



Despite this digital upbringing – or perhaps because of it – Generation Z (aged 14 to 29 today) are increasingly rejecting technology and embracing analog culture. Western Sydney high school students Phoenix Varu, Rettalia Fraser, and Wyntah Rose take a selfie during a photography lesson at UTS. Sitthixay Ditthavong They’re documenting the world through film and digital cameras, rejecting streaming services for CDs and DVDs and hand-writing letters. Many of these are marvels from an era they never knew. A recent study commissioned by music video platform Vevo of 1800 teens, evenly split across Australia, the US and UK, found 65 per cent of Gen Z feel nostalgic for a time in which they weren’t alive or were too young to notice (referred to as “borrowed nostalgia”), while one-third felt they were “born in the wrong generation”. And they are, despite what others may think, the generation most wary of AI, some emerging research suggests. Western Sydney high school students learning photography at UTS. Sitthixay Ditthavong According to a Gallup study from April, for example, Gen Z’s adoption of AI has remained steady in the past year, but enthusiasm for it is dropping and scepticism is on the rise.



For some teens, access to creative mediums is still a barrier. Inside a University of Technology Sydney workshop, 16-year-old Charmonix Vaatuitui from Liverpool has applied the finishing touches to her first short film, titled Plastic. Charmonix Vaatuitui, 16, inside UTS’ filmmaking lab. Sitthixay Ditthavong She created it via an incentive the university runs, whereby any student from western Sydney who completes the week-long creative course is guaranteed entry once they finish their HSC. They can choose from filmmaking, animation, photography and music production, all using the university’s equipment. “My film was just talking about how I feel very connected to my [Samoan and Tongan] culture; however, I can’t speak my language, and then I’m called plastic, which is basically [challenging the stereotype when people say], ‘Oh, you can’t speak your language or not that into your culture’, and just basically feeling ashamed of not being able to work on it,” Charmonix, who is in year 11, says. “Putting like all my thoughts and my own footage into a video has made me open my eyes.” Loading



The experience of learning a craft with her peers, socialising each day and having a reason to be off her phone has been a highlight for Charmonix, who wants to keep pursuing filmmaking but sees herself in the media industry. “Not just having my head just straight into my phone and being out here, leaving home early, going home late, but also making new friends like on the way there’s actually there; it helps with my personal identity,” she says. “It’s not like I did it because I was forced to do it … I wanted to actually make a film about myself.” She has since made another short film based on her and her boyfriend. While Charmonix has begun learning how to create a popular medium, every Saturday afternoon, 17-year-old Arlo Temple spends hours cultivating a centuries-old craft. Sydney teen Arlo Temple, 17, has been learning the art of shoemaking at Sydney School of Footwear for three years. Sitthixay Ditthavong The year 11 student is learning the art of cordwainery (bespoke shoemaking done entirely by hand) at Sydney School of Footwear in Leichhardt – albeit with a modern twist.

World.title: Woman caught in crossfire as police shoot armed man during stand-off
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCrime Woman caught in crossfire as police shoot armed man during stand-off Catherine Strohfeldt July 26, 2026 — 10:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A bystander to a tense police stand-off has been shot after officers discharged multiple rounds at a 28-year-old man carrying knives. Both a 50-year-old woman and the armed man suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries following the incident in the Cairns suburb of Mount Sheridan. Both remained in hospital on Sunday. Assistant Commissioner Graeme Paine said the “very dynamic” situation had escalated quickly. Loading About 5pm on Saturday, multiple residents near Benjamina Street called Triple Zero to report a man in the street armed with knives.



Paine said the 28-year-old had broken into two residences. “The man was confronted by occupants during those break-ins, and it’s alleged that he has stolen two large knives before moving out onto the street,” Paine said. The assistant commissioner said the man was reported to have had blood on him. Polair, the dog squad, and general and tactical officers were sent to the scene. Officers found the man armed with knives about 5.30pm at a nearby roundabout connecting Hardy Road, Foster Road and Lizard Street.



Paine said the roundabout was a “busy residential and traffic area”, and officers first yelled out to the man to drop the weapons, before trying to use their vehicles to block his exits. Far Northern Region Assistant Commissioner Graeme Paine. Queensland Police “The male person was still mobile and still in possession of the knives,” Paine said. Three officers fired at the man, he said. A 50-year-old woman standing by the front door of her nearby property was struck by a stray bullet in the lower leg.



Paine said the 28-year-old man was shot in the elbow and upper leg, suffering “serious but non-life-threatening injuries”. No police officers were injured during the incident. The assistant commissioner would not be drawn on whether the 28-year-old had been moving towards the three officers when they opened fire, but he said he was satisfied they had responded appropriately. “The officers were confronted with a very challenging situation – a dynamic situation with a significant threat level,” Paine said. He said the incident would be “holistically” investigated by the Ethical Standards Command.



“There will be significant investigative strategies implemented, and that will incorporate everything from the versions of the officers, witness statements [and] CCTV.” The Queensland Police Union issued a statement on Saturday night confirming it was providing on-the-ground support for the three officers. Investigations into the alleged break-ins on Benjamina Street were also continuing on Sunday. Police declared crime scenes at the two homes on Saturday, with forensic specialists examining the properties on Sunday morning. Paine said he could not detail anything else that might have been taken from the homes, and urged anyone who had dashcam or CCTV footage, or who might have heard anything, to come forward. World.title: Battered, bruised, then banned from seeing her kids. How did Virginia Giuffre get here?
World.content:
Every day, inside the Perth Magistrates Court, judges make decisions that have life-changing consequences. For Virginia Giuffre, one made without her knowledge on January 14, 2025, was especially devastating. On January 9, the prominent Jeffrey Epstein accuser was allegedly assaulted by her husband, Robbie Giuffre, during a family holiday in coastal town Dunsborough, in Western Australia. Bruised and battered, Virginia later went to the local hospital, alleging he cracked her sternum. When Robbie walked out of the court five days later, it was with a family violence restraining order. But it wasn’t against him. Instead, Virginia had been banned from seeing their children for six months. How?



That question is what Good Weekend senior writer and Walkley Award-winner Melissa Fyfe, and WAtoday journalist Carla Hildebrandt, examine in episode three of The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald’s investigative podcast, Virginia. Robbie had not been charged with assault by police following the events of January 9, but they did serve him with a 72-hour restraining order.



That expired just hours before Robbie went inside the court on January 14, but that information wasn’t disclosed to the magistrate – nor was an incident in Colorado in 2015, when Robbie was charged with assault, jailed and temporarily banned from seeing Virginia by local law enforcement. Related Article Visual story

Domestic violence ‘Mommy pls call’: The secret ‘scrapbook’ of Virginia Giuffre Like many services in Western Australia, the Perth Magistrates Court is under strain from the sheer scale of domestic violence. WA Police attend about 80,000 family and domestic violence related call-outs each year, or one every six minutes. In 2024, the Australian Bureau of Statistics found the state had Australia’s worst rate of family and domestic assaults. In the 20-minute ex parte hearing – done in the absence of alleged abusers in the interest of keeping victims safe – Robbie told the magistrate that he feared Virginia and that his children were at risk.



The magistrate heard Robbie’s case and granted him the order, which meant Virginia couldn’t return home or contact her two youngest children, who were aged 15 and 17, for six months. Virginia and Robbie Giuffre in Europe in October 2023, 18 months before her death. Instagram Virginia sent messages about her marriage to family and friends after the January 2025 incident. Instagram “[The six-month family violence restraining order] was the worst thing that could have happened to her,” says Amanda Roberts, who is married to Virginia’s brother Sky Roberts. “Her children were her life … That was the biggest damage that was done.”



Immediately once she found out, Virginia objected to the order. But because of delays, Virginia’s court hearing was set for six months later, on July 11, 2025. The same length as the order itself. Virginia died before that hearing could take place. New episodes of Virginia are released every Saturday across The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age, WAToday, or wherever you get your podcasts. Listen to the third episode – where hosts Fyfe and Hildebrandt reveal how Virginia and Robbie’s family life in Perth ended in such a bitter place, the contents of Robbie’s seven-page affidavit that made the family violence order possible, and how the Australian legal system is failing domestic violence victims – in the player above, or click here.



A statement released to us by Robbie’s lawyer says: “Due to Virginia’s behaviour in January 2025, it was necessary for the courts to impose protective measures to safeguard Robert and the children from harm.” Robbie’s lawyer also said in a statement that Virginia suffered “significant mental health issues and overreliance on prescription medication” due to the pressure of being in the public eye, and that “this may have led to Virginia’s change of perspective.” Robbie was limited in responding to “various unfounded allegations,” for legal reasons, the statement says, but he and the children just want to “remember Virginia as a loving wife and mother.” If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: Chickens, Chairman Mao and spiced tea with the neighbours: Welcome to ‘the real China’
World.content:
WorldAsiaChina relations Chickens, Chairman Mao and spiced tea with the neighbours: Welcome to ‘the real China’ Lisa Visentin July 26, 2026 — 9:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What in the World, a free weekly newsletter from our foreign correspondents, is sent every Thursday. Below is an excerpt. Sign up to get the whole newsletter delivered to your inbox. Xingming village, China: Perched atop a hill in a small village in central China, Li Zhiying’s family guesthouse has a spectacular view. Just beyond the front door is a vista of a pristine reservoir, ringed by pine forests and framed by mountain ranges flossed with low-hanging clouds. Li Zhiying grew up in poverty in Hunan province in central China and later returned to his hometown to open a guesthouse. Lisa Visentin Along the cul-de-sac that winds past his house, Li’s neighbours tend crops of beans, chillies, pumpkin and corn in small plots near their homes.



Village dogs bark and scrap in the street and chickens roam freely. By the roadside, an elderly man is picking the Sichuan peppercorns that will spice the tea and tingle the tongues of neighbours who will pop by in the evening for a daily ritual of gossip and card-playing. I’ve come to Li’s hometown of Xingming in China’s central Hunan province to spend three days exploring a different side of the modern China story that frequently makes headlines. The ordinariness of rural life. Xingming village, in Hunan Province, central China. Lisa Visentin A snapshot of the so-called “real China” that’s more representative of everyday life for millions of Chinese people than dancing robots, drone light shows and the breakneck speed of AI development that is reshaping tech hubs in Beijing, Shenzhen and Hangzhou. The evening I arrive, we wander down the street to the home of the retired village party secretary, a local Communist Party official, whose wife is serving slices of watermelon and tea in plastic cups to any neighbour who stops for a chat.



“Hello Australia, welcome, please enjoy our village,” one elder tells me, using a translation app. Neighbours pop by in the evening for a daily ritual of gossip and card-playing. Lisa Visentin This is Chairman Mao country, where portraits of China’s former supreme leader hang in the homes of older villagers, his reputation unspoiled by history’s verdict – in the West at least – of the calamity caused by the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution. “Mao is like a god to us,” a local party cadre from the neighbouring province tells me over lunch at the guesthouse. “He understood the ordinary people.” The nearest market is 5 kilometres away in a small, unremarkable township, where everyone is curious about the visiting foreigner (me). There’s plenty of pointing and waving and lots of smiles.



“Never!” an old villager running a pork stall responds when I ask how often foreigners come to the market. Nearby, a man is loading hunks of fresh meat into the boot of his car lined with just a piece of cardboard. Another vendor is selling a freshly slaughtered whole dog, its fur shaved off but skin intact. It’s a confronting sight for the uninitiated, though Li tells me he has never seen dog meat for sale here before. By his own admission, Li forewarns would-be guests that his home is located in a remote rural village that most Chinese people have never heard of. There’s no tourist infrastructure, and quotidian village life is slow-paced and perhaps even boring.



“If you are looking for a comfortable, easy introduction to China, this may not be the place,” he says on the guesthouse website. But he believes visitors will be charmed by the warmth and authenticity of the locals, and the unrefined beauty of the Chinese countryside. Li Zhiying and his friend, Li Mi, paddling on the reservoir that sustains the local village. Lisa Visentin For the most part, this is not the side of China that has bedazzled the wave of influencers who have arrived under the government’s soft-power masterstroke of visa-free travel, which has now been extended to more than 70 countries, Australia included. They have flooded Instagram and TikTok with effusive videos about China’s smartphone-powered megacities, with a cashless economy, gleaming skyscrapers, robots that deliver food to the hotel door, and futuristic electric vehicles that cruise silently around clean streets.



The comparison is stark. There’s little tangible wealth in villages such as Xingming, but community bonds are strong. People eat what they grow, or fish from the reservoir, and share what they have with their neighbours. Some of the older generation speak patchy Mandarin, preferring their local dialect. This has tethered them to their home province and added to the language barriers with outsiders who arrive, as I have, reliant on AI tools to navigate them. ChatGPT, though an impressive translator, struggles with dialects. Villagers fish from the reservoir. Lisa Visentin Younger people, meanwhile, have decamped for the cities looking for work, often leaving behind their children to be raised by their grandparents. “My children have gone to work in the 3D printing industry,” one woman says, as she picks beans from her garden while her granddaughter plays nearby.



But the crushing poverty that once afflicted Xingming, and mired families such as Li’s in destitution, has largely been eliminated. To get to Xingming from Beijing, it’s a five-hour journey on high-speed rail to the nearest station in Yueyang – a small, lower-tier city by Chinese standards with only 5 million people (about the size of Sydney). Then it’s an hour-long drive through the countryside. I’ve come specifically to meet Li, a softly spoken 36-year-old architect turned aspiring AI developer, whose life has skirted the same grooves as China’s own recent trajectory in many ways. Portraits of Mao Zedong are a common sight in the homes of older residents in parts of rural China. Lisa Visentin He rose out of poverty off the back of China’s economic juggernaut, which from the 1990s onwards lifted hundreds of millions of people like him with it. Li then crested the wave of the country’s property boom before crashing with its collapse, shuttering his own construction company within six months of opening it in 2022.



Since then, he’s looked for ways to reinvent himself, firstly in e-commerce, joining a friend’s large online company selling adult products to consumers all over the world on platforms like Amazon and Taobao – a lucrative pivot that was especially profitable in the US market until US President Donald Trump’s tariff war upended global supply chains. Now he’s dabbling in the emerging tech economy, splitting his time between Xingming and Shenzhen – the gravitational epicentre of China’s entrepreneurial classes – where he is teaching himself AI and building a small online game. At the same time, he has been running the guesthouse. The 14-bedroom homestay is a relatively new addition to Xingming, one he designed himself, overseeing its construction in 2016 during the runaway years of China’s real estate bubble. To build it, he scrimped, saved and borrowed money from friends in a bid to deliver on his parents’ dream for their son to return home and share his success with the family. Its minimalist open-plan aesthetic – with sharp lines, exposed brick, timber panelling and floor-to-ceiling glass windows – is a strikingly incongruous landmark in the small village.



It’s also an unrecognisable improvement on the basic brick flat that once stood in the same spot and where his mother cooked over an open wood stove that doubled as heating. As a child, his family was too poor to afford a bicycle, so he and his brother walked two hours through the mountains to attend school, a journey they made twice a week, sleeping at the school quarters in between. “We could only afford to eat meat a handful of times a year. As for clothes, we often wore the same clothes for five or six years, unless we literally outgrew them,” he tells me. “I think everyone in China has felt the economic growth, and people in rural areas have felt it very noticeably too. North Asia correspondent Lisa Visentin has lunch with Li Zhiying’s family and neighbours at the guesthouse in Xingming village. “If you had visited rural China 30 years ago, there was basically not a single paved or asphalt road in most rural areas. All the toilets in the countryside were simple pit latrines. Our waste was used to fertilise the vegetables.”



These days the roads are sealed, and the village has reliable power and sewerage systems. Many of his neighbours have rebuilt bigger, multi-storey houses in recent years, and many families have at least one car. Li’s ticket out was that he was academically gifted, won a scholarship to study architectural design at university and was supported by government policies that helped low-income families. He graduated into a rapacious property market, at one point securing a well-paid job with Country Garden, China’s biggest real estate developer. Related Article China relations Not a solo performance, but a symphony: What China’s leader thinks about AI Laden with billions of dollars of debt, Country Garden has been teetering on the brink of collapse since 2023. Its crisis, along with the implosion of other major developers, has hollowed out China’s middle-class wealth and left an economic wound so deep that even the nation’s breakout AI industries haven’t come close to healing it. When Li’s guesthouse first opened before COVID-19 hit, it was fully booked on weekends, but since then, the slow post-pandemic recovery and lagging domestic economy have seen bookings dwindle as Chinese consumers sit on their savings.



During my stay last weekend, I was the only guest, although more travellers arrived the day I checked out. As China opens up to foreign tourists, Li hopes more will find their way to villages such as Xingming. “If you travel China, 70 to 80 per cent of the places are like this. It is also very beautiful here. Although the big cities are also a real part of China, this is what China truly is.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
