China Lisa Visentin is the North Asia correspondent for The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age based in Beijing. She was previously a federal political correspondent based in Canberra. or email. Connect via X

World.title: This revolutionary rule change would kick-start global domination for NRL
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion This revolutionary rule change would kick-start global domination for NRL Roy Masters Sports Columnist July 26, 2026 — 9:30am

July 26, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NRL boss Peter V’landys thinks big. So, here is a radical, revolutionary suggestion for him to capitalise on his $5.3 billion broadcasting rights war chest and achieve his dream of “global domination” for the code: Allow one attacking kick, or a forward pass, to an offside receiver per set of six tackles. NRL halfbacks are so accurate at finding wingers, often on the run, with pinpoint kicks. They can execute with the boot what an NFL quarterback can with a pass to a deep, wide receiver. Allowing one kick per set to an attacking player in an offside position would make the game more attractive to overseas markets. Getty Images Consider the scenario of, say, tackle three in an NRL game with one offside kick/pass per set. A pair of outside backs rush downfield, quickly followed by defenders. Instead of kicking the ball, the half decides to pass it laterally against a depleted defensive line. The ball is then carried deep into opposition territory. The attack still has the one kick to an offside player to use. If the ball is caught and grounded in goal by a teammate who was onside at tackle three, it’s a try. V’landys has nominated Europe, dominated by soccer, and the USA where NFL wide receivers score most touchdowns, as homes of NRL franchises in the year 2050.



Ask soccer supporters their problem with rugby league and they’ll say “passing backwards”. Ask NFL fans what they admire about rugby league and they’ll say, “playing without helmets and pads.” Allow one kick to a deep offside player per set of six, and the 13 aside game would appeal to Europeans and Americans. Most of the football codes (soccer/American football/Gaelic football) allow forward passes. Peter V’landys is a big thinker and has never been scared to make big calls in the game’s best interests. Dominic Lorrimer However, if V’landys wants to accelerate global domination, he has to apply my suggested rule change to his international franchises. Pay TV partner DAZN, the global streaming company which broadcasts rugby league via Foxtel, has 100 million subscribers. Nearly 30 years from today, it could broadcast the game’s best showing off their skills in New York, London or Miami.



However, back in Australia in the mid-2020s, let’s play with the rules and focus more on the Barassi Line than flirting with the advantage line. The line, named after former Australian Rules VFL champion Ron Barassi, refers to the territory divide between rugby union and league within the states otherwise dominated by Aussie Rules. An accurate NRL kicker could take on an NFL quarterback-style role. AP The line has moved well north of the Murray River since Melbourne academic Ian Turner coined the term in a lecture in 1978. The AFL has teams in NSW (Swans and GWS) and Queensland (Lions and Suns). However, unlike the NRL, which grants the same amount of money to all its 17 clubs, the AFL heavily subsides the Giants and Suns. Furthermore, the AFL pledged to spend 10 per cent of all football revenue on the grassroots game, and is targeting Queensland.



NSW Riverina towns such as Temora, which produced league stars like Liam Martin, Trent Barrett, Zac Lomax and Ryan Hinchcliffe, now have an even split between rugby league and AFL. Yet when their fathers played, the 13-a-side code was dominant. There is some irony in V’landys boasting the NRL’s TV deal has bested the AFL’s contract and then investing in overseas expansion, while the AFL raids the game at home. Zac Lomax would be a beneficiary of my suggested rule change. Getty Images The AFL is on the back foot with the women’s game. Chair Craig Drummond was shocked on the morning of May 15 when he learned that the TV ratings for the second women’s State of Origin match eclipsed the AFL’s top game (Lions vs Geelong) played the same Thursday, 1,009,000 to 663,000. And NRLW will continue to eclipse the TV ratings of AFLW, especially when it moves to two full rounds and is potentially screened midweek. However, the major reason the NRL must invest its TV windfall result in development is to deepen the player talent pool.



NRL players are great athletes but many lack football IQ. Some games produce more tries bombed than scored. Ask any former players the following question: is the top 36 at your club as good as it was 10 years ago? I have posed it many times recently, and the replies were mainly in the negative. Those who prevaricated conceded defence as a skill, as in both tackling and positional play, has declined. Injuries have exposed a weakness in depth at most clubs. The NRL will expand to 18 teams next year with the inclusion of Perth; 19 the following year with the addition of PNG, and is anticipated to move to 20 soon after. We need an extra 108 players to field these three clubs at a time the talent pathways are not producing players as skilful as a decade ago. The choice of Christchurch as the 20th team would certainly help because it would harvest rugby union players. Another source for the NRL is Victoria, where the game broke through the Barassi Line in 1998 and established the Melbourne Storm. The club has been one of the benchmarks in the competition for generating commercial revenues, but has consistently lobbied the NRL for increased investment in participation and pathways to grow the game in Victoria.



Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Benji Marshall has total control at the Tigers. The club thinks that needs to change Danny Weidler Sport columnist Perhaps that’s why the Storm are considering partnering with private equity to raise funds. Cynics would suggest private equity is traditionally interested in profit and the money would be better coming from V’landys’ war chest. Recently departed NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo was always confident he would land a big TV deal. “I knew that our growth strategy would work and that the fundamental valuation would be strong,” he said. “So being able to get the timing right, having implemented the strategy first, was an advantage to us.” The AFL will also go to the broadcasting market with an expansionist strategy in approximately three years, just as V’landys secured his $5.3b during the AFL’s current deal (2025-31).



After all, the most important TV deal is always, as Abdo suggests, the next one. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Iran war spreads to Red Sea and Caspian, Gulf quiet as US forgoes strikes
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Iran war spreads to Red Sea and Caspian, Gulf quiet as US forgoes strikes Raphael Satter and Lefteris Papadimas July 26, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Signs of the Iran war’s spread emerged this weekend despite a pause in US strikes, as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Saudi oil installations along the Red Sea coast and Iran accused Ukraine of targeting an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea. The US military said on Saturday (Washington time) that its naval blockade against Iran “remains in full effect” but did not explain why it halted a streak of 13 nights of escalating strikes. Asked about the pause, a senior official in Donald Trump’s administration said the US president “has always been clear that his preference is diplomacy, but he has shown Iran what will happen if they fail to come to the table in a serious way”. There were also no reports of attacks from Iran on neighbouring countries, like those that have been taking place daily in response to the US attacks. Houthi supporters hold a rally in Sanaa, Yemen, this month against the Saudi-led coalition. The banner in Arabic reads, “All Saudi oil facilities are targets to our missiles and drones”. AP Photo/Osamah Abdulrahman On Friday, Trump told US news site Axios he was considering a “massive attack” on Iran to force it to negotiate a peace deal. But The New York Times reported on Saturday (New York time) that the president had set aside those plans, at least for now, amid concern that ramping up the war could dangerously drain the Pentagon’s shrinking inventory of Patriot interceptors and other air defences.



Despite the lull in the Gulf, fighting between Iran’s Houthi allies and Saudi Arabia on Saturday indicated the war, which has already disrupted energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz,

could affect a second major shipping route and reignite Yemen’s civil war. Related Article Updated

Middle East at war Trump warns of ‘massive attack’ on Iran, Australians urged to rethink travel plans Separately, Iran’s Foreign Ministry accused Ukraine of attacking an Iranian commercial vessel in the ​Caspian Sea, saying it resulted in an explosion that killed ‌a sailor and injured another. Earlier on Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky used a social media post to praise the results of “long-range strikes” in the Caspian Sea, alluding to vessels shipping military cargo, but did not identify the nationality of the targets. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group struck sites belonging to Saudi state oil company Aramco in Jizan and Yanbu. Video shared on social media showed a large column of smoke rising from the direction of the Aramco refinery in Jizan.



Two Asia-based trading sources said they had been informed of potential damage to fuel and oil storage sites at Jizan. Aramco did not respond to requests for comment. In Yanbu, two ballistic missiles aimed at oil installations were intercepted by a US-made Patriot battery operated in Saudi Arabia by the Greek military under an agreement with Riyadh, Greek security sources said. Loading Yanbu, Saudi Arabia’s main Red Sea oil port, has become a key route for Saudi oil skirting the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has blockaded. Up to 400,000 barrels can be processed daily at the oil refinery in Jizan, a city on the Red Sea close to the Yemeni border. In Yemen, the air force of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, which has opposed the Houthis for more than a decade, struck Houthi launch sites and arms depots in the

Marib and al-Jawf provinces, Yemeni officials said.



Earlier, the Saudi-led military alliance said it bombed Houthi military positions on Friday in the Red Sea port of Hodeidah. The Yemeni officials said both sides in Yemen’s civil war were mobilising forces along the front. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea is another crucial global shipping passage. Graphic: Nathan Perri Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling the Houthis for more than a decade since the Iran-aligned fighters captured Yemen’s capital, Sanaa. The Yemeni civil war, during which hundreds of thousands of people died from fighting and famine, has been paused under a ceasefire since 2022. But that truce broke down this month, with the Houthis effectively joining the wider war their Iranian allies have waged since being attacked by the US and Israel.



The Houthis have declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia over the past week, and Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi said all Saudi oil facilities could be targets. On Thursday, the Houthis struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea. American forces recently resumed their own blockade on Iranian ports. US Central Command, whose coverage area includes the Middle East, said it disabled a ship whose crew attempted to run the blockade despite “repeated warnings” on Friday in the Gulf of Oman. An interim truce effectively collapsed two weeks ago, with US forces striking targets in southern Iran in response to Iranian disruption of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. On Friday, Trump said the ‌US and Iran were in talks to ​negotiate an end ​to their conflict, but ⁠repeated that Tehran ​was not yet ready ​for a deal. World.title: Tim Tszyu almost quit boxing. Now he has the chance to cement his legacy
World.content:
SportBoxingWorld Boxing Tim Tszyu almost quit boxing. Now he has the chance to cement his legacy Adrian Proszenko July 26, 2026 — 9:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There was once a time, when his record was unblemished, that boxer Tim Tszyu spoke about retiring his opponents. And yet, it wasn’t so long ago that Tszyu himself almost quit. Worn down by boxing politics, family fractures and a series of beat-downs – including the loss of his world title belt – the Sydney-based pugilist lost the love of a sport that has been his life. Loading “It wasn’t from my losses,” Tszyu explained. “To a certain extent it was the politics of sport, I was thinking, ‘This is not worth it.’ “I joined the sport for the love of it, the thrill of it, the challenge of it. There are a lot of obstacles at certain times trying to stop me from doing that.



“That’s a time when I was thinking of retirement and giving it up … I won’t go into detail, it was just life.” There were several low points. His first loss, at short notice, to Sebastian Fundora, in which a horrific head cut cost him a chance of retaining the WBO super-welterweight world title he had wanted so much. His devastating knockout defeat to Russian Bakhram Murtazaliev, followed by a subsequent KO loss in his rematch with Fundora. Tim Tszyu shadow boxes ahead of his fight against Errol Spence Jnr. Sam Mooy “There were a lot of people in the change room after victory in the Tony Harrison fight, a lot of people for that,” Tszyu recalled, referring to his defeat of the American in 2023 to claim the interim WBO super welterweight belt. “But after what I went through in the Bakhram fight, there weren’t many people in the hospital, let’s just say that. You learn who is there and who is not. You learn about the ugly truth about the sport.”



But Tszyu’s decision to endure has been rewarded. After overhauling his mindset and team – legendary boxer-turned-trainer Jeff Fenech is in his corner – Tszyu will on Sunday step into the ring for the biggest fight of his career. The 31-year-old will take on Errol “The Truth” Spence Jnr in a blockbuster middleweight bout at Sydney’s Afterpay Arena. Spence is a future hall-of-famer, whose only loss was against Terence “Bud” Crawford, who became the first undisputed welterweight champion of the four-belt era. Tim Tszyu is ready for business. Sam Mooy While a world title isn’t at stake, it is a chance for Tszyu to take on the opponent who has been at the top of his hit list. “This is way bigger than a world title,” Tszyu said. “This is hall-of-fame status, we’re talking about one of the fighters of our generation. I get to take him on and cement myself. It’s a blessing.”



When he first rose to prominence, Tszyu was dubbed “The Soul Taker”. But after a wretched run that included three loses in four fights, he has been rebranded as “The Phoenix”. “All these nicknames – I’m Tim Tszyu,” he said. “The Phoenix was like a new chapter in my life to burn from the ashes from what happened and go onto the new. That’s what it is, this new phase of my life.” Tim Tszyu poses for a photograph at the Overseas Passenger Terminal ahead of the fight against Errol “The Truth” Spence Jr. on Sunday. Sam Mooy After a series of team changes, in a bid to start “controlling the narrative more” in his career, Tszyu has settled on Fenech as his mentor. “There’s not many people you can ask for advice who have been there and done that,” Tszyu said. “I’ve never been in a team where someone has felt exactly what I felt.”



It appears a peculiar comment given his father is hall-of-famer Kostya Tszyu, while his brother Nikita is an undefeated fighter closing in on his own world title shot. However, except for grandfather Boris – “he’s stayed with me through thick and thin” – Tszyu has a complex relationship with his family. Kostya has for a long time lived in Russia, there has been a falling out with Nikita and there has been tension with others who were close to him. Errol Spence Jnr has arrived in Sydney in supreme shape. Sam Mooy “Everyone goes through different issues in their families,” Tszyu said. “We are going to get through this fight and then we need to sit down and hug it out.” Fenech, a hall-of-famer who won four world titles in four weight divisions, has noticed a change in Tszyu since becoming his trainer.



“The person I saw in Tim prior to this is someone who had 110 things in his head, said some stupid things about opponents,” Fenech said. “I told him the only thing that will sell fights is not publicity, it’s not shit talk. Your fists will sell fights. “I’m not trying to change Tim. I’m just trying to make him a better Tim. The one thing I have changed is I have a happy guy.” Errol “The Truth” Spence Jr. shadow boxes at the Overseas Passenger Terminal. Sam Mooy Given Spence’s long lay-off – he hasn’t fought for three years – and Tszyu’s poor record in big fights, the loser could be forced into premature retirement. Having previously contemplated walking away from the sport, the Australian believes he is about to leave his mark on it. “I still believed in myself, I still got through it,” Tszyu said. “And here we are, on the verge of doing something special.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: National promises to extend paid parental leave from 26 weeks to 30, if re-elected
World.content:
National has pledged to extend paid parental leave from 26 weeks to 30, if re-elected.

The party is also proposing to revive a policy that allows parents to take some or all of their leave at the same time.

Since 2020, primary carers have been eligible for 26 weeks of paid leave and an additional 26 weeks of unpaid leave.

National has proposed changing the entitlement incrementally, increasing it to 27 weeks in 2027, 28 weeks in 2028, and then 30 weeks in 2029.

Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said the policy modernised paid parental leave, supporting families to give them more financial breathing space while they took on caregiving responsibilities.

"The birth of a child is an expensive time, as families juggle the costs that come with a new baby while their household income is less than when both parents are in paid work," she said.

Nicola Willis at the announcement on Sunday. TU NATANAHIRA / RNZ

"Extending paid parental leave to 30 weeks will ease that pressure and give more parents the option to stay home with their baby for longer."

Leave is currently capped at $811 a week. National's policy did not propose an increase to that, but Willis said the government had increased the cap each year.

National is also bringing back a previous policy that would allow parents to split their leave.

Christopher Luxon speaking to a child at the announcement. TU NATANAHIRA / RNZ

The party used an example of instead of one parent taking 30 weeks' leave, both parents could take 15 weeks together, or both parents could take 4 weeks together, then one parent could take 10 weeks, and then the other parent could take 12 weeks.

Willis said the current law was restrictive and got in the way of families doing what they thought was best for their babies.

"Whether a dad wants to support mum in the first few weeks after birth, or two caregivers want to share paid leave in overlapping instalments, the choice should sit with families and not restricted by outdated government rules."

The policy would be funded out of Budget operating allowances, costing $27 million in 2027/28, $56.6m in 2028/29, and $119m in 2029/30.

That larger extension is timed to coincide with the forecast return to surplus.

National claims its long-term intention is to increase the entitlement to 40 weeks, but it has not put a timeframe on when it would want to achieve this.

The policy announcement comes as National MPs rally around their colleague Katie Nimon.

The Napier MP's would-be challenger, Stuart Nash, resigned as a New Zealand First candidate, after coming under fire for labelling Nimon as lazy for taking nine months off after having a baby.

MPs do not get paid parental leave. Nimon confirmed she took ten weeks of parental leave and returned to Parliament after six months.

Nimon, who was present at the press conference, said Nash called her on Thursday to apologise.

"He just offered his apology for offending me," she said.

The party insisted it had not timed the announcement off the back of the saga, but Nimon said her views on the policy would be the same regardless of recent events.

"I've said a lot this week, there is no right way of being a working parent. We just need to give people the choice. This policy that we're putting forward is really going to give people that choice. I stand by that, whether what happened this week happened or not."

In 2023, Willis proposed allowing parents to share their leave entitlement so they could take time off together. The member's bill was voted down by Labour at first reading.

Labour then went on to campaign for four weeks' paid parental leave for partners.

National had put forward a member's bill this term to allow for split parental leave, in the name of East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick.

It had been unable to get the changes into the coalition agreement or pass them as a government this term. Willis said the responsibility for parental leave rested with the Workplace Relations and Safety Minister, ACT's Brooke van Velden.

"I think it's a shame that it wasn't prioritised within the minister's programme for this term, and we are really keen as a National Party to see this done."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins asked why National should be trusted now.

"They have had three years to make life easier for Kiwis and support families but have instead cut Best Start support for parents, reduced funding for school lunches, cut women's pay, and failed to tackle the cost of living."

World.title: Christchurch Catholic Diocese unveils plans for new $80m Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament
World.content:
The design of Christchurch's new $80 million Catholic cathedral has been unveiled.

The Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament is being built on the Barbadoes Street site of the 1905 original, which was demolished in 2020 after suffering irreparable damage in the 2010 and 2011 earthquakes.

The damaged Christchurch Catholic Basilica, 2019. Peter Fleming

The Catholic Diocese of Christchurch wants to raise $16m from parishioners to help fund the project.

In a pastoral letter on Sunday, Bishop Michael Gielen appealed to Catholic families in Canterbury and on the West Coast to financially contribute.

Gielen announced in 2024 the cathedral would return to the diocese's traditional home on Barbadoes Street and that it would retain the name Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament.

A design rendering for Christchurch's new Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament. Supplied / Catholic Diocese of Christchurch

He said that in the two years since significant work had been undertaken to develop the design in partnership with the architecture firm Warren and Mahoney.

"When I arrived in the diocese four years ago, one of the questions I was most often asked was: 'What is happening with the cathedral?'. That question revealed something profound, the deep love our people have for their Mother Church," Gielen said.

"Over these past four years, through listening, prayer and discernment, that shared vision has taken shape."

A design rendering for Christchurch's new Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament. Supplied / Catholic Diocese of Christchurch

Gielen believed people would see in the design: "a cathedral that glorifies God, that serves as a beacon of faith in our city, that responds to the realities of the present day".

The diocese's cathedral campaign manager, Tony Brazier, said the project had an $80m budget that would cover the 800-seat cathedral, the attached perpetual adoration chapel and the Te Rangimarie community centre.

Brazier said about $45m of the funds needed to build the cathedral would come from insurance proceeds and the sale of diocesan assets.

Of the $35m required through fundraising, more than $19m had already been found, he said.

The proposed site of the Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"Bishop Michael is emulating what Bishop Grimes did, inviting every Catholic family to make a sacrificial offering to build our new cathedral," he said

Gielen said he had heard from many people who had a sense of pride that their grandparents or great-grandparents helped fund the construction of the original Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament.

"It's now our turn to answer the ancient call to build something that will last for generations," he said.

The Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament, Christchurch, as it looked in 2005. Wikimedia Commons

"I have been struck by the generosity of people who recognise what a sign of hope our cathedral will be for Christchurch and our region. That generosity has been seen around New Zealand and from people of other faith traditions."

The diocese said that when half of the remaining $16m had been raised, the project would move towards final preparations for construction.

World.title: Emergency helicopters stood down after false mass stabbing report
World.content:
Police say no arrests have been made following what's understood to be a hoax call out to an alleged mass casualty event in Westport.

Hato Hone St John said it was notified of what was believed to be reports of multiple stabbings just after 8.30pm on Saturday.

It said it responded with two ambulances and four helicopters, but they were all stood down prior to arrival and not required.

A police spokesperson said no arrests have been made.

World.title: Members' Day: The select committee effect
World.content:
MPs returned to Parliament last week after a two-week recess. Plenty awaited them, including the first Members' Day in almost two months.

Members' Days give non-ministerial MPs the chance to propose their own laws.

Four were debated on Wednesday, with three receiving their first readings. One bill expanded its support after a makeover in select committee. A second bill began the same process with hopes of a similar outcome.

T​​he first bill began as the Life Jackets for Children and Young Persons Bill but returned to the House as the Maritime Transport (Lifejackets on Recreational Craft) Amendment Bill, after public submissions fundamentally reshaped what the legislation was trying to achieve.

MPs expanded the bill's scope, then reopened submissions for feedback on their wider vision.

National's Shane Reti, whose bill it is, said, "Two-thirds of submitters requested the scope of the bill be changed from under 15-year-olds to all ages on the basis that the average age of death in recreational boating incidents is actually more towards the age of 50 than 15."

Labour MP Tangi Utikere, who is a member of the transport and infrastructure committee, said that willingness to reopen consultation was a strength of the bill's process.

"The committee sought the permission of the business committee to expand the scope. That was granted, and so the committee went out for round two."

MPs praised each other for changing course because the evidence pointed in a different direction. Among them was ACT's Simon Court, whose party had opposed the original bill but changed its mind after submissions and amendments.

"In fact it was adults … going out in small craft with the hero cap on, feeling invincible, or simply not being prepared for when the conditions changed."

Members' bills can produce unusual alliances. Shane Reti's lifejacket bill had early support from every party except National's coalition partner ACT. The Criminal Records (Clean Slate) (Additional Eligibility) Amendment Bill, from Labour MP Tangi Utikere, had support from every party except National.

"This bill is founded on a simple principle," Utikere said. "People who have genuinely turned their lives around should have the opportunity to move forward with their lives.

"New Zealanders believe in accountability. We expect people who offend to face the consequences of their actions, but I also believe New Zealanders believe in rehabilitation, redemption and second chances."

The bill would extend Clean Slate eligibility to those who had served short custodial sentences (under a year) or had lost driving licences but who had since spent at least 10 years without committing an offence.

National MPs said they agreed with the principle of rehabilitation but questioned whether the law should be extended.

"People fundamentally deserve a second chance," National MP Tim Costley said. "I guess that the question … is what does that look like, and where do we draw the line?"

Costley argued Parliament needed to balance rehabilitation with consequences and deterrence before confirming National would oppose the bill.

While National remained opposed, support from ACT and New Zealand First allowed the bill to pass its first reading.

Labour MP Tangi Utikere. VNP / Phil Smith

Utikere argued that select committee was where questions about a bill's parameters could be worked through.

"We could look at where the line is drawn, what offences should be in, what offences should be out."

Whether National changes its position in committee when it returns for a second-reading debate remains to be seen.

The week showed how public submissions, expert advice and cross-party cooperation in committee can reshape legislation into something substantially different from what was first introduced.

A second bill begins the same journey, with supporters hoping scrutiny and public consultation might hone better law and, as a bonus, pick up unanimous support along the way.

The justice committee is receiving submissions on the Criminal Records (Clean Slate) (Additional Eligibility) Amendment Bill until 3 September. Information on making a submission is available on Parliament's website.

World.title: Urgent need for rules and protections on data centres, Greens say
World.content:
The Green Party wants a one-year pause on consents for new AI data centres, until stronger rules and regulations are put in place.

It comes after New Zealand's first AI factory moves closer and closer to reality.

Singapore-based company Datagrid has been given resource consent to develop a new $3.5 billion data centre in Southland.

The 78,000 square metre factory in Makarewa would use 280 megawatts of power, making it the second-largest electricity user behind the Tiwai Point aluminium smelter.

Its consents would include the ability to draw more than 600,000 litres of groundwater every day, although Datagrid has been adamant it will not use any groundwater, preferring Invercargill's naturally cool air temperatures, and rainwater when needed.

Mercury Energy has recently announced a $53 million investment for a 12.7 percent minority equity stake in Datagrid NZ, following the signing of a 140 megawatt power purchase agreement in March.

Southland's mayor Rob Scott has said the centre would be a good opportunity for the region.

But Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the rules on data centres needed to be written before any concrete was poured.

"Some may argue these AI data centres could build their own renewable energy, or that they're increasingly using closed-loop water cooling systems. That may well be the case, but our current rules don't require any of those things," she said.

"New Zealanders haven't even had the opportunity to discuss and decide whether they want them."

Swarbrick said the Datagrid centre was expected to use about six percent of New Zealand's total electricity supply.

She insisted the moratorium was not a ban on data infrastructure, but a pause on the most resource-intensive developments until intentional regulation was developed.

"Currently, councils get to decide through their planning rules whether to consent these developments. These can be on a non-notified basis with no public input required.

"As other cities and countries are quickly discovering, you can't put that genie back in the bottle. Let's take a moment to figure out the right way to do this."

The Australian government recently announced it would establish an 'Office of AI' within the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, to manage the development of AI standards and force data centres to be net producers of energy and to limit their water usage.

Swarbrick pointed to the Australian example, as well as New York's pause on new hyperscale data centres until a framework was developed, as reason for New Zealand to be cautious.

"If an AI data centre project does not meet basic standards for power, water use, and environmental impact, why should we allow it to be built here? Anyone who argues the opposite needs to explain why New Zealanders should shoulder the cost of something they didn't get any say on."

Prime minister Christopher Luxon said the government would not consider a pause on data centres, but it was looking at an AI strategy.

"Data centres are critical for us going forward to add more value into our economy, to embrace more technology and innovation. But it's also important that we come, as we expand and open up more data centres in due course, with some very good thinking and some good principles about how we do that."

Luxon said the Greens' were being "alarmist," and would turn off investment before it had even arrived in New Zealand.

World.title: Boy racer crackdown sees police issue over 50 infringements, make four arrests
World.content:
Over the weekend in Taranaki police issued over 50 infringements, arrested four people and impounded three cars and a motorcycle for dangerous driving.

Dangerous and unlawful driving was reported on Plantation Road and Main North Road on Friday and Saturday night, police said.

"Police worked hard to stop and deter the burnouts, erratic driving, driving without lights at night and speeding," inspector Mark Miller, Taranaki Area commander, said.

"The Police Eagle helicopter was also deployed to Taranaki for the weekend to assist staff on the ground."

Almost twice the speed limit

Police said on Friday night a driver was driving down the highway at almost twice the speed limit

The driver was spiked near Inglewood and attempted to flee, but was caught after being tracked by a police dog unit.

"In addition to the horrific driving that could have caused a significant crash and harm to people in the area, there were bottles being thrown by an offender.

"One bottle went through the back window of a patrol car, and thankfully, the officer was not injured," Miller said.

The four people were arrested for assault with a weapon, reckless driving, breach of bail and drug charges, and will likely be in court next week.

Police said 59 driving infringements were issued, one car was incorrectly registered and six cars were marked unsafe.

"We're disappointed to see this behaviour in Taranaki.

"Driving like this puts everyone on the road in danger. We've seen the effects of dangerous driving and the very sad impact it can have on the community.

"People deserve to feel safe and everyone on the road is required to follow the same rules, no exceptions. If we see dangerous driving, we will take appropriate action," Miller said.

World.title: Weather: Heavy showers up north, severe frosts in the south
World.content:
It's a story of two islands for Sunday's weather, with heavy showers for Northland, Auckland, and Coromandel and severe inland frosts for most of the South Island.

MetService recorded the lowest temperature at Mount Cook, where the mercury plunged to -6.3C on Sunday morning.

Road snowfall warnings were also in force from the previous day, with Waka Kotahi issuing a slew of them across both islands.

Waka Kotahi said snow and cold temperatures may cause ice to form on roads, making driving dangerous.

"Take extra care and remember to increase your following distance and be prepared for unexpected hazards when driving in these conditions," it warned.

MetService had no weather warnings in place on Sunday morning.

In a forecast issued at 6.18am, it said Northland, Auckland, and Coromandel could expect showers, some heavy, with squally thunderstorms possible about Northland and Great Barrier Island in the morning and afternoon.

World.title: Fresh Mount Maunganui slips close road
World.content:
Mount Maunganui has been upgraded to the highest alert level after three new landslides within 48 hours.

They come six months after a big landslide fell onto Mount Maunganui Holiday Park, killing six people.

Tauranga City Council recovery manager Charlie Rahiri said the alert had been lifted to Level 3, leading to the closing of Adams Avenue at the base of the mountain between Pilot Bay and the Maunganui Road roundabout.

There had been "a major regression" at the site of the original landslide, extending 20 metres with a runout of 100 metres, he said.

The latest landslide had not extended as far as the original runout but the material was "saturated, mobile and fluid", he said.

The council said in a statement that geotechnical engineers were assessing the site, with the closure expected to remain in place until at least Monday.

Residents and businesses could still access Adams Avenue via the southern footpath.

"The closure is a precautionary measure following slips on Mauao overnight, to ensure public safety while the area is at higher risk of further movement."

Six people died in January when a large landslide fell onto the campground below.

The council said Māori Wardens were managing the current closure until temporary fencing was installed later on Sunday.

World.title: Sobers could only do everything — including for SA's Sheffield Shield side
World.content:
The cricketer Sir Garfield St Aubrun "Garry" Sobers was a man who frequently found himself the subject of admiration and wonder.

Widely recognised as the game's greatest all-rounder, Sobers — who died recently at the age of 89 — scored 8,032 runs at an average of almost 58, claimed 235 wickets and snared 109 catches in his 93 Test matches for the West Indies.

But even by the time he was recruited by South Australia, as a 25-year-old in 1961, his talent was already indisputable.

"I don't say this lightly — he's the greatest cricketer, in my opinion, the game has ever seen," said Ken "KG" Cunningham, who played alongside Sobers during the latter's three seasons with SA's Sheffield Shield side.

"He opened the bowling, he bowled first change and bowled left arm orthodox, he was second change with left arm [wrist spin], he'd field like a demon and then he could bat.

"He was five cricketers in one."

South Australian sporting legend Ken "KG" Cunningham vividly recalls batting with Sobers. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

In 1958, Sobers had broken the world record for the highest individual innings when he scored 365 not out against Pakistan in Jamaica — a milestone that stood for more than 35 years.

His arrival in SA the summer after the famous Tied Test series occurred at a time in which there was strong enthusiasm for West Indian cricket.

"It's a little bit murky how it came about, because success always has a million fathers — but it was very much on the back of the 1960/61 West Indies tour, and I think Bradman had a role in it," sportswriter Michael Sexton said of the circumstances that led to SA securing Sobers's services.

"The lure of Bradman was just so important — they got on very well. He used to go and have dinner at Bradman's house in Adelaide."

The front cover of Michael Sexton's book Three Summers of Sobers, about Sir Garfield Sobers's time playing for SA. (Supplied)

Sexton's book Three Summers of Sobers is a tender tribute to the cricketer's SA seasons and their culmination in Sheffield Shield victory.

There are vignettes from his time at Prospect Cricket Club, where Sobers played at grade level, and the book depicts him in his off-field moments as a man who "charged past midnight, wore out barmen, gambled, chased skirts and lit every scene with the sunshine of possibility that beamed out of him".

Light is also shed on the political setting, and Sexton said South Australian administrators had "to bypass the White Australia Policy" to get Sobers into the squad.

It is an irony of considerable gravity that while Sobers was regarded by fellow cricketers as having reached the summit of their sport, cricket authorities were obliged to seek, with delicacy and discretion, special dispensation to keep him in the country.

'So grateful and so lucky'

In person, there was nothing immediately imposing about Sobers, and little to indicate that his frame concealed an inner Hercules. The short back and sides, the pencil moustache and the V-neck sweater hardly betokened the presence of athletic genius.

But Sobers was, in truth, a cricketer of whom it feels apt to borrow a bon mot: he could only do everything.

The paradoxical presence of the word "only" in that statement adds the crucial note of humility that makes it especially applicable to Sobers, whose accomplishments were usually accompanied by grace.

The news that Sobers was destined for SA generated headlines across Australia. (Supplied)

In one of his six sixes in an over for Nottinghamshire at Swansea in 1968, he performed a complete pirouette, spinning like a sprinkler on a parched outfield.

His bowling action was equally aqueous. The rock back and forward sling prefigured the motions of Jeff Thomson, and the ball was released in a cascade of lithe force.

"He was the best player in the world — and he's just turning up at Prospect to go and have a net with the others, because he was in that team," Sexton said.

"It's an astonishing thing that happened to South Australia. It's probably the equivalent of when Bradman came in the 1930s — it's that sort of impact, isn't it? 'What on Earth is he doing here?'"

For his Prospect teammates, the experience was perhaps not unlike that of an amateur dramatic society that persuades a BAFTA-winning lead to join its players, or a garage band that fills the vacant role of rhythm guitarist by recruiting a rock legend, or a model aeroplane club that without warning is gifted possession of an actual Spitfire.

But Sobers's career in South Australia had unpropitious beginnings, and his initial three outings with the bat for Prospect produced a solitary run.

A team photo of the South Australian 1963/64 Sheffield Shield side, including Ken Cunningham, Neil Hawke, Sir Garfield Sobers, Rex Sellers, Les Favell, Barry Jarman and Ian Chappell. (Supplied)

Even so, his cricketing charisma was palpable, and Cunningham still remembers the first time they batted together for SA.

"I walked down the beautiful steps at Adelaide Oval, onto the oval itself, and went to the striker's end," he said.

"I looked up and I saw Sir Garfield Sobers [at the other end] and I said to myself, 'What in the hell am I doing here? I'm just Ken Cunningham. I shouldn't be here'.

"I was so grateful and so lucky to be able to play with the great man."

Sobers's seasons in SA were like the building and breaking of a wave, and triumph came in 1963/64.

A newspaper  from around the time of Sobers's remarkable achievement in the 1963/64 Sheffield Shield season. (Supplied)

Remarkably, he took more wickets and scored more runs than any player in Australia during the summer.

Among the mainstays of that Shield victory was the bowling partnership Sobers formed with leg-spinner Rex Sellers — the former took 47 wickets, the latter 46.

"I s'pose we might have complemented each other," Sellers reflected.

"He was very accurate, I believe I can say I was pretty accurate as well, so we created good pressure on batsmen from both ends."

In SA's final game — a win against Victoria that guaranteed SA the Shield — Sobers made a century and claimed nine scalps.

"He was pivotal because not only was he the best player, but he inspired the others to play better. He gave them a slight swagger and a confidence that they hadn't had before," Sexton said.

"He lived up to all expectations and hopes."

World.title: Pogačar on the cusp of Tour history after dramatic penultimate stage
World.content:
Tadej Pogačar moved to within touching distance of a record-equalling fifth Tour de France title after finishing safely in the penultimate stage overnight.

The Slovenian star heads into tonight's showcase finish in Paris with a lead of six and a half minutes over Belgian rider Remco Evenepoel.

Barring mishap, Pogačar will join Belgian Eddy Merckx, Spaniard Miguel Indurain, and Frenchmen Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault as the only men to win five Tours.

"I have done a really good Tour. Some of our competitors had bad luck," said Pogačar, whose main rival Jonas Vingegaard crashed out of the race.

"We made it through with the team and now there is just one last show left."

The 20th stage was won by Richard Carapaz for his second win at this year's race and third overall. The Ecuadorian rider overtook Sepp Kuss near the end as the American almost crashed out. Evenepoel also surged past Kuss near the line to take second place.

"There was a moment when I couldn't believe what was happening," Carapaz said.

"This Tour de France has been incredible, with all the spectators and all the support I've received from Ecuador, where they'll be jumping for joy."

Pogačar chose not to launch one of his attacks like on Friday's 19th stage.

Stage 20 was a mammoth 171-kilometre alpine trek featuring three hors catégorie climbs, the hardest category, and one category 1 climb.

After three weeks in the saddle, weary riders tackled hors catégorie ascents of Col de la Croix de Fer, Col du Galibier and Col de Sarenne, and the one category 1 climb of Col du Télégraphe, making for 66km of hard climbing in total before a hilly finish to Alpe d'Huez.

Carapaz rode from the front to secure the polka-dot jersey awarded to the Tour's best climber. Pogacar's yellow jersey group was hanging back when Carapaz, Kuss, Spaniard Juan Ayuso and Australian Jai Hindley went over the Galibier together.

Pogačar's priority was ensuring his AE Team Emirates teammate Isaac Del Toro finished third in the rankings, and the Mexican rider is now more than two minutes clear of Frenchman Paul Seixas in fourth.

"It's been an honour to ride for Isaac today," said Pogačar, who gifted Del Toro victory on Stage 2.

"Crossing the finish line together with him has been memorable."

Ayuso was dropped as the former Spanish Vuelta winner Kuss, Hindley and Carapaz — both former Giro d'Italia winners — battled for supremacy in the Sarenne pass.

"It was really, really tough," Carapaz said.

"Sepp, in particular, was a very tough nut to crack."

An exhausted-looking Kuss lost control of his bike going downhill when he mistimed a turn with 5km left and almost tumbled over a roadside concrete barrier. Some netting cushioned him.

Carapaz rode swiftly past him to victory.

"It was absolutely brilliant to win here and in a distinctive jersey," Carapaz said.

"I think I deserve it, because I've fought so hard in this Tour de France."

Pogačar has won five stages on this year's race and 26 overall, meaning he would likely need to compete in at least two more Tours to beat British sprinter Mark Cavendish's record of 35 stage wins. Merckx won 34 and Hinault 28.

He may go for another stage win tonight.

"Let's see how I feel tomorrow. I won't take any risks," Pogačar said.

"But if I have good legs and I don't have to take too many big risks, I'll try to claim victory tomorrow."

The final stage is on an 89km route featuring an uphill dash through the Montmartre district in Paris and finishing on the Champs-Élysées.

The stage was shortened from 133km and its starting point in Thoiry, west of the capital, was changed to Paris to reduce pressure on emergency services combating wildfires in the south-west.

World.title: Aussies won't allow anticipated clash with English defector to distract them
World.content:
Most elite athletes not named Michael Jordan don't need to make things personal to perform at their peak, and that's certainly the case for Leigh Hoffman.

And he wouldn't have to look far for personal animus if he wanted to find some.

The last time the Australian track cycling team was competing in Glasgow, at the 2023 world championships, and the last time he was at the Commonwealth Games, at Birmingham 2022, he was alongside Matthew Richardson.

In fact, the first four major medals of Hoffman's career came in team sprints with Richardson, including bronze at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

But then, as Hoffman told it on his arrival in Glasgow, they "brought a few medals back for Australia and then he went on holiday and never came back".

Leigh Hoffman, Matthew Richardson and Matthew Glaetzer are the reigning Commonwealth Games gold medallists in the men's team sprint. (Getty Images: John Walton/PA Images)

Richardson defected to the country of his birth after the Games and will ride for England at the Commonwealth Games for the first time.

On the way out, he took a few shots at the apparently insufficient Cycling Australia program, with whom he won 10 medals across Olympics, world champs and Commonwealth Games.

"We'd never experienced something like that," Hoffman said.

"You grow up racing with someone and you think you're both Aussies and then he's not. That's life. It is what it is."

Leigh Hoffman and co went through a lot with Richardson (centre). (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Hoffman's cavalier attitude to the impossibly hyped rivalry with Richardson ahead of a potential team sprint final clash next Friday morning makes sense for a couple of reasons.

Firstly, the format of track cycling being so cutthroat, these guys are no strangers to racing each other anyway.

"We'd be racing with each other in the team sprint, and every other event you race as an individual anyway," Hoffman said.

Richardson breaks WR — for Great Britain A year after winning Olympic silver for Australia, Matthew Richardson has become the fastest cyclist of all-time — in the colours of Great Britain.

"So even if he still represented Australia, I'd still have to come against my own teammate and aim to try and beat him and he'd be aiming to try and beat me.

"It's kinda life in track cycling."

The other reason is the amount of turnover across the team.

In addition to Richardson's defection, five-time Commonwealth gold medallist Matthew Glaetzer retired, and Tom Cornish pivoted to the endurance events.

Hoffman has suddenly gone from the young buck at the Birmingham Games to the leader of a new-look sprint unit, with 23-year-old Danny Barber, 22-year-old Ryan Elliott, and 20-year-old Tayte Ryan.

The Aussies have been competing against Richardson relatively amicably the past few years. (Getty Images: Matt Jelonek)

They will relish beating England, but will not be focusing too much on Richardson, because if you're looking the wrong way on the bike, you can easily get passed on your blind side.

"I'm excited to beat everyone in the world, he's just another domino to fall, hopefully," Hoffman said.

"The Australia-England rivalry goes back very far with the Ashes and all our other sports. It's always Australia vs England, [but] for the Commonwealth Games, we've got some really stacked riders.

"Azizul Awang from Malaysia, who's come in in great form; Trinidad and Tobago, Nicholas Paul – there's a lot of great riders.

"But the fans are definitely looking forward to an Australia-England match-up."

World.title: Even Diamonds were cheering for Tonga in the Comm Games netball opener
World.content:
The game was never going to be close between the Diamonds and Tonga, but as Uneeq Palavi hit the Griddy on her way onto court, it was clear the result was only part of the story.

One was the undisputed number-one team in the world and defending champions, the other was on Games debut.

"[Before the game] we were pretty much telling ourselves 'oh, we're gonna beat the diamonds' but it's just a hype up to get around," Palavi said.

Tonga's Uneeq Palavi (right) had plenty of support in the stands at the Hydro. ( Getty Images: Morgan Harlow)

"It's just another step closer to putting our little country on the map and that's all that matters."

As is so often the case, especially at the Commonwealth Games, the gulf in profile and quality meant every Australian goal was met with polite applause and each Tongan bucket led to cheers usually reserved for contests of significantly more consequence.

Only 36 hours earlier, the British King and Queen had elicited a similar reaction in the same venue, Glasgow's colosseum-like Hydro arena.

There was no shortage of physicality on display. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

On Saturday, there was more royalty in the house, with Tongan Princess Lātūfuipeka Tukuʻaho, albeit sitting with the plebs in the stands, rather than in the royal box populated by Charles, Camilla and other dignitaries at the opening ceremony.

"I didn't expect so many Tongans to be out there but that's the crazy thing, no matter where you are in the world there's always Tongans to support and I feel like that's the best thing to have behind us," Palavi said.

The crowd at the Hydro was firmly on Tonga's side. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

And it wasn't just Tongans.

Perched in the upper decks were Diamonds reserves Amy Parmenter and Jessie Grenvold.

Diamonds mid-courter Amy Parmenter was in the stands cheering for Tonga. (Instagram: Jessie Grenvold)

Rather than cheering for their girls in gold, they held a sign reading "Princess Pav", backing their Melbourne Mavericks teammate.

In the second half, Palavi clocked them and any time she managed to have a moment against the vice-like defence of Jo Weston, Courtney Bruce, Matilda Garrett or Sarah Klau, her eyes went straight up to them.

"It was good to see their faces to ground myself and remind myself that, although the loss was tough, it's great to have people around me like that," she said.

Unfortunately, there weren't many chances for those fans to get up and about.

Palavi and Lavinia Lavea got vanishingly few opportunities in the face of the locked-in, well-oiled defence of the Diamonds.

Uneeq Palavi scored 30 of Tonga's 38 goals. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Stacey Marinkovich rolled out her first-choice seven to start the match.

By half-time, Tonga had taken 22 shots for 19 goals. Australia was 52/55, with six intercepts.

In the second half, Marinkovich rattled through different line-ups en route to a 99-38 thumping in a bit of a test case for later group matches against England, South Africa, Malawi and Northern Ireland.

The Diamonds almost cracked 100 against Tonga. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

For Tonga, things should only get easier.

"It wasn't the best, but to come up against the world's best it's obviously gonna be something like that," Palavi said.

"We're not a new team but we're new in this environment. I feel like it's a lot to come up against the world's best and put out what we wanted to do, but I feel like we did good regardless."

World.title: Gold for Aussie gymnasts as Williamson stuns in breaststroke
World.content:
Sam Short roared his delight, Mollie O'Callaghan counted her blessings and Alex Perkins shed her bridesmaid tag as Australia's swimmers banked five more gold medals, turning the Tollcross pool into their own Commonwealth Games pleasure dome.

Short led home a dominant Australian medal clean sweep in the 400m freestyle final to launch the second night of the Glasgow swimming program in dazzling style ahead of his teammate Elijah Winnington and Ben Goedemans.

"It doesn't come around too often and you've got to make the most of it," said the Queenslander of his extravagant flex.

"I saw my idols do that on the lane ropes so I was like, you know, why not?!"

Behind the 22-year-old Queenslander, there was a battle royale before Winnington (3:45.56) pipped teammate Ben Goedemans by a mere one-hundredth of a second — a formidable effort from the defending champion, who revealed afterwards he'd spent most of the previous night over a toilet bowl after a bout of food poisoning.

"It just goes to show the rich history of Australian 400m swimming and it's super special," Winnington said.

Sam Short, Elijah Winnington and Benjamin Goedemans swept the medals for Australia in the men's 400m freestyle. (Getty: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Olympic great O'Callaghan powered to 200m free victory ahead of teammate, 400m winner Lani Pallister, while Perkins annexed a long-awaited gold in the 50m butterfly.

She picked up her second gold, showing no vestiges of the stress fractures and bone bruising in her back that had cast a cloud over her participation.

"Dealing with the injury currently is not the best thing ever, but as an athlete you've got to find ways to adapt," said the delighted Queenslander, who stopped the clock at 1:54.66 to Pallister's 1:55.01, having always been in control.

"That's something that I've done and my team has done and there's been multiple circumstances over the years where I've just had to keep pushing on.

" That's the best part about sport, you get hit with an unlucky stick and then you've got to pick yourself back up. "

Sam Williamson added a fourth gold medal for Australia, upstaging two-time Olympic champion Adam Ramsay-Peaty in the 100m breaststroke.

Flynn Southam, Kyle Chalmers, Shayna Jack and Meg Harris then cemented the Dolphins' spectacular start, winning the mixed 4x100m freestyle relay as Australia backed up their six golds on the opening night.

Godwin adds to legacy, leads women gymnasts to team gold

Georgia Godwin, Kate McDonald, Ruby Pass, Breanna Scott and Emily Whitehead celebrate after victory in the Women's Team Final. (Getty: Naomi Baker)

Georgia Godwin has become Australia's most decorated women's gymnast at the Commonwealth Games, bursting into tears as she guided the nation to a team gold medal in Glasgow.

Godwin won her ninth Games medal to surpass Allana Slater in the record books, with Australia leading from the outset en route to a final score of 158.400 points at Glasgow International Arena.

Canada trailed by 1.100 points for silver, while 2022 Birmingham champions England (154.300) claimed bronze.

Australia's five-woman squad was unrelenting across the four apparatuses — vault, uneven bars, balance beam and floor — to win the nation's first team gold medal since the 2010 Delhi Games.

Four of Australia's gymnasts — Godwin, Kate McDonald, Emily Whitehead and Breanna Scott — were part of the 2022 silver medal-winning team, with 19-year-old Paris Olympian Ruby Pass making her Games debut.

Georgia Godwin in action on the uneven bars. (Getty: Naomi Baker)

Godwin will look to cement her legacy at the Games when she aims to defend her individual all-around and vault titles.

Already boasting three 2018 Gold Coast Games medals, Godwin had drawn level with Slater on eight medals in 2022 after winning uneven bars, balance beam and team all-around silvers.

World.title: Brisbane's premiership defence all but over after Cowboys crash-out
World.content:
Brisbane's premiership defence is done and dusted after North Queensland kept their own finals hopes on track with a deserved 18-10 derby win in Townsville.

The Broncos are set to be the first defending NRL premiers to miss the finals since 2005 champions Wests Tigers missed the top eight in 2006.

Their season of dismal failure was crushed in front of a sold-out crowd in Townsville on Saturday night by a Cowboys outfit brilliantly led up front by club legend Jason Taumalolo.

Brisbane, on 18 points, are now four wins outside the eight and there is a remote "mathematical chance" of making finals, but even if they were to win all remaining six games the best they can finish with is 12 victories.

That simply won't be enough to play finals. Brisbane's for and against is so poor at -132 that even a collapse by the teams ahead of them would not be of any help to their cause.

Coach Michael Maguire is set to come under further scrutiny for his failure to get results from his superstar roster.

"I'm pretty shattered for my players and staff … but it just hasn't been our time," Maguire said.

"We have six games to go and we will focus on the next one."

The Cowboys, in eighth position on 26 points, had all the best players in key positions — including Taumalolo trumping Payne Haas.

North Queensland halfback Jake Clifford was left out of the starting side last week, but returned with a bang with his kicking game the best on either side.

Taumalolo led from the front yet again for North Queensland. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Cowboys centre Tom Chester was scintillating and fullback Scott Drinkwater played with the composure that Broncos opposite number Reece Walsh lacked.

North Queensland coach Todd Payten lit the fuse before the clash with his statement that "everyone hates the Broncos" and his players delivered.

"I'm very happy for the team, the town and the club," Payten said.

"It was a good performance by our lads. We started fast and physical."

The hosts also dealt with adversity far better.

Cowboys hooker Reed Mahoney was concussed and ruled out in the seventh minute.

Taumalolo, in his 31st derby clash, rumbled through the middle of the Broncos and five-eighth Jaxon Purdue's pinpoint grubber was swooped upon by forward Heilum Luki for the opening try.

Broncos No.6 Ezra Mam had the perfect riposte with a grubber of his own for edge forward Xavier Willison to score out wide.

Both sides bombed tries over the line, but on the cusp of halftime Drinkwater's cutout pass sent winger Braidon Burns steaming down the touchline. He came to Walsh and knocked him clean over before offloading to Clifford for a 14-4 lead.

The Cowboys got out to a 12-point lead before Walsh forced an error from Burns with a towering bomb. The Broncos fullback threw the money ball for Mam to power his way over to score a cracker.

Mam went within a whisker of adding another, but Brisbane winger Josiah Karapani gave away a penalty and the hosts went back out to an eight-point lead.

The Broncos' most experienced players Adam Reynolds and Ben Hunt were off the pace in the big moments.

Cowboys co-captain Reuben Cotter was awarded the Carl Webb Medal as man of the match, in honour of the late legend of both clubs who lost his battle with Motor Neurone Disease in 2023.

There was a lot of heat in the match with North Queensland trio Griffin Neame, Purdue and Heilum Luki all on report, while Brisbane duo Preston Riki and Kotoni Staggs were also booked.

In the day's other matches both Canterbury (18-6) and Canberra (56-10) kept their finals hopes alive with wins over the Warriors and Tigers, respectively.
